The two of them were walking when they came upon a particular door. Several people were waiting outside. Suddenly a young man came bursting out, face flushed with elation, gripping a slip of paper, muttering excitedly to himself — "The road to the heavens, the road to the heavens..."
Jiang Mi watched him rush off with an uncomprehending look. "What is 'the road to the heavens'?"
"That door is the 'All Wishes Granted' room," Su Jingchen said. "There is a Master Zhu inside. If the price is right, he will provide a solution for anything. Quite a few people have come out very satisfied."
He lowered his voice. "What that young man was muttering — 'road to the heavens' — that means the imperial examinations."
Jiang Mi's expression sharpened. "The examinations? Impossible. They would never dare leak the questions openly like this!"
"It is not as severe as leaking questions — they would not be so brazen as that. What a friend of mine bought was a note on a particular examiner's preferences and temperament. He went to the capital and used it accordingly — knew exactly how to make an impression, had a far better chance of being noticed than others. As for rising from there — that still depends on one's own abilities."
Jiang Mi went very still. Was this not serious enough? She found it deeply alarming.
Who could compile such detailed intelligence on officials of the imperial court?
"Miss Jiang — would you like to go in and see?"
She shook her head. There was no need. She would go back and write to her aunt immediately. She also wanted to ask Xiang Yun whether it was possible to reach Sister Xuan, and get a letter to her.
"Then let me take you to the hundred-flower garden to spend some time with A'Rong and the others. Miss Jiang — just think of today as a flower-viewing excursion."
She knew there were things that could not be said here, and that two visitors leaving so quickly after arriving would arouse suspicion. She went with Su Jingchen to the garden.
At the entrance to the hundred-flower garden, Su Jingchen ran into an acquaintance who immediately began pressing him to come for a drink.
Jiang Mi could see he was torn and told him to go ahead, asking one of Yǒuyuán's maids to lead the way.
She had barely entered the garden when the layout gave her an odd sense of familiarity. Gardens often resembled one another — it was nothing unusual.
She had not gone far when she spotted the Su sisters and A'Rong playing under the peach trees in the distance. She paused, then said to the maid, "Take me to change."
The maid bowed and led her off toward a side courtyard.
Jiang Mi came out again quickly. The maid was waiting ahead. She was just about to walk over when she heard a burst of small urgent chirps — thin, quick, anxious.
She looked around. At the foot of a tree near one of the garden's decorative rock formations, a small dark bundle was hopping frantically, flapping its wings but unable to fly.
A fledgling bird.
She spotted a nest in the branches above — it must have fallen from there.
Jiang Mi walked over, cupped the fluttering little creature gently in her hands, and stood on her toes to lift it back into the nest.
The moment she let go, an urgent voice came from the other side of the rock formation.
"Young Master, young master — please stop running this way. If the master finds out, this servant will be punished."
Jiang Mi turned to look.
A maidservant had placed herself in the path of a small child, who had just lifted his face.
That face. Jiang Mi could not forget it no matter how many times she tried.
She had seen it at the Duke Zhen State's manor. She had seen it on the ship. She had seen it in nightmares.
Why was this child here?
A low male voice cut through the air. "How did you let him run out here? If the wrong eyes see him — a stranger catching a glimpse that should not be seen — you will not keep your life."
The maid dropped to her knees, head knocking the ground in supplication.
A slightly older voice said, "The Young Lord shows mercy in sparing your life. Now take the young master away quickly."
The maid scrambled up and hurried the child away.
In the instant that voice had sounded, Jiang Mi had pressed herself into the rock formation.
She could not collect herself. The man who was supposed to be in Suzhou — how was he here in Jinling, in this Yǒuyuán?
Through a gap in the rocks, Jiang Mi saw Xue Jinglin in a deep sapphire robe. Standing beside him was an elderly man in grey.
The old man said, "Young Lord — Xu Shiming is very displeased that you killed Yang Da in Cangzhou and destroyed everything they had built there. Particularly with the court's deliberate commendation of you — that faction now suspects you of divided loyalties. Though this old one actually thinks it is fortunate that your cover was not truly blown."
Xue Jinglin's mouth curved in a cold smile. "That was merely a test. I let them come to collect the child — and two factions within their own camp both tried to take him. Xu Shiming sent Yang Da to seize him, thinking that one child was all it would take to make everything fall into place."
The old man said, "The Young Lord is meticulous. By disguising the young master as a girl and scattering several children to flee separately, you exposed their intentions completely."
Xue Jinglin said, "Master Zhu — I have been feeling uneasy of late. The others need reining in. If any of them start entertaining ideas again, kill them outright. We will lie low for now. I have a few things to arrange, and then I will return to the capital."
The old man stroked his beard. "The Young Lord need not worry. Xu Shiming cannot make much of a wave. The lesson you gave him will keep him quiet."
Xue Jinglin said nothing.
The old man continued, "This old one did happen to meet with Official Gao a few days ago. The official seems somewhat displeased about the Young Lord's betrothal. He had apparently had a mind to seek an alliance with you."
Xue Jinglin gave only a faint smile and looked at the plants growing between the stones.
The old man said, "There is no hurry on this matter. Once things are done, it can be discussed at leisure. The Young Lord's betrothal to the Cheng'en Marquessate has both advantages and disadvantages — all in all..."
Xue Jinglin snapped his head up and looked directly ahead. "Who is there?"
Jiang Mi held her breath, utterly motionless.
She heard footsteps approaching. Her face went white, her heart hammering.
"My greetings to the Young Master. This servant came to find someone — it seems the young lady is not here. I will take my leave."
Jiang Mi recognised the voice of the Yǒuyuán maid who had been showing her the way.
Xue Jinglin waved a hand, dismissing her.
The old man said, "Young Lord — the garden has many visitors today. This is not a good place to talk. Shall we go to the Cāngfēng Courtyard?"
Xue Jinglin did not refuse. He turned and walked away with the old man.
Only when their footsteps had faded completely did Jiang Mi dare to breathe.
Her hands and feet had gone to water.
She could not believe what she had heard.
That Xue Jinglin was a stranger to her. Utterly unlike the man she thought she knew.
She had not even begun to piece together what it all meant when a hand shot from the shadows and seized her by the throat.
Jiang Mi struggled with everything she had.
The hand at her throat — which should simply have snapped her neck — paused. For some reason it reached up and lifted her veiled hat instead.
Jiang Mi looked at the face before her. Tears spilled without her permission.
Xue Jinglin released her at once. Jiang Mi sagged against the rock formation, coughing, unable to speak through the pain in her throat.
Xue Jinglin slowly closed his hand. He looked down at her in silence. "How did you come to be here?"
That was precisely what Jiang Mi wanted to ask him.
The old man stepped to Xue Jinglin's side. He looked at the woman's face and could not conceal his surprise. "Young Lord — you know her?"

chapters.title: Eighty-one
chapters.content:
Jiang Mi sat in silence and watched Xue Jinglin push a cup of hot tea toward her.

He smiled pleasantly. "Miss Jiang — have some tea and settle yourself. I assure you, there is nothing added to it."

Jiang Mi did not move.

Seeing this, he did not press her. He set the cup on the table.

Xue Jinglin looked at the red-purple marks around Jiang Mi's neck. "Does it still hurt? I will have a maid fetch some medicine."

He turned and gave instructions to the maid standing at the door.

Jiang Mi could not understand how he was able to carry on as though nothing had happened.

"You need not trouble yourself, Young Lord." She forced herself to sound composed, though she felt no steadiness inside. "When does the Young Lord intend to release me?"

Xue Jinglin sat down across from her. His smile was soft, his tone light. "We have not seen each other in some time. Is there nothing to talk about?"

"What does the Young Lord wish to talk about?"

"Oh — how much Miss Jiang saw. How much she heard. How much she knows."

What little colour remained in Jiang Mi's face drained further.

She knew she had no way out of this.

She gave a thin, bitter smile. "If I said I saw nothing and heard nothing, the Young Lord would not believe me."

Xue Jinglin poured himself a cup of tea and drank. "If I could, I would like to believe it. Unfortunately, I had actually brought a gift back from Suzhou for you. I wonder whether Miss Jiang is still willing to accept it now."

There was no point in circling around it. Jiang Mi decided to ask plainly.

"Young Lord." She kept her voice low. "Did you think of the Grand Princess and Ningzhu before doing all this? You hid that child and brought him all the way to Jiangnan. What is it you are trying to do?"

Xue Jinglin set down his cup and looked at her unhurriedly. "The boy Mu'er does bear some resemblance to the Prince of Qi. I thought, given your age and how few times you had seen the Prince of Qi, that you would not have recognised him so quickly."

He was not going to answer her question. He was deflecting. Jiang Mi pressed the question that had been circling inside her for the longest time:

"Young Lord Xue — at the flower banquet at the Duke Zhen State's manor, I was pushed into the water by Xie Mingshan. While I was in the water, a servant woman grabbed my legs trying to drown me. Was that because I had seen the child — and that was what brought that attempt on my life?"

Xue Jinglin studied her for a long moment before he spoke. "Miss Jiang, it would have been better for you if you were a little less perceptive."

A chill swept through her. At the time she had traced the person who pushed her in and the person who drugged her — but had never been able to find the one who had tried to drown her from below.

She had not imagined, not for a moment, that meeting that small child at the lakeside could have provoked Xue Jinglin into wanting her dead. She had not even connected the child to the Prince of Qi at the time.

Deep fear rose in her.

She knew this much. There was no way Xue Jinglin would let her go.

Jiang Mi laughed without humour. "And what does the Young Lord intend to do with me this time?"

Xue Jinglin's expression became complicated. "Miss Jiang — you can only blame yourself for knowing too much. It is not that I am without compassion, but I have no choice except to make you disappear."

He turned to the maids. "Come — bring the miss a clean set of clothes to change into."

Two maids came in carrying clothing and moved toward Jiang Mi.

When she refused to undress, they looked to Xue Jinglin for instruction.

"Why are you standing there? Can you not help the miss change?"

The maids seized her arms. As one of them reached to undo her clothes, something small and golden fell from Jiang Mi's sleeve.

Xue Jinglin walked over and picked it up. He looked at it for a moment. "A palace-made wrist crossbow. Was this from Xiao Huaiyan?"

He turned it in his fingers. "When did he give it to you?"

Jiang Mi pressed her lips together and said nothing.

"Let me guess — the day of the betrothal? No — Xiao Huaiyan would not have had the presence of mind for that. Speaking of the betrothal — you may not know this, but that same night Xiao Huaiyan had second thoughts and came to tell me he wanted to betroth An'yang to me instead. Isn't that amusing?"

Jiang Mi kept her eyes down.

Xue Jinglin turned the crossbow over in his hand. "Or was it the day you went to nurse the Empress Dowager? I heard you went to the Qianqing Palace with broth? But why would he give you a crossbow out of nowhere? Unless — have the two of you met again at some other time?"

Jiang Mi looked up at him. "That question is absurd, Young Lord. I have been in danger repeatedly — is it so strange that my aunt would provide me with something to defend myself? I have not had the luck of a Princess An'yang, to be rescued by the Young Lord at a lantern festival."

Xue Jinglin saw the redness creeping into her eyes, saw the pitiful, fragile impression she made. He half-believed her, half did not. But Xiao Huaiyan was in the remote north performing the imperial sacrifice — he could not possibly have come to Jiangnan to meet her in person.

Jiang Mi could feel him still watching her. She gathered her disordered clothes and said quietly, "Young Lord Xue — for Ningzhu's sake, at least let me go with some dignity."

Xue Jinglin looked at her for a long moment, then said to the maids, "Stay with the miss while she changes."

Jiang Mi heard his footsteps leaving. She did not know what he intended to do with her, or why changing clothes was part of it.

......

In the hundred-flower garden, Jiang Rong grew more and more anxious as Jiang Mi failed to appear. She kept running to the garden gate to look, and sent Qiuyu to inquire.

Not long after Qiuyu left, a Yǒuyuán maid appeared and addressed the Su sisters. "Young Misses — a Miss Jiang found herself a little tired from walking around and has gone to wait in the carriage. She said she would like to head back a little early."

The Su sisters had not quite had their fill, but seeing Jiang Rong's distress, they all agreed to go.

The third Su daughter told her maid, "Go find Second Young Master and tell him the girls are all tired and waiting in the carriages. Ask him to come quickly."

The maid went off to do so.

Jiang Rong hurried with Qiuyu and Xiang Yun to the carriage. Qiuyu lifted the curtain, preparing to help Jiang Rong in — and found the girl she thought was her mistress lying on her side under a blanket, saying, "I am a little tired. I would like a moment to myself."

Qiuyu paused and looked at Jiang Rong.

Jiang Rong quickly said, "Of course, Elder Sister — rest well. I will go squeeze in with Third Cousin-Sister."

Jiang Rong did not get in, and Qiuyu and Xiang Yun both followed in the carriage behind.

When Su Jingchen arrived, Jiang Rong gave him a reproachful look. "Second Cousin-Brother — where did you take my sister? She has worn herself out completely."

Su Jingchen thought of all the time spent examining calligraphy and antiques — that sort of thing did take it out of you. He felt genuinely guilty. "It is entirely my fault. I will make it up to your sister when we get back!"

Jiang Rong shook her head. "That — that is really not necessary."

Su Jingchen smiled, swung up onto his horse, and led the party down the mountain.

The winding mountain road had a way of making everyone drowsy. The Su sisters and Jiang Rong, worn out from a day of entertainment, were all beginning to nod off — each of them thinking they would wake up closer to home.

No one was prepared for what happened next.

The carriage carrying Jiang Mi, which had been moving smoothly and quietly, suddenly lurched and bolted out of control. The black horse that drew it went wild, charging straight ahead — toward a cliff with a sheer drop to nothing below.

The change was so abrupt that no one had time to react.

Xiang Yun seized a horse from one of the attendants and rode in pursuit, but she could not close the gap. She could only watch, helpless, as the runaway carriage plunged off the edge of the cliff.

The crash that followed made everyone's blood run cold.

Jiang Rong stumbled forward, screaming and crying. "Elder Sister! Elder Sister!"

Su Jingchen stood frozen.

It had taken only a breath. And it had become a catastrophe.

Su Jingchen looked at the bottomless drop, sank to his knees, and struck himself hard across the face. He hated himself. Why had he brought Jiang Mi to Yǒuyuán? Why had he asked her to help him? He had been cheated out of money — fine, let him be cheated. Why had he needed to understand it?

What was he supposed to do now?

How was the Su family to explain this to the Jiang family — to the Empress Dowager — to the Duke Zhen State's manor?

Su Jingchen was shaking from head to foot. The Su family was finished.

Jiang Rong had collapsed at the cliff's edge, screaming in grief. Su Jingchen crawled over and held her back — one person had already gone over; he could not let a second follow.

Xiang Yun, who everyone had stopped noticing, stood with trembling hands. Her master had sent her to protect Miss Jiang. She deserved to die ten thousand deaths for letting this happen.

She took out a signal whistle and blew it.

......

Yangzhou.

At the banquet table, Xiao Huaiyan held his wine cup and found his thoughts elsewhere.

Gu Chang rose and lifted his cup in a toast. "Your Majesty — Jingyuan's safe recovery owes everything to your strategy. If not for your plan, we might never have found where he was being kept, hidden away and unable to leave."

Xue Jingyuan raised his cup as well. "This subject also owes Your Majesty his life."

Xiao Huaiyan could not account for the unease that kept pulling at him. This was meant to be a welcome-back banquet for Jingyuan, and yet he kept losing the thread. The feeling made him deeply uncomfortable.

He drained his cup. "Jingyuan — the account books and evidence you gathered represent a real achievement. You were confined for so long. You have suffered."

Xue Jingyuan did not dare claim credit. Splitting the rebel faction from within, exposing the officials who had colluded with them — all of it had been the Emperor's orchestration. Those beneath him had only carried out orders.

"Since Your Majesty has already laid the groundwork — when do we move to bring the traitors all in at once?"

Xiao Huaiyan was about to answer when his right eye gave a sudden, violent twitch.

At the same moment Chengzhong came running in, his face ash-white, a letter clutched in shaking hands, his voice barely holding together. "Your — Your Majesty — word has come from Jinling. Miss Jiang's carriage has fallen off a cliff. It is feared the worst..."

Chengzhong knelt.

The wine cup in Xiao Huaiyan's hand dropped to the floor. He looked at Chengzhong with a gaze that could have drawn blood. "Say that again."

Chengzhong was shaking so hard he could barely form words. "Miss Jiang — with the carriage — fell off a cliff. It is feared the worst."

The entire banquet hall went utterly silent.

The trusted men gathered around Xiao Huaiyan were struck dumb. Had Miss Jiang not been sent to the Su family in Jinling? How had she ended up falling off a cliff?

Xiao Huaiyan felt a pain in his head as though it were being split apart.

And through that pain, as if from somewhere impossibly far away, came a thin, wailing sound in a drawn-out pitch — a voice grieving and calling: "Your Majesty... Consort Jiang has been long ill and did not recover... she passed three days ago..."

Xiao Huaiyan pressed his hand to his forehead. His eyes had gone bloodshot. The memories came in like a tide.

chapters.title: Eighty-two
chapters.content:
The ninth month of the fifth year of Yuanxi. Xiao Huaiyan returned from suppressing the rebellion.

He had just entered the palace, still in his black armour, when that keening voice reached him: "Your Majesty... Consort Jiang has been long ill and did not recover... she passed three days ago..."

Xiao Huaiyan's expression froze. His gaze went somewhere vacant for a moment.

He raised his hand and lashed the whip. The announcing eunuch's skin split open.

Xiao Huaiyan's eyes were cold as ice. "Spreading false and disorderly words. Take him away and beat him to death."

The palace maids and eunuchs around him trembled in terror, not daring to say a word.

Xiao Huaiyan walked toward Héngwú Palace, fury radiating from every line of him.

Consort Jiang could not possibly be gone.

When he had left for the campaign, she had been ill, but already showing signs of recovery. She had given him a sachet when he departed, wishing him an early return.

She had said that if he came back before the Longevity Festival, she would present him with a special gift at the birthday banquet.

He had kept his promise. He had returned before his birthday.

He had told her to wait for him. She owed him that promise in return.

She must be angry with him for the way he had dealt with the Jiang family. She was deliberately frightening him.

Xiao Huaiyan stood before Héngwú Palace, staring at the funeral banners hung at the door. Inside, sounds of weeping reached him.

He walked in. In the main hall, a coffin had been placed. The crying around it grew louder.

That crying hammered at his head until it was unbearable.

The maids and consorts inside came out to greet him. Xiao Huaiyan drew the sword from his side. "Get out. All of you — get out."

The murderous intent in his voice made legs give out beneath those who had been about to approach him. They fled, supported by their maids.

Xiao Huaiyan walked, step by step, to the coffin. He saw his Consort Jiang.

She lay quietly — as though she had only fallen asleep.

He reached out and touched her face. Ice cold.

The blood in his body turned to stone. His hand shook beyond his control. He bent low and whispered, "Consort Jiang — I am back."

The person in the coffin slept on in silence. Not the slightest response.

Those hands that held life and death over all beneath heaven, afraid of waking her, yet unable to stop themselves from nudging at her gently. "Tangtan — I am back. Wake up..."

Xiao Huaiyan slept every night in Héngwú Palace. But Jiang Mi never came to him in his dreams.

He thought the palace must be too loud. That was why she would not come. It was the noise.

He did not remember how many people he had killed, how many he had had executed by the cruelest method. The palace grew quiet at last.

But still she did not come to him in dreams.

Even as he thought to keep her near him with ice — the monks from Qiānshuāng Temple came to the palace to tell him she should be given a proper burial.

Xiao Huaiyan looked at the person in the coffin. He placed a golden relic beside her.

He drew a knife and cut his palm, letting his blood flow onto the relic. Only when the golden light of it had faintly taken on the colour of blood did he withdraw his hand.

His bloodstained fingers traced her lips, leaving them red as a blooming lotus.

He looked at her for a long time, his eyes full of broken vessels. "Is it because you resent me that you will not come?"

He closed his eyes, fighting for control. His voice came out desolate. "You have every right to resent me."

He wound a lock of his hair around Jiang Mi's little finger, his voice gone hoarse. "Even if you resent me — I am unwilling to let go. In the next life, let us bind our hair together again."

......

Xiao Huaiyan opened his eyes. The pain cut to the bone.

He had been given a second chance — and yet he had heard of Jiang Mi's death again.

Xue Jingyuan, Pei Chi, and the others could see that His Majesty's head ailment had returned and that something was badly wrong. Disregarding court hierarchy, they stepped forward to support him and called out for the imperial physician.

Xiao Huaiyan waved them off. "Close the net. We move to Jinling."

He would find her alive. Or if she was—

No. She could not be dead.

......

In the space of a single night, Suzhou, Yangzhou, and Jinling were shaken to their foundations.

The office of the Governor-General of the Two Rivers was raided and searched. Numerous officials and prominent families were swept into the investigation. No one knew when or where those soldiers had appeared. The generals leading them carried imperial edicts and made arrests on the spot.

The streets were full of soldiers and Embroidered Guards hunting down rebel conspirators. Citizens barred their gates and did not dare venture out.

Yǒuyuán — that garden which the people of Jinling had spoken of so fondly — was quietly surrounded by a heavy cordon.

Xiao Huaiyan stood on the cliff's edge and looked down into the abyss. It was from here that Jiang Mi's carriage had fallen.

Xiang Yun, covered in wounds, knelt nearby. Her bloodied hands held out a small object. "Your Majesty — this is what this servant found at the bottom of the cliff."

Xiao Huaiyan looked. It was a small wrist crossbow — made for a woman's hand.

There was no question it was the one he had given Jiang Mi.

And yet to Xiao Huaiyan, that crossbow was a thing of horror. Every second he looked at it sharpened the pain.

"Where is she?"

Xiang Yun thought of the disfigured body she had found. She had not wanted to tell him. That a woman so beautiful had been reduced to that.

After Miss Jiang went over the cliff, she had contacted the shadow guards and they had gone down to search for her.

When the body was found, it was beyond recognition.

Xiang Yun did not dare disobey.

In a dark room packed with ice, a body lay in a coffin.

Xiao Huaiyan stood before it for a long time without moving.

He faced Jiang Mi's death a second time.

His spine was rigid. The smell of blood hung in the air even through the incense.

He stood for a long, long time. At last, bearing the pain of it, he made himself look at the person lying inside.

One look. And something shifted in his eyes.

It was not her.

Xiao Huaiyan stepped forward and lifted the wrist to examine it.

He spun around. "Pei Chi — burn all of this."

Pei Chi did not understand but would not defy the imperial will.

Xiao Huaiyan wiped his hands with a cloth and went directly to Yǒuyuán.

After a night of fierce fighting, the situation there had been resolved.

What had once been a beautiful garden was now soaked in blood everywhere one looked, with bodies strewn across the paths.

Gu Chang came forward. "Your Majesty — all have been captured. Those who resisted have been executed on the spot. The Prince of Qi's former strategist Zhu Mo attempted to flee with the young child, but was intercepted by the Embroidered Guards."

Gu Chang hesitated before asking, "Your Majesty — as for Young Lord Xue of the Duke Zhen State's manor — how do you wish to handle him?"

"Bring him to me." Xiao Huaiyan said.

Gu Chang went to carry out the order. He could not understand why a man of Xue Jinglin's standing had chosen to wade into these waters.

Xiao Huaiyan sat in the main hall and watched as Xue Jinglin was brought forward, hands and feet bound in chains.

Xue Jinglin's expression was calm.

He looked up at Xiao Huaiyan and let out a low laugh. "So that is how it is. A decoy. You never went to the northern mountains for the imperial sacrifice at all — you set up a stand-in and fooled us all."

Xiao Huaiyan said, "Where is she?"

Xue Jinglin looked puzzled. "She? Who?"

He seemed to remember something, and smiled again. "Are you speaking of my not-yet-wedded wife, the Jiang girl? She lost control of her carriage and went over a cliff — there is nothing left of her. Surely Your Majesty knows this already?"

Xiao Huaiyan's patience was nearly spent. His eyes were full of dangerous intent.

An arrow flew and pierced straight through Xue Jinglin's knee.

Xue Jinglin's face showed pain as he crumpled to the ground.

Xiao Huaiyan pressed his brow down over his eyes, restraining his desire to kill, and asked again. "Xue Jinglin. Where is she?"

Xue Jinglin gave a low laugh. "So you are capable of rage after all." He had grown used to Xiao Huaiyan's composed, undisturbed face; seeing him like this was genuinely novel. "She is dead, Your Majesty. From a height like that — how could anyone survive..."

Before he finished speaking, a second arrow went through his shoulder. He looked at Xiao Huaiyan's expression and thought: if he had any less control over himself, that arrow would have gone through his throat.

"Victory to the victor, ruin to the vanquished — I have been prepared for this outcome for a long time. There is no need for your hand." Xue Jinglin spoke, and blood began to flow from the corner of his mouth. "Everything was done by me alone. No one else is responsible. I am willing to pay with my life."

Xiao Huaiyan felt nothing at all about whether Xue Jinglin lived or died. He said, "And you think that will spare the Duke Zhen State's manor? Your father, your mother, your sister — even your grandmother. All of them will be found guilty because of you. The Xue line will be destroyed by your hand."

Xue Jinglin's eyes went unfocused. He knew — anyone who takes up the idea of rebellion, if they fail, brings ruin to their family. But ever since he had learned of his own origins, the ambition inside him had been growing, day by day, gnawing at him.

If even a discarded son like Xiao Huaiyan — born of a consort whose honour had been smeared — could reach the throne, then why could he not? Why could he not seize any chance that came to him?

If only he had been given a little more time. He and Zhu Mo had laid so many years of plans. He could not accept falling this suddenly.

He did not even know where he had slipped up — what had made Xiao Huaiyan keep his suspicion on him all along. Under that suspicion, he had only grown more reckless, more desperate to bite at any opening he could find.

The poison was taking effect. His vision was beginning to blur, his hearing to fade.

But he knew what Xiao Huaiyan wanted to know.

Xue Jinglin smiled, triumphant even now. More blood came. He opened his mouth, and moved his lips without sound: "You will not find her."

Through the blurring of his eyes he seemed to see a face — luminous, lit from behind, like something from another world — and he raised his hand as if to touch it.

Then he fell, and did not move again.

Xiao Huaiyan watched without feeling.

In his last life, his confrontation with Xue Jinglin had been on a battlefield.

Even then he had not imagined that the one buried deepest inside the rebel forces was him.

In that last life, at the hunt at Fengchi, Xue Jinglin had presented a white tiger he had caught in the forest. The beast had been gentle at first, drawing admiration from the court officials as a blessed omen. The moment Xiao Huaiyan drew near, it had lunged at him. Xue Jinglin had stepped in front and killed it, then apologised. Afterward, whispers spread — if even a sacred beast had tried to attack the Emperor, could it be that he lacked the virtue to rule?

In this life, because of the incident at the Duke Zhen manor's flower banquet, the white tiger was never presented. Instead there had come the wolf attack and the assassination attempt.

What Xiao Huaiyan hated most was this: in his last life, Xue Jinglin had hidden the Prince of Qi's son by a concubine and sent the boy to rebel-held territory. Later, the child's name had been raised as a banner for legitimacy in open revolt. And in that same campaign, to taint Xiao Huaiyan's birth, the circumstances of his mother's death had been dragged into the open for all the world to know.

Xue Jinglin deserved ten deaths over.

He did not believe a word the man had said.

Xiao Huaiyan walked out and gave orders to Pei Chi, Gu Chang, and the others. "Turn this garden over stone by stone. Pry open the mouths of every traitor. Search every stretch of mountain and every village in the surrounding area. Find her."

He would find Jiang Mi no matter what.

......

After being made to drink a bowl of medicine, Jiang Mi had fallen unconscious.

When she came to, she found herself inside a narrow underground passage.

It was dark. Only in the small space immediately around her did a candle give off a faint glow.

Jiang Mi looked around, frightened. Behind her was a sealed stone wall.

Ahead was endless dark. She had no idea where it led.

She carefully shielded the candle flame and bumped into something. She looked down. A bundle.

Inside: a water bladder, dried provisions, and a fire-starter.

Had Xue Jinglin left this? What had he intended by bringing her here?

Jiang Mi picked up the bundle. She searched the stone wall behind her for any hidden mechanism and found nothing.

She looked at the limitless dark ahead. The only way was forward.

She lifted the candle and shielded the flame with her hand, and stepped carefully into the dark.

The passage was far longer than she had imagined.

When she was hungry she took a small mouthful of provisions. When she was exhausted she stopped to rest.

She watched the fire-starter dwindle. The provisions dwindled. She could not tell where the darkness would end.

Her fear deepened. If she finished the provisions, and the fire-starter, and had still not reached the end of this passage — what then?

Would she be trapped here?

She forced herself to stop resting, enduring hunger until she absolutely could not before allowing herself a small bite.

Then — she felt something. Wind.

When she ate the last mouthful of provisions, she noticed the dark ahead was not quite as absolute. A faint thread of light was filtering through.

Jiang Mi quickened her pace. Before long, she saw the way out.

She pushed aside weeds and branches and stepped through the opening.

The sky outside was already dimming — which explained why the light inside had seemed so faint.

She had no idea where she was. Trees in every direction.

She wanted to find a path out while there was still a little daylight.

She spotted the flicker of torchlight ahead — someone was over there. She did not dare go directly.

She crept to a spot at a safe distance and hid behind a tree, easing the leaves aside to look.

A great number of soldiers carrying torches were searching the area. Others were interrogating a group of kneeling captives. Among them stood a man in a white brocade robe, his back to her, a bloodied sword hanging from his hand, looking on at the suffering before him with cold indifference.

Jiang Mi had thought she might be able to call for help — but the scene before her made it impossible to approach.

As though sensing something, the man in white suddenly turned his head and looked directly toward her.

Jiang Mi threw herself behind the tree, not daring to breathe.

But the man's long, narrow phoenix eyes held steadily on that direction. He walked toward her, sword in hand, and pushed aside the branches.

He found the person he had been searching for.

He thought for a moment that he was seeing another hallucination — and was afraid that this one too might vanish.

Xiao Huaiyan let the sword fall from his hand. He seized her and held her fast.

"Tangtan..."

chapters.title: Eighty-three
chapters.content:
Jiang Mi had barely managed to drag herself out of the underground passage, and the sight she had just witnessed had left her like a startled bird.

She was still pressed behind the tree, heart hammering, when she heard a small sound. She looked up — before she could make out anything clearly, she felt a figure pull her into an embrace.

The arms around her held firm. She could not break free.

The scent of dragon's blood incense — that same oppressive fragrance — entered her breath just as the embrace did.

And in the same moment, a murmur against her ear, low as a sigh.

"Tangtan..."

Jiang Mi went completely rigid.

She found it all preposterous. She began to wonder if she had never truly left the passage at all — if this was a dream conjured by sleeping too long in the dark.

How could Xiao Huaiyan possibly be here.

How could he possibly be calling her by her pet name.

It was all too strange.

No — she could not keep dreaming. She had to get out of the dark. She needed to wake.

Jiang Mi was trying to raise her wrist to bite herself awake when the arms around her suddenly loosened. Hands gripped her shoulders, and eyes bore into her.

Jiang Mi met that gaze and felt a chill run through her.

The look in his eyes was like something that wanted to swallow her whole. The Xiao Huaiyan of her dreams kept getting stranger.

Xiao Huaiyan held what felt like a vision, held it as tightly as he dared, afraid that if he let go it would disappear.

He could feel the thing in his arms struggling. It was not cold. It had warmth. It had a heartbeat.

Xiao Huaiyan came back to himself with a lurch. He looked down at the person he was holding.

A pale, small face with a smear of dust across it. A pair of wide, water-filled almond eyes, wide with fear.

He reached out and touched that face.

It was warm.

There was breath.

"Tangtan." Xiao Huaiyan's voice was raw and dry. "It is you."

Jiang Mi swallowed nervously.

What did it matter if it was her? She could not think straight — she did not dare make a sound. She had heard somewhere, in some dream, that if someone calls your name you must not answer.

Xiao Huaiyan closed his eyes and opened them. The person before him had not disappeared.

After several breaths, he brought the surging tide of feeling under control, and bent to press a kiss to her forehead.

Then he scooped that slight body up into his arms.

......

The people left behind watched as their Emperor emerged from the darkness of the forest. In the torchlight, they could see a woman held in his arms.

When his close attendants and trusted officials made out her face, every one of them was struck silent.

They had all largely accepted, by this point, that Miss Jiang was likely gone. They had interrogated so many of the rebel conspirators and not a single one had any knowledge of her whereabouts — it was as though she simply did not exist to them. Only Zhu Mo had known — and he had claimed, under initial questioning, that she had been given poison and her body left in the wilderness. Only under severe torture had he finally admitted, with great difficulty, that Yǒuyuán might contain a hidden passage — but only the garden's master knew of it. And the garden's master, Xue Jinglin, had taken poison and died. No one knew where the passage was or where it led.

The Emperor had sent men to turn Yǒuyuán apart, stone by stone. A passage had been found, but it had been sealed. If they forced it open with explosives, the tunnel itself would collapse.

With soldiers, they had searched every reachable part of that mountain and found no trace.

They had all come to believe that a young woman as fragile as Miss Jiang had almost certainly perished.

The Emperor had not slept at all, circling several sections of the surrounding mountain himself, dragging rebel captives along to confirm what they knew, one by one.

The search area he had enclosed overlapped, as chance would have it, with the base of the cliff where Miss Jiang's carriage had fallen.

Hope had felt remote. And yet — as night fell, the Emperor had suddenly gone still, staring at one particular spot, and then walked straight toward it.

He had come out of that wild tangle of trees carrying a woman in his arms.

If they had not seen it with their own eyes, they might have thought it a forest spirit summoned by the force of his obsession.

......

Jiang Mi sat in the carriage, listening to the hoofbeats outside and looking at the man seated across from her. And at the cup of hot tea in her own hands.

She was beginning to accept that she was not dreaming.

She had truly walked out of that dark underground passage.

And she had been found again by Xiao Huaiyan.

Jiang Mi kept her eyes down on the tea, fingertips pressed tight around the cup. She tried to push away the warmth that still lingered on her forehead from before, in the darkness.

She became aware of a shadow leaning toward her and instinctively turned her head away.

But she was too weak. Even with the will to dodge, she could not quite manage it — something soft brushed across her face.

Jiang Mi looked up. Xiao Huaiyan's hand was suspended in the air, holding a cloth. He had apparently been trying to clean her face.

The look in his eyes was strange — it unsettled her for a reason she could not name.

She was aware of how wretched she must look. Her clothes and face were certainly smeared with dirt.

Jiang Mi turned to the side and bowed her head. "This — this subject has been indisposed. I beg Your Majesty's pardon."

Xiao Huaiyan saw that she was still afraid of him, still pulling away.

And yet the fact that she was sitting here in front of him, alive, was enough to make his heart overflow with something he could not name. He could see her. She was here.

"You have not been indisposed." Xiao Huaiyan held down what he wanted to do, reined in his urgency.

He set the cloth down beside her and leaned back against the carriage wall and closed his eyes.

The carriage carried the scent of tea, and her particular faint fragrance — and the splitting pain in his head, which had been like a blade tearing, slowly began to quiet.

Jiang Mi felt the pressing gaze disappear. Xiao Huaiyan had stopped speaking.

She glanced over. He seemed to have fallen asleep.

She looked at the cloth beside her — hesitated for a long time — and then, turning her back to him, used it to wipe her face.

She ran it across her skin twice. When she looked at it, it had come away grey.

Jiang Mi frowned and tucked the cloth into her sleeve.

Whether it was exhaustion or simply relief at having escaped danger, her body finally eased — and sleep crept up on her. She drifted off without realizing it.

......

Jiang Mi's sleep was uneasy. When she opened her eyes, the carriage had stopped. She moved to get up and found her wrist held in a firm grip.

She looked. Xiao Huaiyan still had his eyes closed — but at some point he had taken hold of her wrist.

Jiang Mi tried to pull free. Several attempts, all unsuccessful. In the process she knocked an empty tea cup off the blanket.

The sound was small and did not wake Xiao Huaiyan — but it alerted Chengzhong, who had been keeping watch outside. He lifted the carriage curtain, thinking he had been summoned.

He found that Miss Jiang had woken.

Chengzhong saw her movements and assumed she was trying to get down. He lowered his voice: "Miss — please wait a little longer. His Majesty has not slept for days and nights on end searching for you. Let him rest a while longer."

Chengzhong withdrew.

Jiang Mi sat in silence and looked at the wrist being held.

When the maids had been forced to change her clothes, she had thought she would die. But Xue Jinglin had let her live. He had come back once, spoken a few words, then had the maids pour a bowl of medicine down her throat.

In that one moment before the medicine hit her, so many people and so many things from this life and the last had flashed through her mind. She had thought of Xiao Huaiyan too.

In her last life, he had led the campaign in person and told her to wait for his return.

In this life, in Xuzhou, he had also told her to wait for him to come for her.

Twice. Both times she had not waited.

There was too much between them — too many people, too many things.

Walking alone through that black passage, she had been terrified, helpless, not knowing whether moving forward would lead anywhere at all.

But something — she did not know where it came from — had kept her going. Some quiet insistence: let me see how far I can walk.

She could never have expected that walking out of that dark passage would bring her to Xiao Huaiyan again.

Jiang Mi sat quietly.

She did not know how much time passed. When she opened her eyes again, she was lying in a bed. Warm morning sunlight came through the latticed window in bars of gold. Birds were calling in a small bright noise. A soft breeze carried the faintest trace of flowers.

Qiuyu, keeping watch at the bedside, saw Jiang Mi's eyes open and cried out in joy. "Miss! Miss! Do you feel any pain anywhere?"

Jiang Mi shook her head.

Qiuyu quickly brought a cup of warm honeyed water to her lips. "Miss — drink something. I am going to go and fetch Madam and Fourth Miss."

The moment Qiuyu left, Jiang Mi noticed the room was not the one she had been sleeping in at the Su estate. And she had been changed into clean clothes.

If not at the Su estate — then where?

Before she could think further, Su-shi and Jiang Rong came hurrying in.

Both of their eyes were red. Jiang Rong flung herself toward the bed calling for her sister.

Su-shi wiped her tears with a handkerchief. "You are awake. You are all right. That is all that matters."

She patted Jiang Rong. "A'Rong, do not throw yourself on your sister — her injuries are not yet healed."

Injuries? What injuries?

Jiang Mi felt a small confusion. Where was she hurt?

Su-shi sat at the bedside, emotions running high. These past days had been almost unbearable. She had very nearly gone to prostrate herself before Jiang Mi's father in apology.

Looking now at Jiang Mi, alive and breathing, she could only say with relief, "Thank heaven for that elderly couple who found you, and thank heaven for the general whom the Emperor sent to suppress the rebellion passing through in time. A true miracle."

"Elder Sister had Buddha's protection! Falling from such a height and landing in the trees — Elder Sister has been blessed by fortune!" Jiang Rong added.

Su-shi nodded earnestly. "Tangtan — the elderly couple who rescued you, I have already sent gifts of thanks. You just rest and get better. In a little while we will all travel back to the capital with the Emperor."

Jiang Mi recalled what Xue Jinglin had told her: that he had made her carriage fall off the cliff, and that she would simply vanish from the world. But what Su-shi was saying was that she had fallen but been found and rescued — that she had sustained injuries and recuperated at that couple's home, and a general coming through to put down the rebellion had brought her back.

She thought she was beginning to understand.

This way, her ordeal and her rescue had nothing whatsoever to do with the rebel conspiracy.

From what they were saying, they seemed to know about the suppression of the rebellion — and to know that Xiao Huaiyan had come as well. Had his identity been made public?

Jiang Rong noticed her sister's prolonged silence. "Elder Sister — are you tired?"

Jiang Mi shook her head. "Madam has been through so much trouble on my account," she said softly.

"Of course not. Not at all."

"I wonder — how is Young Lord Xue?"

Su-shi's expression shifted slightly, then she smiled. "These past days everything outside has been in chaos with the arrests and executions of rebel criminals. The Young Lord is probably still in Suzhou — perhaps we will have news in a few days. Do not worry."

Jiang Mi gave an imperceptible nod.

As she had suspected. Su-shi did not know that Young Lord Xue had been one of the conspirators.

Had Xiao Huaiyan suppressed the truth about Xue Jinglin to protect the Grand Princess and the Duke Zhen State's manor? Or was it also, in part, for her?

Su-shi, worried she might overthink things, said, "Tangtan — you are recuperating at the Prefect's residence for now. The Emperor's party is also lodged here, and there is a palace physician in attendance. His Majesty will certainly have the physician give you proper care and attention out of regard for the Empress Dowager."

The Prefect's residence. So that was where she was.

Su-shi added, "Oh — and Tangtan, that physician's apprentice-brother you asked me to help you find before — there are some leads now. When you are feeling stronger, I will have him come to see you."

That was good news.

Su-shi and Jiang Rong stayed for a little while longer, then took their leave.

On the way out, Su-shi murmured to Jiang Rong, "Not a word about the Young Lord in front of your sister, do you hear?"

Jiang Rong said, "I know, Mother. I do not want Elder Sister to be sad."

Su-shi sighed. "What a pity. Such a pity."

......

In the study, Xiao Huaiyan finished the last of the memorials and had a rider carry them back to the capital at speed.

Pei Chi stood below him and said, "Your Majesty — this subject has already put out word that Xue Jinglin died at the hands of the conspirators. As for his remains — how do you wish them handled?"

Xiao Huaiyan suppressed his fury. In his final moments, Xue Jinglin had played one last hand.

He had deliberately provoked him with words — and then, in the same breath, traded Jiang Mi's life for the last thread of survival for the Duke Zhen State's manor.

Because of the Cheng'en Marquessate's betrothal connection with the Duke Zhen State's manor, Xiao Huaiyan had been forced to keep things buried — to protect Jiang Mi's name from being tainted by association with a traitor.

Xue Jinglin had begun gambling the moment he arranged to send the Prince of Qi's son to Jiangnan.

And against all expectation, the gamble had paid off.

Xiao Huaiyan's gaze went cold. "Take his remains back to the capital and present them before the Grand Princess of Zhaoyang. Tell her, in full, exactly how he died."

Only a slim chance of survival — and it would not let the guilty escape punishment.

Pei Chi: "By your command."

After Pei Chi left, several more trusted officials came in sequence to report. When it was finally over, Chengzhong came in to refill the tea and heard the Emperor cough again.

"Your Majesty," Chengzhong said carefully, "let this servant bring Physician Song's medicine. Please drink a little."

Xiao Huaiyan said evenly, "No need. Has she woken?"

Chengzhong hurried to answer. "She has, she has. Madam Su and Fourth Miss Jiang have both been to see her. Physician Song also went — he says Miss Jiang had a bad fright but her body is unharmed. A calming draught and she will be fine."

Xiao Huaiyan said nothing more.

Chengzhong watched the Emperor return to his work — and the cough seemed to have grown a little worse.

He was fretting inside. The Emperor would fret over Miss Jiang well enough, but refused to take his own medicine when he was sick. Really...

He wondered whether fetching Miss Jiang to come and persuade him would do any good.

chapters.title: Eighty-four
chapters.content:
In the deep quiet of the night, Xiao Huaiyan sat on the edge of the bed, his gaze moving greedily over the sleeping face before him.

Only at moments like this could he look his fill without restraint.

That she was still alive was the greatest mercy heaven had ever shown him.

He thought of the carriage — how she had turned away from his hand when he tried to wipe her face, how she had avoided his eyes.

He had been afraid of making her uncomfortable. So he had closed his eyes and feigned sleep.

Now, with her, he was like someone holding a piece of glass that could shatter — he could neither grip it too tight nor too lightly.

He did not know what to do with her.

He had wound one of her strands of hair around his finger and was watching her sleep, seemingly unable to look enough.

Xiao Huaiyan raised his hand to his lips and gave a quiet cough. He looked at her sleeping face — she had faintly frowned — and smothered the itch in his throat. He released the strand of hair and stood.

He lowered the bed curtain and walked out of the room.

Chengzhong, keeping watch outside, saw him emerge. Before long, the Emperor coughed again, trying to muffle it.

"Your Majesty," Chengzhong said in distress, "please let Physician Song come and take another look. This illness seems to be getting worse." He had watched it unfold in growing alarm. Ever since the Emperor heard that Miss Jiang was in danger, he had not slept — not stopped for one moment — dealing with the rebel conspirators and searching that mountain himself. The wind-cold that had taken hold of him was severe, and yet he refused to drink the medicine. Now his cough was worse.

Xiao Huaiyan paid Chengzhong no attention and walked alone into the dark.

Inside the room, behind the lowered curtain, Jiang Mi slowly opened her eyes. She stared at the strand of her own hair, lost in thought.

......

The following day, Jiang Mi was in reasonable spirits. She and Qiuyu walked through the garden.

The crabapple blossoms at the Prefect's residence had opened. Jiang Mi stood beneath the flowering trees and listened as Qiuyu told her everything that had happened outside while she was missing.

Then someone came down the other path.

The trees where Jiang Mi stood blocked the view from the other side, but she could see them clearly.

A girl of about fifteen or sixteen walked among the group — fine-featured and composed, her face carrying a blush, attended by maids who were teasing her.

The girl's face went redder. "Father said His Majesty has a cough — I do not know if this autumn pear paste of mine will do any good. And His Majesty has imperial physicians looking after him already. If I go and present it uninvited, will he find it tiresome?"

The shorter maid said, "Miss — with your looks and your accomplishments, who could find you tiresome? This is a rare opportunity. Do not let it pass."

The taller maid added, "Miss — your autumn pear paste is the finest remedy there is for a cough, and it soothes the lungs too. The Old Madam, when her cough was at its worst, was healed by the paste you made with your own hands. Stop worrying. Go now, before any of the other sisters get there first and steal the advantage."

At those words the girl's face showed clear anxiety. She knew the Emperor's party was a guest in her family's home — the whole household was walking on eggshells. Among the sisters, every one of them had an eye out for an opportunity. The Emperor had not yet chosen an Empress or taken consorts. If any of them could catch his favour, she would be going to the capital with him. She had heard her father say that whenever past emperors came south, they always brought back some beauties with them. She and her sisters must not let the chance slip by.

Worried about her sisters getting there first, she forgot her own propriety and quickened her steps.

Jiang Mi watched them move away and withdrew her gaze. She picked up a crabapple blossom that had just fallen and turned it in her fingers.

Qiuyu told her, "Miss — that was the Prefect Sun's daughter, Sun Ruoyue — fourth daughter, second legitimate daughter." She had been moving around the household and had gathered some information.

Jiang Mi paid it little mind and gave a small nod.

Qiuyu hesitated, then ventured, "Miss — from what they were saying, it seems His Majesty is not well. Would you like to go and visit?"

Jiang Mi turned the flower bud in her hand and shook her head. "I will not add to the crowd."

Xiao Huaiyan had imperial physicians attending him and would not lack for people eager to show their concern.

Jiang Mi looked at the girl who had gone to bring the autumn pear paste and saw herself, in her last life, reflected back. Herself and all the other consorts and concubines whose shadows she carried.

In these recent days she had not been unaware of Xiao Huaiyan's intentions. She had been avoiding thinking it through directly.

But she was truly afraid.

She had neither the courage to compete with so many other women for his favour, nor — with the Jiang family's secret hanging over her head like something unspoken — the audacity to try.

How could she dare fall for Xiao Huaiyan again.

......

After returning from the garden Jiang Mi did not go out again. She lay on the daybed with a book, flipping through it without quite being able to settle her mind.

She gave up and put the book aside, closed her eyes to rest.

She fell asleep before she meant to.

Her sleep was uneasy. She found herself back in that dark underground passage, holding a small failing light, terrified, walking and walking and never reaching the end, and finally sinking down and crying in despair.

"Tangtan."

"Tangtan."

A voice calling, over and over, drawing nearer from somewhere far away.

Jiang Mi raised her head. The dark passage had inexplicably grown bright. Xiao Huaiyan stood before her in white, his hand held out, calling again in a quiet voice: "Tangtan — I have finally found you."

Jiang Mi's eyes snapped open.

She pressed her fingers to her temple and sat up slowly. The blanket slipped from her shoulders.

The room had been lit. Outside it was dark. Had she slept this long?

Jiang Mi was about to call for Qiuyu when she heard voices outside.

"Eunuch Cheng — Miss is still sleeping. You cannot go in."

Chengzhong was frantic but did not dare force his way. "Qiuyu — please go in and wake her. I have truly urgent business with Miss Jiang."

There was something wrong with Chengzhong's tone. Jiang Mi said toward the door, "Qiuyu — let Eunuch Cheng in."

Chengzhong came inside and said at once, "Miss Jiang — His Majesty has a high fever and it will not break. Please come and look in on him."

Jiang Mi tightened her hands around the cloth she was holding. She thought of what she had seen that morning. "Are the physicians not with him? Eunuch Cheng — I am no physician. I would be of no use even if I came."

Chengzhong thought: how could she be of no use — the Emperor only needed to lay eyes on her and that would be worth more than any physician.

"Miss Jiang," Chengzhong said, "ever since His Majesty received word that you were in danger, he has not rested — not for a moment. He has been relentlessly dealing with the rebel conspirators, searching that mountain himself, all to find you. The wind-cold he caught has come on very hard. I have served His Majesty for many years — no matter how severe the injury, he has never looked like this. Please have mercy on him. Please come and see him."

Chengzhong said this, and wiped his eyes.

He did not understand why Miss Jiang resisted the Emperor so. But what the Emperor had done for her, those of them in service had all seen.

He looked at Miss Jiang sitting there without speaking, apparently unmoved. He felt the weight of it.

He also knew the Emperor would rather die than disturb Miss Jiang. Coming to find her like this was already a great transgression on his part.

"It is my fault for coming and troubling you, Miss," he said quietly. "I will go back now."

He turned to leave.

"Wait."

Jiang Mi let out a quiet breath. She said to Chengzhong, "Lead the way."

......

Jiang Mi followed Chengzhong into the courtyard where Xiao Huaiyan was lodging. The guards were many and strict.

Inside, it was not what she had imagined. She had expected the Prefect Sun to have his household gathered outside anxiously — but the courtyard, apart from its guards and a handful of inner attendants, was empty and quiet.

When she entered the room, a strong smell of medicine met her.

She went around the screen and first saw Physician Song standing at the bedside. Her gaze moved to the bed.

Xiao Huaiyan appeared to be asleep. His colour was poor.

Physician Song saw her arrive and clasped his hands in a bow. "Miss Jiang." He stepped quietly to one side.

Jiang Mi returned the courtesy and asked, "Physician Song — how is His Majesty's condition?"

"His Majesty suffered a severe emotional upheaval and extreme exhaustion, which allowed the wind-cold to enter. He then refused to take medicine, causing the illness to worsen. The fever has not broken, and he will not keep the medicine down — just overturned a bowl. I must go and brew another. Miss Jiang — I will ask you to keep watch here for a moment."

After the physician left, the room contained only Jiang Mi and Xiao Huaiyan.

Jiang Mi stood at the bedside. She looked at him — seemingly unconscious, brow furrowed even in this state, forehead glistening.

She had never seen him like this.

Xiao Huaiyan was forceful. He was merciless. He was elevated far above ordinary people. How could he ever be this weak from illness?

He had taken the full force of a fallen lamp stand across his back to shield her, and with injuries that severe he had still been capable of cold, menacing threats.

Jiang Mi sat down by the bed. He was insensible, and yet his brow was still pulled tightly together.

She took a cloth and wiped the sweat from his forehead. She could not avoid touching the skin there.

It burned.

She noticed a copper basin set nearby. She wrung out the cloth inside and laid it across his forehead.

Then she heard his lips moving. A murmur. Too indistinct to catch.

She was about to change the cloth when the murmur grew a little louder.

"Tangtan..."

Her hand stilled.

"Tangtan..."

Xiao Huaiyan's eyes opened suddenly.

His gaze had no focus — and yet it had found Jiang Mi.

The tight knot of his brow slowly released.

He looked at her as though she were something he could not bear to look away from. "Tangtan — I missed you."

Jiang Mi felt something sting at the back of her nose. She looked away and asked in a stiff voice, "Your Majesty — are you awake?"

Xiao Huaiyan watched her expression. Clarity was returning to his eyes.

Not a dream.

His Tangtan was right here in front of him.

Xiao Huaiyan coughed quietly. He took in the room full of medicine smell and asked, a little uncertain, "Did you come to bring me medicine?"

Jiang Mi was afraid of being misunderstood. Before she could think, she said, "Your Majesty does not lack for people to bring medicine. Physician Song has gone to brew another bowl."

Xiao Huaiyan lay still and listened to her voice. He smiled without making a sound. "No matter who brings it — the only medicine I am willing to drink is what you bring me, Tangtan."

Jiang Mi stepped back. She lowered her head. "Please do not call this subject by her pet name, Your Majesty."

She felt panicked, and something else that she could not name was pressing against her chest.

She did not know why. She wanted to cry.

Those two syllables — in her last life she had wanted so desperately to hear them.

Xiao Huaiyan looked at the small figure about to cry in front of him. "All right," he said gently.

And Jiang Mi's tears fell anyway.

chapters.title: Eighty-five
chapters.content:
Physician Song came in carrying the medicine and found the Emperor already awake. Miss Jiang stood quietly to one side, her eyes visibly red.

As one of the Emperor's closest confidants, Physician Song had not missed how much His Majesty's feelings toward this young woman had come to affect him.

He assumed she had cried out of worry for the Emperor's illness.

Without giving it another thought he walked over and placed the bowl of medicine directly in Jiang Mi's hands. "I will leave this to you, Miss Jiang."

He did not dare try to persuade the Emperor to drink again. When the Emperor had been stationed at Yunzhou and suffered serious injuries, he had endured them without a sound. But getting him to take medicine was another matter entirely — no amount of persuasion ever worked.

Having offloaded the problem, Physician Song stepped back and quietly withdrew.

Jiang Mi looked at the steam rising from the bowl. She knew Xiao Huaiyan disliked taking medicine — in her last life she had made no small number of promises to coax him. "Your Majesty — your health is bound to the welfare of the realm and all who live in it. Please take care of yourself." She spoke softly and held the medicine out.

Xiao Huaiyan thought about how carefully she was choosing each word, how if he tried to draw closer she would only pull further away. He wanted to be near her. He wanted her to feed him the medicine herself. But if he asked for that, she would retreat.

He smiled pleasantly and said, in an easy tone, "All right."

Jiang Mi had expected him to raise some condition, the way he had when she changed his dressings. She had not expected him to agree so readily.

She looked up just in time to catch that faint smile. She pressed her lips together and looked away, and placed the bowl in his extended hand.

Xiao Huaiyan drank a calm mouthful. His brow creased slightly. "I find myself missing the osmanthus cakes you made at the Empress Dowager's palace."

Jiang Mi understood — he found the medicine bitter. "Good medicine is bitter, Your Majesty. Please drink it while it is hot."

He said nothing more and finished the bowl.

"It is not so bitter after all."

"When I was small, I once took medicine for a wind-cold and then suffered terrible cramps — nearly did not survive. I have not been fond of medicine since."

His tone was easy, as if telling a passing story.

Jiang Mi took the empty bowl from him, and paused.

So that was why he had always resisted medicine. In her last life when she had been at his sickbed, she had once asked him if it was because he feared the bitterness. He had given her a sharp, cold look, and she had not dared raise it again.

This was the first time she had ever heard him speak of his childhood.

After Consort Jin passed, Xiao Huaiyan had been only seven years old. How had he survived those years in the palace?

Jiang Mi did not know what to say. Or whether she was supposed to say anything.

This version of Xiao Huaiyan felt unfamiliar. He made her chest go tight.

His gaze had not left her. In the last life, when he was ill, she had been anxious and fussing — she would stay close, she would want to be near him. Now she stood properly to one side, every word she spoke measured and composed, not the faintest presumption.

Xiao Huaiyan gave a silent, bitter inward smile. "Do you still have nightmares at night?"

Jiang Mi shook her head instinctively. Then wondered — how would he know?

Xiao Huaiyan read her expression and offered an explanation before she could ask. "In the carriage the night I brought you back — there were signs that you had woken from a bad dream."

He had learned later that she had walked a path through total darkness to find her way out. She had always had a timid spirit. She must have been terrified in that passage.

Xiao Huaiyan slipped a string of prayer beads from his wrist. He reached for Jiang Mi's hand and pressed them into her palm. "These beads have been blessed with incense by a high monk. If you wear them, they will calm the spirit."

Jiang Mi stepped back and refused. "Your Majesty is ill — you have more need of something to ward off ill and settle the spirit. I thank Your Majesty for the thought."

The beads were placed back in Xiao Huaiyan's hand.

He was at something of a loss. She would not let him use her pet name. She would not take his things.

Jiang Mi curtseyed. "Your Majesty should rest. This subject will take her leave."

"Tang..." He stopped himself. "Tomorrow — "

Whatever he had been about to say, he let go of it. "Never mind. Go and rest."

Jiang Mi pressed her lashes down, curtseyed once more, and withdrew.

The moment she stepped outside, a fit of sharp, urgent coughing came from the room behind her.

Jiang Mi's step became heavier. She kept walking.

Until she could hear nothing more.

......

The coughing inside gradually subsided. Chengzhong brought tea.

Xiao Huaiyan closed his eyes and rested against the headboard, turning over in his mind each word she had said and every expression she had worn.

Something she had said stayed with him.

She had said he did not lack for people to bring medicine.

Xiao Huaiyan asked, "Did anyone come to this courtyard today with anything?"

Chengzhong startled. How had the Emperor known?

He replied with great care, "Yes, Your Majesty. Prefect Sun's daughter came to the gate with autumn pear paste and a soup to soothe the lungs. But this servant sent them away before they could enter."

Chengzhong had taken one look at the Prefect's daughter all dressed up and known exactly what she was about. But the Emperor's face was not so easily sought.

A chill came over Xiao Huaiyan's expression. "This Sun Youchang has no sense of what is and is not appropriate."

Chengzhong thought privately that the Prefect was likely about to receive a severe dressing-down.

......

The next morning Jiang Mi woke in a drowsy haze, turned over — and felt something press into her hand.

She opened her eyes. It was a string of prayer beads.

She held them up, puzzled, and called out, "Qiuyu."

Qiuyu came in quickly.

"Where did these come from?" Qiuyu had kept watch through the night; she would know if something had appeared at her pillow. If Qiuyu did not know, then Xiao Huaiyan had come again in the night.

"After you fell asleep last night, Miss — Eunuch Cheng brought these over. He said they ward off ill and settle the spirit, and since you kept being startled awake from bad dreams, I took it upon myself to place them by your pillow. And it is strange — you slept very peacefully through the whole night."

Jiang Mi turned the thought over quietly.

These were the same beads she had refused when Xiao Huaiyan offered them to her last night.

Jiang Mi rose and washed, changed into a spring gown, and drank the congee Qiuyu brought her.

Qiuyu poured her tea, and noticed the miss had been looking out the window for some time. She looked too — and saw a pair of sparrows hopping and chirping in the treetops. "Miss — would you like to go out for a walk later?"

"Have the pear blossoms opened in the east garden?"

"Yes — when the wind blows it looks like snow falling."

Jiang Mi smiled.

Before long, she was standing under the old pear tree. Qiuyu bent a branch down so Jiang Mi could pick the clean blossoms from it.

It was a mature tree, heavy with flowering branches, and before long the basket was more than half full.

When she had enough, she turned to go back.

Walking along the covered corridor, she caught pieces of a conversation between two young maids.

"I don't know why the master flew into such a rage — he sent both the Fourth Miss and the Fifth Miss off to the villa and said they're not to come back for some time."

"Strange — the master always spoils those two. I heard Madam and Lady Liu were scolded too. Anyway, let's just be careful and keep away from places we shouldn't be."

The two maids were walking quickly and disappeared around a corner before long.

Jiang Mi looked at the blossoms in her basket. She said to Qiuyu, "Let us go to the small kitchen."

Qiuyu brightened. "Miss — are you making pear blossom cakes?"

Jiang Mi rinsed the petals clean in clear water, combined her prepared ingredients, folded the petals in.

The finished cakes were pale and translucent, delicate in appearance.

Qiuyu thought they were too beautiful to eat.

"Pear blossom soothes the lungs and eases a cough," Qiuyu said. "Miss — are you going to bring these to His Majesty?"

Jiang Mi had not actually wanted to insert herself into that crowd.

But there were things that needed to be said plainly.

She picked up the food box and went to the southern garden. Chengzhong, hearing the announcement, came out to meet her with a wide smile.

"Miss Jiang — please come in."

Xiao Huaiyan saw Jiang Mi enter carrying a food box. He was genuinely surprised — he might even have called it delight.

He set down his memorials.

Jiang Mi had not expected to find him in the study working through his illness.

She curtseyed. "Long life to Your Majesty."

"No need for ceremony. Sit down."

"This subject has brought a small confection for Your Majesty." She set the small plate out from the box.

Xiao Huaiyan looked at the delicate cakes on the plate and recognised at once that they were pear blossom cakes. The smile at the corner of his mouth would not be suppressed.

He took one and tasted it.

Sweet without being cloying. A trace of floral fragrance.

That gentle sweetness dissolved on his tongue.

Xiao Huaiyan was still smiling, about to speak —

Jiang Mi reached into her sleeve, took out the prayer beads, and placed them beside the plate of cakes.

She bowed toward him. "Your Majesty saved this subject's life. A small confection is what this subject is able to offer in return. But certain things are too precious — this subject does not dare accept them, and cannot accept them. Please take them back."

The smile faded from Xiao Huaiyan's face. The sweetness in his mouth turned to something else.

She was not talking about the prayer beads. She was using the prayer beads to say what she meant to say about him.

Jiang Mi bowed again. "This subject wishes Your Majesty a swift recovery — which is a blessing for the realm."

Xiao Huaiyan's face was entirely still now. He looked at her quietly.

"There is nothing you cannot accept," he said.

Only things she was no longer willing to accept.

He walked toward her and placed his hands on her shoulders. He felt her flinch. He held himself still and said, "Tangtan. Do not be afraid of me."

chapters.title: Chapter 86
chapters.content:
How could she not be afraid?

There had been the cheap little stall in Linzhou, sitting beside him, eating wontons while watching the crowds pass by.

The solitary figure at the riverside in Xuzhou, standing in the lantern-light.

Pouring jars of plum wine together in offering to Consort Jin.

The single bowl of yangchun noodles they had split between them.

And then: walking out of the darkness, and seeing him come toward her through the light, and finding her. She could not have been unmoved in that moment.

All of it — every protection, every rescue — was real.

How could she not be afraid?

She was afraid of being unable to escape, unable to flee the warmth that had come to matter to her.

She was afraid of falling in again, and never finding a way back out.

Jiang Mi thought she would almost prefer his coercion to this — the slow grinding of a blunt blade. At least then she could not be swayed.

Without warning her body went light. He had lifted her and set her on the edge of the desk.

Jiang Mi looked at the memorials and books swept to the floor and felt a flicker of panic. Her legs pushed to slide down, but Xiao Huaiyan's hands pressed them still.

He leaned in and looked directly at her.

"Tangtan. Look at me."

Jiang Mi kept her head bowed. The position made her think, inevitably, of the things Xiao Huaiyan had done in the imperial study in her last life. And yet, strange as it was — though she felt panicked — she did not feel the same helplessness and terror she had felt then.

Xiao Huaiyan felt her silent resistance.

But if he did not make things plain, she would only retreat further next time.

He let out a quiet breath. "Tangtan — you have the courage to push me away again and again. You had the courage to face the dark alone and walk out of that passage. Why will you not look at me?"

Her lashes trembled, but her eyes stayed down.

Xiao Huaiyan took her hand. "I will not let you go. But I will not force you either. If there is something you are unwilling to accept — tell me. If you say nothing, I cannot know what you are thinking. Can we try again — the two of us?"

"Tangtan — if you truly found me so repellent, you would not have made those cakes. And that string of prayer beads — if you did not want them, you could have thrown them into the river. Why bring them back to me with your own hands?"

"Tangtan. You cannot bring yourself to let go either."

Jiang Mi was shaking badly. She raised her hands to push him away, but he wrapped his arms around her and held fast.

"Tangtan — I cannot let go either. I am unwilling to release you, and more unwilling still to hand you to anyone else."

Jiang Mi shook her head without making a sound, eyes full of grief.

She looked up. "Your Majesty is only taken with the novelty of this. There will be others in time — others Your Majesty will be equally unwilling to let go."

"There will be no one else. I only —"

He did not finish. Something came surging up from deep in his throat. He turned away, covering his mouth, coughing — and in that moment, released her.

Jiang Mi saw him turn his back to her.

But she had already seen it: the thread of red leaking between his fingers.

Jiang Mi slid down from the desk. She went toward him, and called uncertainly, "Your Majesty..."

Xiao Huaiyan forced the blood back down. "I am all right," he said calmly.

The words had barely left his mouth when the room swayed. He caught himself — and felt a slender pair of arms reach out to steady him.

......

Jiang Mi stood to one side and watched Physician Song work the needles into the acupuncture points along Xiao Huaiyan's body — long silver needles placed one by one.

When the physician withdrew them at last, Jiang Mi asked, "Physician Song — what is truly wrong with His Majesty?" She could not believe a simple wind-cold had brought him to this.

Physician Song said, "This is an old injury flaring up. When His Majesty received word of your accident, it triggered an episode. Without that — a wind-cold alone would not have felled him like this."

"Miss Jiang — you may not know this, but while His Majesty was stationed at Yunzhou, the attempts on his life — stabbings, poisonings — were too numerous to count. This old injury is what he has carried from those days. His Majesty is suspicious by nature, and I believe you may be the only person he has ever let his guard down around. I need to go and prepare another decoction. Would you be willing to keep watch over him for a little while?"

Jiang Mi sat quietly at the bedside, Xiao Huaiyan's words still turning in her head, her thoughts a tangle.

......

Xiao Huaiyan became aware of a very soft sound of breathing near his ear. He opened his eyes and saw the figure slumped asleep at the edge of his bed. Looking at her peaceful sleeping face, the ache in his chest seemed to ease.

His Tangtan — her heart was always this tender.

Not wanting to wake her, Xiao Huaiyan pulled his outer robe around himself and leaned back against the headboard. He thought: if things could always be like this.

When Jiang Mi woke and looked over, Xiao Huaiyan appeared to still be asleep — but his colour seemed somewhat better than before. The medicine had done some good.

A glance at the window told her the light was nearly golden. Dusk.

It was time to go.

Jiang Mi slipped out of the room. Chengzhong, keeping watch outside, did not dare try to detain her.

She stepped out of the courtyard and walked directly into someone.

She looked up, recognised the face, and called out, "Official Xue — a moment, please."

Xue Jingyuan had been on his way to inquire after the Emperor's old injury. He had not expected to encounter Jiang Mi here.

He stopped and clasped his hands. "Miss Jiang — what is it?"

Jiang Mi asked carefully, "Official Xue — might you know how Young Lord Xue is faring?" She had asked Su-shi, and she had asked Qiuyu, but neither of them seemed to know that Young Lord Xue was connected to the rebel conspiracy. The truth had clearly been suppressed from above — only someone close to the Emperor would know it.

Xue Jingyuan was not entirely surprised.

After Miss Jiang had woken, any trace of Xue Jinglin's existence had been quietly erased at every level. Without the Emperor's word, no one would dare tell her.

"If I am not mistaken," Xue Jingyuan said, "Miss Jiang encountered him at Yǒuyuán — you saw him in league with the rebel conspirators, and that is why he detained you?"

Jiang Mi nodded in silence.

"Then, Miss Jiang — do you hate him?"

She was startled. Did she hate him? She hated the murderous intent he had turned on her. She hated being used. She hated that the Jiang family had been drawn into it. And yet, in the end, he had left her a way out.

She could not name what she felt.
