Xue Jingyuan, seeing she did not speak, said, "For secretly harbouring the Prince of Qi's son and colluding with rebel conspirators in a plot to overthrow the throne — the traitor has been brought to justice."

Jiang Mi's feelings were a bitter tangle.

She thanked Xue Jingyuan with a bow.

Xue Jinglin had always known, she thought, that if it ever came to light, the end could only be this. But her heart went to Ningzhu — what would become of her? How much grief would she bear? Whatever Xue Jinglin had done in the world outside, however many crimes he had committed — to Ningzhu, he had only ever been her most beloved elder brother.

Jiang Mi could not help asking, "Official Xue — do you know how His Majesty intends to deal with the Duke Zhen State's manor?" Xue Jingyuan had come from that house himself — and yet he was a credited hero of this suppression.

Xue Jingyuan said, "That I do not know. Perhaps the innocent will be spared."

Jiang Mi knew she should not have asked. She thanked him again.

Xue Jingyuan did not leave immediately. He had something to say.

"Miss Jiang. I have told you the true cause of Xue Jinglin's death. Ordinarily, every crime he committed would have been proclaimed to the world — he would have been condemned before all people, and everyone associated with him drawn into it. But do you know what is being said outside? People know only that the Young Lord died at the hands of rebel conspirators. You are not the unbetrothed fiancée of a traitor. The Cheng'en Marquessate has not been implicated in any way by association with him. Your name has been kept clean."

Xue Jingyuan paused. "Does Miss Jiang understand His Majesty's intention?"

He clasped his hands and took his leave.

Jiang Mi stood where she was, her mind somewhere far away.

She did not know how she found her way back to her own courtyard.

Qiuyu had been about to go looking for her and came hurrying over. "Miss — what took you so long? It is dark already, I was worried sick." She had expected the miss to return quickly after delivering the pear blossom cakes to the Emperor.

Qiuyu saw the pallor on her face and took her arm, guided her to the daybed, and brought a cup of hot tea. "Miss — are you all right? Do you feel unwell? Shall I fetch a physician?"

Jiang Mi shook her head. "No need. I am only a little tired. I will rest."

She leaned against the daybed. As she raised her arm, she noticed something on her wrist.

The prayer beads — the ones she had returned to Xiao Huaiyan — were on her wrist again.

Jiang Mi turned the beads slowly between her fingers. She closed her eyes.

......

A day passed. Su-shi arrived with Jiang Rong.

Jiang Rong spread an assortment of snacks and confections on the table in front of Jiang Mi. "Elder Sister — try some Jinling snacks! I rather liked all of these."

Su-shi smiled. "You bought everything you liked yourself and brought it to your sister — with no idea whether your sister will like them at all."

Jiang Mi tried a piece of lily-paste pastry and said it was delicious.

Jiang Rong delightedly pushed the lotus root with osmanthus fragrance toward her. "Mother — see? If I like it, Elder Sister likes it too."

Su-shi shook her head, laughing.

She had proper business to discuss. "Tangtan — the person you asked me to find. I have brought him."

Jiang Mi brightened. "Where is he?"

"Waiting in the pavilion outside. I'll have him come in now."

Before long, Su-shi led in a clean-featured young man of around twenty.

"This is Physician Duan — Physician Gu's apprentice-brother."

The young man clasped his hands toward Jiang Mi. "Greetings, Miss. I received my senior sister's letter — may I ask what matter brings you to seek me out?"

Jiang Mi showed him the prepared incense formula and asked, "Physician Duan — Physician Gu warned me that costus root and rose dew cannot be used together. I wonder whether this formula might also have a problem?"

Physician Duan examined it carefully. "Is this formula used by the miss herself, or by another?"

"A senior member of my family."

"Does your elder often use sandalwood incense?"

Jiang Mi thought of her aunt, who spent hours each day in the small Buddhist hall, where sandalwood incense burned constantly.

"My elder has prayed at a Buddhist shrine for many years."

Physician Duan pointed to one ingredient. "The problem may be this — the purple karaya leaf. It is a fragrant ingredient from a foreign land that closely resembles the cloud-sorrel plant in appearance. Cloud-sorrel has a mild toxicity and cannot be used alongside sandalwood. If your elder has been around sandalwood incense over a long period of time, the two will clash and worsen her condition."

Jiang Mi felt her heart tighten. So that was it.

"Physician Duan — is there an antidote to cloud-sorrel's toxicity? Can the damage to the body be repaired? Would long-term use of such incense cause someone to die of illness in just a few months?"

Physician Duan considered. "Both the costus root and rose dew, and the cloud-sorrel and sandalwood — all of these require a long period of time to degrade the body. They are agents that worsen existing conditions and make them difficult to detect. Death within a few short months, as you describe, would be unlikely — unless the person already had another concealed ailment."

Having seen many such cases, and aware of his senior sister's connection with this young woman, Physician Duan offered one further observation: "If you described a person who appeared outwardly healthy, gave no visible sign of illness, suffered no sudden acute episode, and yet experienced extreme physical deterioration in just a few months — with no evidence of being poisoned by another — there is one other possibility. She may have been taking a slow-acting poison of her own will, without wishing to live."

Jiang Mi's whole body shook. That was impossible.

Her aunt had the old complaint of the heart, and those incense blends had weakened her further — that explained the frailty.

But she could not help remembering her aunt's manner in those days. Always soothing her, always assuring her that the Emperor would bring her into the palace, that she would not be mistreated. Jiang Mi had told herself: even if the Emperor did not care for her, her aunt would be there to watch over her, and life would be bearable.

Her aunt had petitioned for her admission to the palace on her deathbed.

Jiang Mi's thoughts were suddenly chaos. She began to wonder — was it possible her aunt had truly not wished to go on living?

But why?

Jiang Mi told Physician Duan, "Would you be willing to travel with me to the capital? I would like you to look after my elder's health."

Physician Duan did not refuse. "As it happens, I have business in the capital. I can come and take a look. I should warn you, though — restoring the body to health will take a great deal of time, and the damage already done cannot be fully reversed."

He added with a sigh, "The use of these incense blends should have been forbidden long ago. At one time, there was only one physician in Xuzhou who was familiar with these compounds."

"Xuzhou?"

chapters.title: Chapter 87
chapters.content:
The moment Physician Duan mentioned Xuzhou, Jiang Mi's eyelid gave a sudden twitch.

Xuzhou — the very place where Consort Jin had met her end in the tenth year of Yongshun.

Without quite knowing why, she thought suddenly of her aunt's face the day the calming incense was mentioned — that complete loss of composure.

After she saw Physician Duan out, Su-shi came back.

Su-shi had been present throughout their conversation and had grown more and more unsettled the longer she listened.

This seemed to concern the safety of the Empress Dowager herself.

Su-shi said with quiet worry, "Tangtan — this..." She was not sure whether she should ask.

Jiang Mi rose and curtseyed formally. "Madam — I have a favour to ask."

"There is no need for such ceremony," Su-shi said quickly. "Whatever it is — if I can do it, just say the word."

Jiang Mi hesitated for a moment, then said, "Madam — I would like someone to go to Xuzhou and look into a matter. The background of the fragrance physician Physician Duan mentioned — and whether anything can be found out about what happened there in the tenth year of Yongshun."

Su-shi's expression shifted. She glanced nervously around her and lowered her voice. "Tangtan — why are you digging into that?" What had happened in the tenth year of Yongshun had been a forbidden subject since the previous Emperor's reign, and it was no less so now.

"Madam, please do not alarm yourself. I know this cannot be investigated openly. Since it was suppressed at the time, there are surely very few people left who know anything. I only thought — the Su family has been in commerce for many years, and it may be possible to gather impressions from ordinary people about the late Emperor's southern journey in the tenth year of Yongshun, and the party's stopover in Xuzhou on the return. But the most important thing is simply to look into the background of that fragrance physician."

Su-shi breathed a small sigh of relief. "All right. I will have Jingchen take care of this. He has felt dreadful guilt ever since taking you to Yǒuyuán put you in harm's way. Let him make it right."

After Su-shi left, Chengzhong arrived before long.

Chengzhong bowed respectfully. "Miss Jiang — His Majesty will be returning to the capital in three days. If you have things to pack, please have them ready in advance. When the time comes, this servant will send people to help with your luggage."

Jiang Mi had not expected Xiao Huaiyan to return so quickly — he had coughed up blood and collapsed from his old injury only the day before.

She looked at the prayer beads on her wrist and asked quietly, "Eunuch Cheng — has His Majesty been taking his medicine?"

Chengzhong felt a leap of hope. "Miss — if you are worried about His Majesty, why not go and look in on him?"

Jiang Mi said nothing. She walked to the windowsill, where a crabapple branch had been placed in a vase not long before. She lifted it out of the vase and held it out to Chengzhong. "His Majesty's rooms must feel heavy. Please take this over for him. And convey to His Majesty, Eunuch Cheng, that this subject hopes he makes a swift recovery."

Chengzhong received it in both hands, consoling himself that though he had not persuaded Miss Jiang to come in person, a branch and a few words were something he could bring back.

Three days passed quickly.

Jiang Mi and the Jiang family members watched from a distance as the officials of Jiangnan came out to see Xiao Huaiyan off to his ship. He wore white imperial robes and a jade crown — noble and striking, carrying about him the faint, habitual air of cool remove.

Those long, narrow phoenix eyes swept suddenly in her direction.

Jiang Mi startled slightly and shifted her gaze elsewhere, keeping her face still.

Even so, her peripheral vision caught the faint curve at the corner of his mouth.

They waited until the crowd had dispersed before boarding their own vessel.

Su-shi was quietly thrilled to be travelling back to the capital under the protection of the imperial procession — no more fear of river pirates or accidents.

The deep sound of horns, the roll of drums, and the ships began to move away.

The return journey was calm and unhurried.

Jiang Mi stood on the deck watching the churning river, the scenery drifting past on either bank. Her state of mind was entirely different from the journey down.

At some point a kite drifted across the sky.

It flew high — just barely recognisable as a sand-swallow kite — and Jiang Mi found herself staring at it, lost in thought.

On the other side of the deck, Xiao Huaiyan had been standing quietly for some time.

He watched Jiang Mi, her skirts lifting in the river breeze, and thought she looked as though she might be carried off with the mist.

He followed her gaze up to the paper kite drifting in the sky.

Something came across his expression then — a shadow.

Among the things she had left behind in his last life, he had found a faded butterfly kite.

Her maid had told him she had treasured it since she was ten years old. In those days she had told anyone who would listen, with great happiness, that a prince had given it to her.

And that time, in the peach grove at the travelling palace, she had asked him: "Your Majesty — do you remember once giving a kite to a little girl?"

Each word was a precise blade carving into him.

He had carefully taken out that butterfly kite — and the old, fragile thing had crumbled in his hands, turning to dust, scattered by the wind.

Xiao Huaiyan felt the redness creep to the corners of his eyes, and the old pain came pressing back.

After a few breaths, he opened his eyes again and walked toward Jiang Mi.

Jiang Mi heard footsteps behind her and looked around. Seeing it was Xiao Huaiyan, she was not entirely surprised.

She was about to curtsey when he stopped her.

"What are you looking at?"

Jiang Mi shook her head. "Nothing in particular, Your Majesty."

Xiao Huaiyan looked up at the kite swaying in the wind and recited softly: "In the second month, when grass grows long and orioles fly, willow branches trail across the dike, drunk on spring haze. Children come home early from school, rushing to fly their kites while the east wind holds."

He turned and looked at her. "Tangtan — do you remember someone once giving you a kite?"

Something crossed Jiang Mi's eyes. Her fingers tightened around the handkerchief in her hand. She said slowly, "This subject... does not remember."

Xiao Huaiyan studied her for a long moment. "Very well. If you have forgotten, you have forgotten."

He took her hand. "Come with me."

Jiang Mi was led inside — into what she recognised at once as his shipboard study, memorials still piled on the desk.

She did not know what he said to Chengzhong, but an attendant came and cleared the desk.

Xiao Huaiyan spread a sheet of paper, picked up a brush, and began to draw.

Before long, a butterfly hovered on the page.

Jiang Mi watched in silence as he worked through each step — sketched the design, fitted the bamboo frame — and in a short while a butterfly kite appeared in his hands.

He held it out to her. "Do you like it? If you smile — just once — the kite is yours."

Jiang Mi's eyes stung. She drew a breath and said, "Your Majesty — I am long past being a child. I no longer want butterfly kites."

Xiao Huaiyan was quiet.

After a moment, he set the kite in her arms. His voice came out slightly lower and rougher than usual. "It does not matter. You do not have to like it."

Jiang Mi looked at the kite in her arms — identical to the one she had torn apart. Of course it was identical; they had come from the same hands. But why had he made her another? He had said himself that he did not remember.

"When we return to the capital, I intend to issue an edict to have you —"

Jiang Mi cut across him in alarm. "Your Majesty — please give this subject a little more time."

He tipped her face up toward him. "Tangtan — I have already given you time."

Since their last exchange, he had not sought her out. This was the first time they had been alone since then. He knew he could not press too hard — and yet he could not let her retreat again entirely.

Jiang Mi still shook her head.

"I can agree to wait a little longer," Xiao Huaiyan said, looking down at her. "But you must know, Tangtan — I will not let go."

Every concession he made came with a single condition: Jiang Mi could not keep running.

Jiang Mi understood perfectly what he meant.

She calculated the days in her mind. Around this time in the last life, Ruofei — the Yielding Consort — should already have reached the capital. After Xiao Huaiyan returned, he would see his maternal aunt and cousin.

How long, she wondered, would his reluctance last?

"Your Majesty — I have one more request."

"Speak."

"This subject would prefer that family and others not know for the time being."

A rather odd expression came across Xiao Huaiyan's face. He turned her words over uncertainly. "Tangtan — are you asking me to keep myself hidden from daylight?"

She did not want her family to know. She did not want outsiders to know. That meant he could not show his feelings in front of others. Could not let anyone see what she meant to him.

In public, they would have no connection at all.

And if she changed her mind, she could cut herself free of him without a trace.

But he had made a promise. If he had agreed to let her set the terms — he would have to live with them.

Besides — in this life, he would not let her enter the palace the way she had in the last.

Xiao Huaiyan thought: it was like picking up a stone only to drop it on his own foot.

He had wanted to keep Jiang Mi close. Wanted her to try again with him. He had made promises.

He pressed his tongue against his back teeth, and smiled, pleasantly and warmly. "All right. I agree."

Jiang Mi looked at his expression and felt vaguely uneasy — but she had heard him agree and quietly exhaled.

Before she had fully let that breath out, she heard him say, "I have agreed to all of that. But, Tangtan — you must at least give me something to set my mind at ease."

"Something to set your mind at ease?"

Xiao Huaiyan leaned down, breathing in the faint fragrance from her. Her clear, liquid eyes were full of puzzlement — there was something sweet and entirely unguarded about the way she looked.

One hand settled at her waist so she could not step back. He bent his head and pressed his lips to hers, light and unhurried.

He felt resistance — and released her.

Jiang Mi had not expected that this would be what he meant by setting his mind at ease.

She was so indignant her whole face went red. She shoved him away and fled from the room.

Coming out, she heard his low laughter from behind her. She looked down and found she was still holding the butterfly kite — and briefly wanted to throw it straight into the river.

Inside the room, Xiao Huaiyan's laughter faded. He rubbed his fingertips together and reminded himself, once more: be patient. A little more patient.

He could not frighten her again.

......

Late in the fourth month, the ships reached the capital.

The imperial guard led the way through the city. Officials of every rank came out to receive the Emperor.

Jiang Mi and Su-shi's party stayed in the hold and did not emerge. She could hear the unbroken waves of "Long live the Emperor" rising from outside and could imagine the sea of people it represented.

True to his word, Xiao Huaiyan had become once again that mild, distant sovereign in public — and Su-shi's party noticed nothing out of the ordinary.

Su-shi had spent the journey quietly marvelling at the Emperor's grace and consideration in allowing them to travel back with the imperial procession. She credited it entirely to the Empress Dowager.

In front of Jiang Mi she had praised the Emperor more times than Jiang Mi could count.

Jiang Mi only smiled.

Once the welcoming party had dispersed, Jiang Mi and Su-shi were assisted into the carriages the Cheng'en Marquessate had sent to collect them.

Returning to the Marquessate, she could feel the looks — pitying, sympathetic, or waiting to see what would unfold.

News of the death of Young Lord Xue of the Duke Zhen State's manor at rebel hands had reached the capital long before their return. The Duke Zhen manor had quickly sent back the betrothal gifts and dissolved the engagement.

But whispers had also begun spreading — that Jiang Mi was fated to bring ill-luck, that she had brought death to her intended husband.

The Marchioness of Cheng'en gathered Jiang Mi close and said many words of comfort, urging her to rest and not let it trouble her.

Jiang Mi returned to the Yuanzhǐ Courtyard. Though she had been gone only a few months, it felt as though years had passed.

A white shape suddenly burst from the undergrowth and came charging toward her.

Jiang Mi crouched and gathered it up. She weighed it in her arms, then tapped the little pink nose. "Mianmian — have you gotten fatter?"

Chun Hui, the maid who had stayed behind in the capital, said, "She absolutely has! Miss — Mianmian has kittens on the way."

Jiang Mi held Mianmian more carefully at once. She felt the roundness under her palm.

New life. At least that was a happy thing.

chapters.title: Chapter 88
chapters.content:
Jiang Mi finished bathing and settled on the daybed while Qiuyu dried her hair, listening as Chun Hui gave her account of what had been happening in the capital and in the household.

"After you and Madam left for Jiangnan, word came very quickly that His Majesty would be making the imperial sacrifice at the northern mountains. This servant heard that the Marquess and the Master both went to see the procession off."

Jiang Mi thought: so that was the reason Xiao Huaiyan gave for going to Jiangnan.

"After that, this servant doesn't know what happened, but soldiers arrived with imperial edicts and arrested a great many people. The Ying Duke's manor was raided and searched. The Duke and his heir were sent to the imperial prison to await His Majesty's judgment. The women of the household were all sent to the teaching ward. Anyone with any connection to the rebel conspirators met with disaster. The whole capital has been uneasy, with everyone afraid of being caught in it."

Even the telling of it made Chun Hui frightened. The Ying Duke's manor, which had once lorded itself over the eldest miss so insufferably — to have come to this. Thank heaven the eldest miss had severed that marriage when she did.

"Miss — you cannot imagine. Any family that could be linked to the conspirators, even relatives by marriage, was also investigated and held to account."

Jiang Mi was shaken too. She recalled what Xue Jingyuan had said to her: Miss Jiang — do you understand His Majesty's intention?

She closed her eyes.

In the last life, after years of consolidating power in Yunzhou, Xiao Huaiyan had risen on the pretext of removing treacherous elements. Among the great families of the capital, many had placed their bets on the Prince of Qi or the Prince of Jin. He had been swift and generous in absorbing and pacifying the court — but within the noble houses, hidden loyalties to the rebel factions would always be a danger. He was using this suppression to purge them.

Young Lord Xue had privately harboured the Prince of Qi's son, established Yǒuyuán in Jinling as a source of funding for the conspirators, and participated directly in a plot to seize the throne. The death penalty was inescapable — and the Duke Zhen State's manor would likely share the fate of the Ying Duke's manor, along with the Jiang family.

Chun Hui, noticing the miss had gone quiet, kept back what she had not dared say aloud: that when news of the Young Lord's death at rebel hands reached the capital, she had thought — what is to become of the miss now?

Not wanting to bring up painful things, Chun Hui moved on to lighter matters — which household had welcomed a new daughter-in-law, which family had welcomed a new child.

Jiang Mi said, "Tell me what has been happening in the household."

Chun Hui hesitated and said, "A few days ago — Second Miss and — and the son of the Assistant Minister of Revenue — they were betrothed..."

Jiang Mi slowly opened her eyes. "That is good news. Sister Yi has found a good match."

Chun Hui felt the sting of it on the miss's behalf. The eldest miss had once had a fine match of her own — and now she carried the name of one who brought ill-fortune to her husbands.

Jiang Mi called Xia Ruo and asked her to go to the storeroom and select a few suitable gifts to send over to her cousin-sister first thing in the morning.

Jiang Mi's hair was nearly dry. Qiuyu was helping her pin it up when one of the small maids came to announce, "Miss — the Master is here."

Jiang Mi tidied herself and went out to greet the man drinking tea in the main hall. "Father."

Jiang Qingxuan said, "Come and sit."

In the two or three months since he had last seen her, Jiang Qingxuan thought Tangtan looked thinner. He had learned about her ordeal in Jinling through Su-shi's letters. He had been furious — what had the Su family been thinking, allowing her to go somewhere like that and nearly losing her life?

And then had come the news of Young Lord Xue's death. He had not known how to comfort her.

"Tangtan — pay no attention to the gossip outside. Just rest and take care of yourself."

Jiang Qingxuan slid a rosewood box across the table toward her. "This is the Su family's compensation to you. Your mother asked me before daring to pass it on."

Jiang Mi opened it. A box full of silver notes and land deeds.

She pushed it back. "Father — I cannot accept this." Her accident had been unforeseeable even from the Su family's side. All they knew was the fiction Xiao Huaiyan's people had constructed — that she had gone over a cliff and been found by a passing couple.

Jiang Qingxuan said, "Take it. Their conscience will not rest until you do. Keep it to add to your dowry."

He paused, then said carefully, "Your affairs — your father will keep watch. I will not allow you to be treated unfairly."

Jiang Mi felt a sting at the back of her throat. "Father — I do not mind. If this were to damage my sisters' names and prospects, I would rather go to the family temple..."

Jiang Qingxuan said sharply, "Nonsense. Your eldest sister withdrew from a marriage and can still be matched again. You were only engaged. Idle gossip is the work of small people — do not let it into your heart. Do not ever speak of that again."

Jiang Mi was rarely permitted to see her father's emotions show so plainly.

Jiang Qingxuan considered for a moment, then said what he had to say: "Your aunt's health has been declining. She sleeps more often than not now. You may be summoned into the palace tomorrow."

Jiang Mi had intended to send in a request to visit the palace herself the following morning. She had brought Physician Duan back from Jiangnan precisely to have him examine her aunt.

When she had left the capital, her aunt had seemed all right. How had she deteriorated so quickly in such a short time?

......

The next day, Mama Cui came to the Cheng'en Marquessate and conveyed the summons.

Jiang Mi told Mama Cui she wished to bring someone into the palace to see the Empress Dowager.

Mama Cui met with Physician Duan, and hearing that Miss Jiang had gone out of her way to find him in Jiangnan, she decided — though it was not customary to bring male physicians into the inner palace — that the Empress Dowager's condition left little choice.

As they neared the Ci'ning Palace, Jiang Mi saw a group of people coming out from inside.

She stopped when she recognised them.

At the front walked a handsome woman of middle age, with a slender, willowy young woman beside her.

They had noticed Jiang Mi's group as well, and looked with mild curiosity.

Mama Cui, standing beside Jiang Mi, explained, "Miss — that is His Majesty's maternal aunt, Lady Liu, and her daughter, Miss Shūróu."

Jiang Mi stepped forward and curtseyed. "Lady Liu. Miss Shū."

Lady Liu gave a gracious nod. The young woman leaning on her maid's arm returned the courtesy.

Lady Liu's manner was warm and pleasant. She said to Jiang Mi, "You must be the niece the Empress Dowager is so fond of. We have come at an inconvenient time — Her Highness has not yet woken. When Her Highness is feeling better, Róu'er and I will come again to pay our respects."

Lady Liu then led Shūróu and the rest of their party away.

Jiang Mi continued toward the Ci'ning Palace without comment. She had known she would encounter Shūróu again.

Only she had not expected it to be quite so soon.

Mama Cui quietly watched the miss's expression — which remained entirely composed throughout — and said, "Lady Liu and Miss Shū arrived in the capital some days ago. Her Highness received them once when she was feeling well enough, but since her condition worsened she has not been seeing visitors. His Majesty had not yet returned when the Worthy Dowager Consort invited Lady Liu and Miss Shū to stay as guests in the palace. They are presently lodged at the Lǎnyuè Pavilion."

......

On the other side, Shūróu glanced back over her shoulder and said to her mother, "So that is the Jiang Mi Princess An'yang always talks about. I did not expect her to look like that."

Lady Liu smiled. "That Miss Jiang is beautiful, certainly. Are you worried you cannot compare?"

Shūróu covered her lips with her handkerchief, her voice low. "I know Cousin does not care for women who are precious and affected. No matter how beautiful she is — she cannot compare to the years of closeness Cousin and I share."

Lady Liu laughed softly. Her eyes moved toward the Qianqing Palace. "That is true. His Majesty's feelings for you are different. Know it yourself, but do not let it make you jealous of things you need not be jealous of. His Majesty has no fondness for Miss Jiang — and she has a dead fiancé to her name. She will not be an obstacle. I only hope His Majesty finishes his pressing business soon and finds time to grant us an audience."

Shūróu blushed and protested, "Mother — I am not in any hurry."

Lady Liu said, "You are, and you know it. My sense is that once His Majesty has settled the matter of the rebel traitors, he will be choosing an Empress and taking consorts. You may not be able to take the Empress position — but you should hold at least a Noble Consort's rank. To have the Emperor's care and protection for life — that would ease my mind greatly."

Shūróu felt a small pang of regret at that, but the thought of remaining at her cousin's side was enough to make her heart content.

......

In the Ci'ning Palace, the palace staff spoke and walked softly, afraid of disturbing the Empress Dowager's rest.

Jiang Mi kept watch at the bedside.

When Empress Dowager Jiang opened her eyes, she found Jiang Mi slumped asleep against the edge of the bed.

She moved her lips. A thin voice: "Tangtan..."

Jiang Mi's eyes opened at once. Seeing her aunt awake, she said quickly, "Aunt — do not speak yet. First drink some water."

She helped her aunt take a few sips of warm water.

Empress Dowager Jiang lay back, looking at Jiang Mi. "Tangtan — is this aunt dreaming?"

Jiang Mi shook her head. "No. Tangtan has come back."

The Empress Dowager settled with a look of deep relief. "Back safely. That is all that matters."

Jiang Mi's eyes reddened. "Aunt knows to hope for Tangtan's safety — so why does Aunt not care for her own?"

The Empress Dowager had never seen gentle Tangtan look at her with something approaching anger.

She was very weak, and speaking cost her effort.

Jiang Mi fed her a little congee, and that helped.

Jiang Mi sent the attending palace staff out of the room. She wiped her aunt's brow and said, "Aunt — why have you done this? Why would you take cinnabar? What has happened that you would throw your own life away?"

The Empress Dowager was silent.

Jiang Mi was not willing to let her retreat from this anymore. She also needed to know, finally, what crime the Jiang family had truly committed.

She pressed forward. "Aunt — is the Jiang family connected to the death of Consort Jin? What did the Jiang family do in the tenth year of Yongshun?"

Even if there was guilt — she wanted to understand it plainly.

chapters.title: Chapter 89
chapters.content:
Xiao Huaiyan came up the steps and glanced at the man kneeling outside the door.

Physician Duan, his head bowed, felt a chill at the back of his neck. He thought: these are not easy people to serve.

Xiao Huaiyan did not pause but went directly inside. The eunuch supervisors and attendants behind him stayed back at the threshold.

From behind the screen came the sound of broken sobbing, soft and wretched.

Xiao Huaiyan walked past the screen and saw the slender figure hunched over the bedside — and something in him was brought instantly back to the last life.

Then, too, the Empress Dowager had been gravely ill. Then, too, Jiang Mi had been sitting at the bedside, crying quietly.

And the Empress Dowager, even at the very end, had not forgotten to take one last measure — to press one last of the Jiang family's daughters into his inner palace.

When he had agreed, the girl had looked up at him through her tears — timid and bewildered, soft and helpless.

Xiao Huaiyan pressed down the pain. He called, "Tangtan."

Jiang Mi turned slowly. Her eyes were filled with tears, just as they had been in that other life.

Xiao Huaiyan bent forward, hand reaching.

Jiang Mi flinched as though stung, and threw her arm out sharply.

They were very close. She moved fast. Her fingernail caught his face and drew a thin line of red across his cheek.

Both of them went still.

Xiao Huaiyan's expression did not change. Jiang Mi's eyes filled with fear.

His gaze darkened. He caught her hand and said in a mild voice, "Do not worry. I have already sent for the physician Zhang. I will find a way to help the Empress Dowager recover."

Jiang Mi was still trying to pull her hand back. "Thank you, Your Majesty."

He did not let go. "I will first have Chief Physician Gu come to attend to the Empress Dowager. The physician you brought — if you trust him, he may remain as well. But — you cannot be cold with me."

Jiang Mi looked up, expression complicated. "Your Majesty — you made a promise."

"The Empress Dowager has not woken. I have not broken my word."

Mama Cui came in just then with tea. Jiang Mi shoved Xiao Huaiyan away in a panic.

Mama Cui entered and noticed the Emperor standing at the bedside, quite close to the young miss — though both were looking toward the Empress Dowager. There was something in the atmosphere she could not quite name.

She reflected quietly that since returning from Jiangnan, His Majesty had remained entirely in the outer court. Coming to the inner palace at all, let alone directly to the Ci'ning Palace — that was remarkable.

If Her Highness knew, it would bring her great comfort, surely.

But when Mama Cui stepped forward to present the tea and the Emperor turned his head, she nearly dropped the cup.

There was a scratch on the Emperor's face. How had that happened?

Mama Cui kept her eyes carefully lowered.

At that moment Jiang Mi spoke. "His Majesty has ten thousand matters of state pressing upon him. This subject will care well for her aunt."

Xiao Huaiyan had the cup of tea but had not yet drunk from it. He heard the meaning in her words. She was trying to send him away.

So determined to keep him hidden that even her aunt's own attendant could not be allowed to notice?

He could not let himself be seen to show any trace of feeling?

He had given her his word, and he would hold to it. Besides — in this life, he would not allow her to enter the palace the way she had in the last.

Xiao Huaiyan set the cup down. "The Empress Dowager's condition came on suddenly and severely. I am deeply concerned. I would be more at ease if I could see her take her medicine."

With that, he settled himself nearby and had Chief Physician Gu sent for.

Gu Tanghai's language was considerably more guarded than Physician Duan's — he would not presume to make a direct statement about the Empress Dowager's condition.

Xiao Huaiyan had both Gu Tanghai and the waiting Physician Duan write a combined prescription and prepare the medicine together.

Jiang Mi watched Xiao Huaiyan move through all of this and thought he would grow impatient and leave in displeasure. She had not expected him to stay.

She glanced at him. Their eyes met. Her gaze skimmed over the mark on his cheek and moved away.

Before long, Qingxue brought the medicine and curtseyed. "Your Majesty, Miss — this is the combined prescription from Chief Physician Gu and Physician Duan. It should be given to Her Highness now."

Jiang Mi reached for the bowl, meaning to ask Qingxue to help prop up the Empress Dowager while she fed it.

Xiao Huaiyan stepped over. The sound of "Tang —" had barely begun to form on his tongue when he met a pair of wide, alarmed eyes.

He gave a quiet click of his tongue and changed course: "Miss Jiang — hold the Empress Dowager. I will give the medicine."

Spoonful by slow spoonful, the medicine went in. Jiang Mi followed alongside, dabbing at the Empress Dowager's lips with a cloth whenever any spilled. She looked at Xiao Huaiyan several times, biting back the urge to say she could do it herself.

Fortunately, the bowl was nearly empty.

Jiang Mi helped ease the Empress Dowager back against her pillows and tucked the quilt.

Seeing the tiredness on Jiang Mi's face, Xiao Huaiyan said, "Miss Jiang should rest when she is tired. I will come to see... Her Highness, when I have an opportunity."

Without waiting for her to curtsey, he walked out.

......

Li Fu had expected the Emperor to make only a brief visit. He had not imagined he would stay so long.

When he finally saw that figure emerge, Li Fu hurried forward — and with his sharp eyes caught the mark on the Emperor's face instantly. He was inwardly appalled. Who had been injured? Who had dared injure the Emperor?

Xiao Huaiyan gave Li Fu a cool look. Li Fu bent his head immediately and called for the imperial palanquin.

Back in the imperial study, Xiao Huaiyan finished the remaining memorials and summoned Pei Chi.

Pei Chi came in, bowed — and the surprise showed briefly in his eyes before he composed himself. He said, "Your Majesty — the person has been found."

Xiao Huaiyan's vermilion brush paused. He nodded. "Keep watch. Continue following the trail."

Pei Chi thought of the subject of his investigation, and of the threads of evidence turning up — each one more difficult to believe than the last. They reached back to what had happened in the tenth year of Yongshun.

He did not know what sort of plan the Emperor intended to make.

As the Emperor's instrument, Pei Chi had never asked why. He only received orders and carried them out.

As he passed Li Fu on his way out, he remarked, without particular intent, "Did His Majesty go to the training ground today?"

Li Fu was momentarily startled, then understood what Pei Chi was asking about.

He shook his head. "The guards at the training ground could not touch a hair on His Majesty."

Pei Chi said no more and walked away.

Li Fu watched him go. Even Commander Pei had noticed the mark — and not dared ask a single question.

That scratch was shallow, nothing more than a surface graze. On any ordinary person it would be entirely unremarkable — perhaps a quarrel with one's wife, perhaps a brush against something in passing.

But this was the Emperor. Who could possibly have the audacity?

And how was it that the Emperor was willing to let it go?

......

In the Changchun Palace, the Worthy Dowager Consort was hosting Lady Liu and Shūróu warmly.

"The palace is quiet," she said. "There have been no new arrivals for some time. I do hope His Majesty moves swiftly to name an Empress and take consorts. I have taken a great liking to Miss Shū from the first moment I saw her — what a beauty, and so accomplished and refined. You can see at a glance that she is a woman of fortune. This palace and she are meant for each other."

Shūróu sat demurely beside Lady Liu, colour rising in her cheeks.

Lady Liu demurred graciously. "Dowager Consort flatters her too much. If you keep praising her like this, the child will not know what to do with herself. There are so many noble daughters in the capital — Shūróu hardly compares."

"You are too modest, Lady Liu. On the strength of your connection to His Majesty alone, which of the capital's noble daughters could claim precedence? His Majesty is the most filially devoted of sons — you and the late Empress Yīzhēn were sisters, and the resemblance is striking. The bond is different from anyone else's."

Lady Liu only smiled. She could not very well respond to that.

The Worthy Dowager Consort thought: after ascending the throne, the Emperor had posthumously elevated his birth mother Consort Jin to the title Empress Yīzhēn, and had shown great favour to his mother's family. Lady Liu bringing her daughter to the capital must have her sights set firmly on a position among the imperial consorts.

With the Xie family having no daughter to offer, cultivating good ties with the Liu family was entirely advantageous.

At that moment, one of the Worthy Dowager Consort's senior palace maids came in and bowed. "Dowager Consort — His Majesty visited the Ci'ning Palace and attended to the Empress Dowager himself. He is said to have personally fed Her Highness her medicine."

The moment the words landed, the expressions in the room shifted slightly.

His Majesty had been occupied entirely with the outer court since returning from Jiangnan, and had not yet called on Lady Liu and Shūróu. And now, stepping into the inner palace for the first time — he had gone straight to the Ci'ning Palace.

There was something worth considering in that.

The Worthy Dowager Consort said coldly, "That side has only managed to claim the name of adoptive mother, and by chance alone. If Empress Yīzhēn were still here, there would be no occasion for those Jiang people at all."

Lady Liu felt some sourness of her own. By rights, His Majesty ought to have summoned her and Shūróu first — they were his own maternal kin.

She remembered that, in the past, His Majesty had hardly mentioned the Empress Dowager at all. From what she had heard in those days, the Emperor was supposed to have no love for the Jiang family. Even after his accession, whatever regard he showed that adoptive mother was surely only the appearance of propriety.

So why had he personally fed her medicine?

Lady Liu withdrew with Shūróu, her thoughts troubled.

The Worthy Dowager Consort saw them out to the palace gate and offered words of comfort. "Lady Liu need not worry — perhaps His Majesty will call on you tomorrow. Your stay at the Lǎnyuè Pavilion puts you close at hand."

Lady Liu smiled. "Many thanks for the good word, Dowager Consort."

On the walk back to the Lǎnyuè Pavilion, Shūróu noticed her mother's expression and asked, "Mother — what is wrong? Is it because Cousin has not called on us yet?"

Lady Liu shook her head. "It is not that."

She had no real grievance at not yet being summoned. What puzzled her was the Emperor's attitude toward the Jiang family.

......

In the Ci'ning Palace, the palace staff moved in careful quiet.

Jiang Mi kept her vigil at the Empress Dowager's bedside.

When Empress Dowager Jiang opened her eyes, the first thing she saw was Jiang Mi, slumped asleep at the edge of the bed.

Her lips moved. A faint whisper: "Tangtan..."

Jiang Mi's eyes opened at once. Seeing her aunt was awake, she said quickly, "Aunt — do not speak yet. Drink a little water first."

She helped the Empress Dowager take a few sips of warm water.

The Empress Dowager eased. She looked at Jiang Mi. "Tangtan — is this aunt dreaming?"

Jiang Mi shook her head. "No. Tangtan has come back."

The Empress Dowager lay down again. Her expression softened with relief. "Back safely. That is what matters."

Jiang Mi's eyes reddened. "Aunt knows to care about Tangtan's safety — then why does Aunt not care for her own life?"

It was the first time the Empress Dowager had ever seen her gentle, mild Tangtan say something so close to a reproach.

She was very weak. Speaking was an effort.

Jiang Mi fed her a little congee. That helped somewhat.

She sent the palace attendants from the room and wiped her aunt's brow. Then she said, "Aunt — why have you done this? Why take cinnabar? What could be so terrible that you would throw your life away?"

The Empress Dowager was silent.

Jiang Mi was not willing to let her go on avoiding it. And she had to know what crime the Jiang family had truly committed.

She pressed on. "Aunt — is the Jiang family connected to the death of Consort Jin? What happened in the tenth year of Yongshun?"

Guilty or not — she wanted to understand it clearly.

(TL: this last part seems to be a repeat of another scene, but that is how the author placed it, so...)

chapters.title: Chapter 90
chapters.content:
The Empress Dowager heard, once again, those pressing questions. What had truly happened in the tenth year of Yongshun?

She had intended to carry this secret with her to the grave.

But looking into Jiang Mi's clear, earnest eyes — she could not quite bring herself to do it.

The Empress Dowager let out a long sigh. "Tangtan — knowing will not be a blessing for you. Not knowing, and you will live more lightly."

Jiang Mi said, "Aunt — I want to know. I want to understand, clearly and honestly, where the Jiang family went wrong. Even if there is guilt — running from it is no answer."

The Empress Dowager listened to these guileless words and gave a quiet, bitter smile.

Her gaze drifted unfocused toward the canopy of the bed, her thoughts far away.

The late Emperor's inner palace had been full of beautiful women. He showered favour on the Noble Consort, showed consideration for the Virtuous Consort, and brought in fresh faces through the triennial selection.

One beauty in particular had come from Jiangnan — the Lady Liu, delicate and lovely, her waist willowy, speaking in the soft lilt of the south. She had captured the Emperor's heart swiftly and completely. Within a year of arriving she had become pregnant, and after delivering a prince she was raised to a consort title.

Under her care, the prince grew sharp and precocious, outstanding in the schoolroom at only five years old, leaving the other princes looking dim by comparison. The late Emperor often said the boy was just like himself.

In those days Consort Jin had favour, had a son — she was by any measure flourishing.

A murkiness came into the Empress Dowager's clouded eyes — something that might have been old envy.

Jiang Mi saw her aunt drift and a tear slip down her face. She reached to wipe it away. The Empress Dowager turned her head.

"Tangtan — you truly want to know?"

Jiang Mi nodded, steadily.

The Empress Dowager began, her voice slow and measured. "In the early spring of the tenth year of Yongshun, the late Emperor announced a southern tour. The Noble Consort, the Virtuous Consort, the Third Prince, the Fourth Prince, and others were all on the itinerary — and Consort Jin and her prince were included as well. Consort Jin had always been respectful toward this Empress — she came often to pay her respects, and she knew that this Empress had long relied on a particular calming incense to help with sleep. In those weeks she had been sleeping poorly. Worried she might not be able to attend properly to the Emperor during the journey, she came to ask for some of this incense to take with her on the ship."

"This calming incense was a familiar formula — nothing precious about it. Seeing how worried she looked, I gave her some."

Looking back on it now, the Empress Dowager thought of Consort Jin in those days — happy, one hand resting at her waist as she left. It had stung, watching her go like that, so full of good fortune. And so the Empress Dowager had said nothing — no word of caution.

Being chosen to travel with the imperial procession was a mark of favour — but it also carried risks, particularly for a woman who had concealed a pregnancy. The palace had so many eyes; she may have believed she had hidden it well, but she had already become a target.

She had thought at worst the child would not survive. She had never imagined the woman herself would die in that beloved Jiangnan.

Jiang Mi held her breath and listened, understanding as the account unfolded: the calming incense must have been connected to what happened to Consort Jin.

The Empress Dowager continued. "The tour passed without incident. The late Emperor enjoyed Jiangnan enormously — all the consorts in attendance received gifts — and on the return journey, the party stopped at Xuzhou. Consort Jin's own younger sister had married into Xuzhou, and Consort Jin missed her. She petitioned the Emperor to have her sister brought to see her. Such a small thing — of course he agreed, and not only had her brought, but allowed her to stay in the garden residence for a few days so the sisters could spend time together. No one could have foreseen that disaster would come from Xuzhou."

The Empress Dowager paused, her breath coming slowly. "I could never have imagined that what happened to Consort Jin would involve this Empress and the Jiang family in any way."

"From what I know: that day, the prince had just returned from archery practice and encountered the late Emperor in the garden. He invited the Emperor to come with him to visit his mother. The Emperor was fond of the boy and had been meaning to see Consort Jin — so they went together. When they arrived, the serving maids who should have been waiting outside had all been sent away. And from inside the room came certain sounds."

"The young prince was eager to see his mother. He pushed open the door. The late Emperor followed him inside — and found Consort Jin with a man, in the most compromising situation. The Emperor's fury was immense. He had both of them dragged from the bed."

"Under interrogation, the man insisted he and Consort Jin had been conducting an affair — that they had been overcome by feeling when they met. Consort Jin wept and denied it. She said she did not know this man at all — that she had fallen into a very deep sleep, and by the time she realised something was wrong she had been unable to resist. She cried that someone had done this to her, that she could never have betrayed the Emperor, that she had been framed. Unable to bear the dishonour, Consort Jin took her own life before the Emperor and her own son."

"Consort Jin died to prove her innocence. The Emperor saw the blood on her skirts and realised for the first time that she had been with child. This shook his certainty enough that he ordered an investigation. First, the imperial physicians examined the incense she had been burning — and pronounced it ordinary calming incense, nothing unusual. Then the food she had consumed that day was examined — also nothing. There was no sign of drugging."

"The serving maids who had been sent away had all departed for reasons that seemed perfectly legitimate, all merely coincidental. The man turned out to be a palace guard. At this point the Emperor began to doubt Consort Jin again."

"The only reason the prince survived was that he had the Emperor's face."

"Two of Consort Jin's personal palace maids did not trust the physicians' verdict. They took the remaining incense and brought it to a local physician who specialised in fragrances and asked him to examine it. That physician gave an entirely different verdict from the imperial doctors: the incense had been altered. Though it looked like ordinary calming incense, something had been added that would cause the user to sleep far more deeply than usual and to become dependent on it. Long-term use would damage the body."

Jiang Mi's voice trembled. "Aunt — was the calming incense the one you gave her?"

The Empress Dowager looked at her. "I did give Consort Jin calming incense. But it was meant only to aid sleep — it would not cause a sleep so deep. Tangtan — if I tell you I added nothing to it, will you believe me?"

She did not wait for Jiang Mi to answer. She shook her head herself. "No one would believe it. At the time Consort Jin's personal maid did not believe it, and was going to take the incense and that physician to present her findings before the Emperor. Your great-uncle happened to be among the Emperor's travelling party. He knew what was happening. Afraid it would implicate this Empress and the Jiang family, he had the maid and the physician silenced. With those two gone, no one remained who knew that Consort Jin had come to this Empress to ask for calming incense."

Jiang Mi felt as though her four limbs had been submerged in ice water. She was shaking.

And yet the evidence that might have proved Consort Jin's words — that could have vindicated her — was gone.

The Empress Dowager, having said all of this, grew visibly more exhausted. "At that time, the Noble Consort and the Virtuous Consort were both waiting for this Empress to make a mistake, so they could pull her down from her position. Had the matter of the calming incense come to light, everyone would have assumed it was this Empress's doing. I had no son — with Consort Jin dead, it would have been entirely natural for this Empress to take in her prince. Regardless of whether the incense was altered or not, the suspicion alone would have dragged this Empress into it. So to avoid that appearance of guilt, I did not come forward to ask for the prince. He stayed for a time in the Worthy Consort's palace, then moved to the princes' quarters on his own."

Jiang Mi felt the cold seeping through her. So this was the secret her aunt and great-uncle had been carrying.

Xiao Huaiyan's birth mother had died in such a brutal way. And Jiang Mi's great-uncle had silenced the women who might have proven her innocent.

How could he not hate the Jiang family?

Jiang Mi said in pain, "Aunt — is this the reason you and great-uncle always wanted me to enter the palace? Because the moment His Majesty learned the truth, he could never forgive the Jiang family, could never forgive me —"

All the scenes of her last life came rushing back. "Aunt — why did you ever think that giving His Majesty a woman would make up for any of this? I could not protect the Jiang family. I was never able to protect them..."

The Empress Dowager said, "That incense was not my doing. Consort Jin was not killed by this Empress. The chain of cause and consequence — I am willing to accept it all. Tangtan — this aunt had thought that a body already breaking down had nothing left to live for. Better to offer a life in return."

"You are so good, and so gentle. Staying beside His Majesty, you would eventually soften his heart. Even if he learned the truth later, he might show leniency toward the Jiang family for your sake. The Jiang family did not harm Consort Jin. This Empress did not harm her either. If the Noble Consort and Virtuous Consort had used the incense matter to direct suspicion toward this Empress, it would have been the same ruin for the Jiang family at that time too. What your great-uncle did was out of self-preservation — truly with no other choice."

Jiang Mi felt wave after wave of cold pass through her. From childhood her aunt had been good to her — watching over her, spoiling her, teaching her things, always the first person to think of her when something new and lovely appeared. Her aunt had been like a mother to her. And all that tenderness, all those careful lessons in how to be pleasing, all those quiet instructions on how to attract the Emperor's attention — had it all been, at its root, an attempt to appease Xiao Huaiyan's hatred? To preserve the Jiang family?

The Empress Dowager raised a trembling hand, trying to reach Jiang Mi's face to wipe her tears. She murmured, "Tangtan — do not cry. This aunt has wronged you. This aunt has made you suffer. This illness of mine — there is no point in treating it..."

Jiang Mi's eyes were filled with grief.

She turned her face away. She rose and drew the quilt up over her aunt and said quietly, "Aunt — do not think like that. You must get better. Did you and great-uncle do nothing more to investigate what happened in those days?"

The Empress Dowager said, "The late Emperor's fury made it a forbidden subject. That garden was sealed. Those who had attended Consort Jin all died one by one in the following years — as if in devotion to their mistress. Every trail went cold. To investigate further would only have alerted the Noble Consort and Virtuous Consort." Even in later years, when fragments of evidence emerged — that the palace guard had been arranged by the Noble Consort, that the serving maids outside had been sent away by the Virtuous Consort — the incense itself remained unexplained. It was never known whose hands had altered it.

Jiang Mi could not help wondering: had Xiao Huaiyan, in his last life, known? How much had he known?

When the Jiang family was later exposed and brought down — stripped of their title and rank, reduced to commoners, but their lives spared — she thought of that, and could not read him.

Xiao Huaiyan — what were you thinking?

chapters.title: Chapter 91
chapters.content:
Xiao Huaiyan sat at the bedside and watched Jiang Mi sleep — restlessly, fitfully.

Her lips were moving. She seemed to be murmuring something.

Every so often came a small, stifled sob.

Xiao Huaiyan gently touched her forehead and waited for her to settle.

Jiang Mi knew she had fallen into a dream. She dreamed that Xiao Huaiyan was going to lead the campaign in person, and she wanted to see him off.

She had only just recovered from her illness — still weak and unsteady, she leaned on Qiuyu and had barely made it out of Héngwú Palace before she was breathless.

She stood looking at the palace wall, grieving that she could not go to him in person.

When she turned in disappointment, she found him striding toward her, already in his armour.

His face was cold. He swept her up without a word and said sternly, "You have barely recovered and you are already running around. Do you think you have not drunk enough medicine?"

But she had been happy then. He had not yet left.

He carried her back inside. She took a sachet from beside her pillow and held it out to him. "Your Majesty — please come home safely."

She had been so anxious, terrified he would not accept it.

And then the weight in her hand was gone. He had taken it.

She looked up and found him saying: "Rest and get your strength back. Wait for me to return."

His gaze held something complicated. She had always felt that he meant to say more.

She could only watch as his figure grew smaller and smaller in the distance.

What had he wanted to say?

She had wanted to call out to him — I may not be here when you return. What was it you still wanted to say?

Jiang Mi opened her eyes slowly — and found, sitting at her bedside, the very person she had been trying to call back in her dream.

She was not sure yet whether she was awake.

Xiao Huaiyan asked, "Did you have a nightmare? What were you dreaming about?"

Jiang Mi said, half to herself, "You."

An unreadable expression crossed Xiao Huaiyan's face.

"Is that so? What did you dream about me?"

Jiang Mi closed her eyes and thought for a moment. "I dreamed that Your Majesty told me to wait for you to return — but you had not finished speaking before you left. I wanted to ask what else it was you wanted to say."

Xiao Huaiyan's eyes went very still. His throat felt tight. He said in a low, roughened voice, "Wait for me to come back — and we should have had a child by then."

Jiang Mi laughed softly. "Your Majesty is teasing. The Empress has not even entered the palace — how could a consort be with child first."

"And if you were the Empress?"

She laughed again, her voice quiet. "Your Majesty is telling stories. That could never happen."

She still had her eyes closed, and murmured the words again: Your Majesty is telling stories.

A warmth pressed close. Her lips were taken in a kiss — deep and unhurried, swallowing the words she had just spoken.

The breath was stolen from her. Her fingers were locked between his.

She felt as though she were being drowned, pulled under by still water. She could barely breathe.

Then she was released all at once. Jiang Mi parted her lips and drew in air.

A warm breath still lingered at her throat. "I am not telling stories, Tangtan."

She appeared to fall asleep again. Xiao Huaiyan watched her for a while, tucked the quilt around her, and walked out.

In the still of the night, when the footsteps outside had long faded, Jiang Mi opened her eyes.

The pet name — Tangtan — brought her gradually back to herself. The Xiao Huaiyan who had appeared in her dream would never call her that. She lay with something unresolved turning in her chest. Why had he answered on the dream's behalf?

......

Word spread through the palace that the Kūnníng Palace was undergoing repairs and renovation.

It meant the Emperor was on the verge of selecting an Empress. The Kūnníng Palace would soon have a new mistress.

The palace and the outer court alike were full of speculation about which family the new Empress would come from.

Petitions urging the Emperor to name an Empress and take consorts had been submitted — and this time the Emperor had not dismissed them as quickly as before.

Jiang Mi heard the palace maids discussing it in the Ci'ning Palace.

Something about it felt odd. In her last life, the Kūnníng Palace had not been renovated at this time — Consort Duān, Consort Rúo, and the others had entered the palace one after another instead.

She had not seen Gu Xuan since that night they drank together — she wondered whether Gu Xuan had returned to the capital. And Shūróu was already staying in the palace. If things followed the pattern of the last life, she would soon be made Noble Consort Róu.

Perhaps because Xiao Huaiyan's journey south to suppress the rebellion had taken up time, the schedule was running later than it had in the last life.

Jiang Mi looked at the flower petals scattered across the ground by the rain and let the thought drift away.

She gave no weight to what Xiao Huaiyan had said. It was not what she was afraid of.

What she truly worried about was the Jiang family. She did not know how much Xiao Huaiyan had learned, or what could be done to protect them. Counting the days, the Su family's letter should be coming soon. She wondered whether Su Jingchen had found anything.

She carried the medicine into the Empress Dowager's chamber.

Empress Dowager Jiang had woken a little earlier than yesterday and was resting against her pillows. Jiang Mi helped her take the medicine and they sat together for a while.

Mama Cui came in to announce: "Your Highness — Princess An'yang and Miss Shū have come to pay their respects."

The Empress Dowager said tiredly, "Tangtan — go and receive them for me. I am weary."

Jiang Mi went to the flower hall, where Princess An'yang and Shūróu were talking. Maids came forward with tea.

Shūróu was listening patiently when the smile on An'yang's face suddenly stopped, and she directed a cool look at whoever had just entered.

Shūróu turned. A beautiful woman in moon-white skirts walked in, moving with effortless grace. Her eyes came to rest on that exquisite face — and she recognised the Empress Dowager's niece, the Jiang girl.

She could not account for it, but from the first moment she had seen this young woman — only once — she had felt an inexplicable hostility toward her.

Jiang Mi curtseyed. "Your Highness, Miss Shū — the Empress Dowager has fallen asleep. I will ask you both to return another time."

Princess An'yang stood. "Is Her Highness any better? I have not been able to see Her Highness these past days and I am quite worried."

Jiang Mi was mildly surprised at An'yang's manner — she had braced herself for sharp words. "Her Highness's illness still requires rest and quiet."

An'yang turned to Shūróu. "Since Her Highness is not allowing visitors, we shall have to come back another time."

As she passed Jiang Mi, An'yang gave a thin, cold smile.

But Shūróu had not moved. Her eyes were locked on the string of beads at Jiang Mi's wrist.

Under that intense gaze Jiang Mi felt deeply uncomfortable. She slipped her wrist behind her sleeve.

Shūróu stepped forward, apparently forgetting An'yang entirely. "Miss Jiang — might I see those prayer beads for a moment?"

Jiang Mi frowned slightly. She had no wish to involve herself with Shūróu. "I am afraid these have been blessed with temple incense, Miss Shū — it would not be appropriate for others to handle them."

At those words, something seemed to hit Shūróu — she went very still, as if she could not quite take in what she had heard.

An'yang, growing impatient, recalled her mother's instructions and called out again. "Shūróu — why are you still standing there?"

Shūróu came back to herself and followed An'yang out, her thoughts clearly elsewhere.

Jiang Mi watched them leave, puzzling over that expression. Had she said something wrong? Or was there something particular about the prayer beads Xiao Huaiyan had given her?

......

Outside the Ci'ning Palace, An'yang asked, "Shūróu — what is so remarkable about those beads? The mere sight of that woman is bad luck enough, never mind anything she happens to be wearing."

Shūróu managed a thin smile. "I must have been seeing things. Your Highness — why do you dislike Miss Jiang so?"

An'yang said, "It is all that little wretch's fault. If not for her, the Young Lord would not have met his end in Jiangnan. She is a curse."

Shūróu listened to An'yang catalogue Jiang Mi's faults all the way back.

Then she heard An'yang mention something about the Longevity Banquet and the guqin.

Shūróu asked again: "Your Highness — you are saying His Majesty bestowed the Lüqì on her?"

An'yang remembered Shūróu had only recently arrived in the capital and would not know the history.

She saw Shūróu's face go completely white. "Yes — who knows what Imperial Elder Brother was thinking. Why do you look like that?"

Shūróu said, "Your Highness — I feel a little unwell. I would like to go back to the Lǎnyuè Pavilion."

An'yang had always known Shūróu was delicate. She did not press her. "Go on then. Come back to the Ci'ning Palace with me another time — perhaps we will run into Imperial Elder Brother."

Shūróu took her leave and walked back to the Lǎnyuè Pavilion, weighed down with thoughts.

She wanted to speak with her mother, but a maid told her Lady Liu had gone out on a visitor's pass provided by the Worthy Dowager Consort.

Lady Liu did not return until evening.

Shūróu went to her at once, not noticing the unusual look on her mother's face. "Mother — I need to talk to you."

Lady Liu saw Shūróu's agitation and sent the maids away.

"What is it, Róu'er?"

"Mother — today I went with Princess An'yang to the Ci'ning Palace. I was hoping we might encounter Cousin. But I saw the Empress Dowager's niece, Jiang Mi, wearing a string of prayer beads — identical to the ones Cousin wore when he was young. Every bead exactly the same."

Lady Liu said, "That cannot be. You must have been mistaken. Your cousin never parted with those beads when he was studying away from home. He refused to let even you look at them closely."

Shūróu shook her head. Something she had treasured in her memory all this time — she could not have seen wrong. And the words Miss Jiang had said were precisely what Cousin had told her once.

"Gānnán sandalwood prayer beads — every bead carved with beast markings. One of the beads has a little wear on it. I remember every detail. There is no other string of beads like that in the world."

Lady Liu's brow furrowed. She began to take Shūróu's words seriously.

"Mother — Princess An'yang also said Cousin bestowed the Lüqì on her. Mother — that is the Lüqì I have dreamed of all my life. How could he give such a thing away so easily? The Lüqì is something one gives only to the one closest to one's heart."

Shūróu began to cry. "Cousin has been back from Jiangnan and has not come to the inner palace at all — and then as soon as that Jiang woman came to the Ci'ning Palace, Cousin appeared to visit the Empress Dowager. Is that not too much of a coincidence?"

"Does Cousin like Jiang Mi, Mother? What am I to do?"

Lady Liu thought for a moment. "Do not panic. Tomorrow I will seek an audience with His Majesty. I will find a way to have your name settled first."

But how could Shūróu not panic? If she had never seen those prayer beads, she would not have worried so much.

......

The next morning, Jiang Mi had barely finished helping her aunt take her medicine before she meant to go and ask Physician Duan how much longer the treatment would take before there was improvement.

She had not walked more than a few paces when she came face to face with Li Fu.

Li Fu was all smiles. "Miss Jiang — His Majesty requests your presence." He added quickly, "The way has been cleared. No one will know."

Jiang Mi weighed the situation. If she declined, Xiao Huaiyan would only come here himself.

She followed Li Fu to the imperial study — but not through the main entrance. Li Fu led her in through a side door at the back.

It puzzled her. She stepped inside and found the room connected to another through a screen that divided the space.

Then she heard voices from the other side of the screen.

"Your Majesty — I come today to ask a favour for Róu'er."

Jiang Mi went still. That was Lady Liu's voice. She and Xiao Huaiyan were speaking. So why had she been brought here? She looked toward the door she had come through — Li Fu had already closed it.

Then she heard Xiao Huaiyan's voice.

"What favour does Aunt wish to ask?"

She could not go out, could not make a sound. She had no choice but to listen.

Lady Liu said, "Róu'er damaged her health as a child when she accidentally consumed some medicine. Many physicians have seen her over the years. She will never be able to bear children. With such a constitution, married life in any family would be difficult."

"Does Aunt wish me to arrange a match for Shūróu?"

Lady Liu's voice rushed to correct him. "Your Majesty — Róu'er has loved and admired you since she was small. I come to ask whether Your Majesty might give her a place to call home."

Silence fell after those words. Even Jiang Mi, behind the screen, held her breath.

Everyone waited for Xiao Huaiyan's answer.

"What I understand Aunt to mean is that she wishes Shūróu to enter the palace?" Xiao Huaiyan's voice gave nothing away.

Lady Liu was genuinely nervous. The young man she remembered was not the same as the Emperor before her now.

She steeled herself. "Your Majesty — for my elder sister's sake — please give Róu'er a place where she will be looked after. Only among family can I feel at ease."

Behind the screen, Jiang Mi thought: given how much Xiao Huaiyan revered his birth mother, he would certainly agree to let Shūróu enter the palace. He had given her a consort title in the last life. She had simply never known the reason.

Just as Jiang Mi and Lady Liu both braced themselves for his answer —

Xiao Huaiyan's voice came, and it carried a chill. "She is willing — even with no favour, only an empty title?"

Lady Liu was struck speechless. She said, "With Your Majesty's care and protection, the palace is better than anywhere else."

She told herself this must be only talk. Shūróu was beautiful — how could she have only an empty title and no affection? That was what people said at the outset. Over time such things ceased to hold.

As long as the Emperor agreed to let Shūróu enter and gave her a rank — everything else could follow in due course.

Xiao Huaiyan heard her answer. He gave a quiet, brief laugh.

He said, "If I have no intention of naming an Empress, one more person or one fewer in the inner palace makes no difference to me."

"However — I have now found someone I intend to make Empress. The favour Aunt is asking, I cannot grant."

Lady Liu's expression changed completely. She had thought this as good as certain — and the Emperor had refused her.

She tried again. "Your Majesty — even in naming an Empress, you will still be taking consorts. The Empress must have magnanimity and tolerance. Róu'er asks only for a quiet corner."

She knew, as soon as the words were out, that she had overstepped.

Lady Liu recovered quickly. "This subject congratulates Your Majesty on finding a candidate for the Empress. I wonder which family's daughter is so fortunate."

Xiao Huaiyan said, "The candidate is in this register. What does Aunt think?"

Lady Liu received the register in both hands. She looked at the name on the page. Her heart gave a lurch.

Her trembling hands returned it. "Whoever Your Majesty has chosen — it will be perfectly fitting."

chapters.title: Chapter 92
chapters.content:
After Lady Liu left, a deep quiet settled over the room. The faint scent of dragon's blood incense drifted through the air.

Xiao Huaiyan's fingers tapped lightly on the desk. He stood and went around the screen.

Jiang Mi was standing in the corner — her expression still unguarded, still carrying the traces of surprise and bewilderment. At the sight of him she went visibly flustered.

He walked over, drew her into the crook of his arm, and settled her hands on his shoulder.

He carried her back to the desk and sat down in the imperial chair — with her on his lap.

Jiang Mi tried to get up, but his arm was firm around her waist and she could not move.

"Did you hear all of it?"

She looked up at him. He knew perfectly well that she had.

He had sent Li Fu to bring her here precisely so she would hear his exchange with Lady Liu.

She saw the faint smile in his eyes as he asked again, "I am to name an Empress. Will you not congratulate me?"

Jiang Mi pressed her lips together. She lowered her gaze. "This subject congratulates Your Majesty."

She knew he was naming an Empress. She believed she knew who he had in mind. In this life, Miss Shen would enter the palace earlier than she had in the last — and before that happened, Xiao Huaiyan would take no consorts, a mark of the regard he held for his chosen Empress.

She could feel that he was pleased. He was clearly satisfied with this choice.

She could not quite describe what she felt — something between having never hoped and therefore feeling no disappointment.

Xiao Huaiyan looked down at her. "That is all — just a congratulation? You do not wish to ask who she is?"

She did not understand why he had to press her for an answer.

"Your Majesty has already decided. This subject does not presume to guess at the imperial will."

Xiao Huaiyan wound one of her loose strands of hair around his finger. "Not presume — or not willing?"

Jiang Mi simply stopped speaking.

Xiao Huaiyan breathed in the faint sweetness that was hers alone, and watched her lower her head again rather than answer.

His gaze drifted to the small curve of her earlobe, the pendant swaying with her every small movement. He said, "The Board of Rites has drawn up a list of candidates for Empress and consorts. Would you like to see it?"

Of course — if he was naming an Empress, of course he would also be taking consorts. That would simply happen after the Empress entered the palace.

Jiang Mi shook her head. "This subject does not presume to overstep."

Xiao Huaiyan did not allow her to refuse. He placed the register in her hands. "I want you to look."

Jiang Mi glanced down at the register in her hands, something bittersweet settling in her chest. The consort list would probably include her name — given Xiao Huaiyan's manner these past weeks, he was surely going to bring her into the palace.

After a moment she raised her hand and opened it.

The pages where the names, family backgrounds, ages, and descriptions of noble daughters should have been listed were completely blank.

Jiang Mi's gaze went still.

What did this mean? Had he given her the wrong register by mistake?

Xiao Huaiyan took her hand in his and looked at the register with her. "What were you thinking just now? Were you expecting to find your name on a consort list?"

He tipped her face toward him so she had to look at him.

"Tangtan — why do you not dare ask who I intend to name as Empress? Who do you think it will be? Who else could you imagine me naming? Tell me — what are you thinking?"

Question after question. She had no ground to stand on. She felt the rising urge to flee.

She shook her head without a sound.

Xiao Huaiyan held her still and looked at her with absolute steadiness. "The one I want to marry is right in front of me."

He had never been this calm. "When I name an Empress — there will be no one else. Tangtan — do you understand what I am telling you?"

Her eyes ached with the effort of holding back tears.

She had never allowed herself to imagine it. Had never dared to. Had never let herself want it.

He was telling stories again.

He had told her stories when she was half-asleep, and now he was telling her stories again.

If he knew what the Jiang family had done, he would regret every word he had just spoken.

The ones who had been the true architects of Consort Jin's ruin — the Noble Consort and Virtuous Consort — had had their entire clans wiped out, and not only because the princes they had backed failed in their bids for the throne. It was because of Xiao Huaiyan's hatred.

In the fifth year of Yuanxi, the Jiang family's actions were exposed. That would come in this life too — there was no escaping it. Which meant there was still someone with knowledge of what had happened, someone who could make the charges against the Jiang family stick — confirming that her great-uncle had killed the witnesses who might have vindicated Consort Jin. By then her aunt would be gone, and there would be no one left to argue in their defence.

The blade hanging over them would fall in the end.

How could she dare respond to him? She did not dare fall for him. She did not dare hope.

Xiao Huaiyan watched her quietly — she was fighting back tears, and still shaking her head.

She bit her lip and shifted her eyes away from his. "Your Majesty — you promised to give me time."

Even though part of him had expected this answer — she looked soft and gentle, but there was iron in her too.

She did not want him — so she would certainly not be drawn by the prospect of an Empress's title. From the moment she woke with her memories of the last life, she had been running from him at every turn.

"Yes." Xiao Huaiyan's voice carried a desolation he could not quite name. "I did promise that. How much longer do you need me to wait?"

How much longer? Jiang Mi had not thought about it.

Perhaps when the Jiang family's crimes came to light, he would no longer be asking.

"Your Majesty — my aunt will be waking soon. This subject should return."

Xiao Huaiyan did not release her.

"Tangtan — I need something to set my mind at ease."

Jiang Mi went rigid. This was the second time he had asked her for this.

Last time she had been able to push him away and run...

Her lashes trembled. Cool fingers came to rest at the side of her neck, stroking slowly, making her shiver.

Warm breath fell at the corner of her lips — pressing, unhurried, deepening by degrees.

The hands she had pressed against his chest grew weak.

The slow, unhurried, deliberate way of it — she was forced to tilt her head back to breathe.

His hand moved to her waist, and as in the last life, he kept up a steady, coaxing pressure — and she trembled wherever he touched.

She kicked her legs trying to rise. He did not move at all. A silk slipper fell from her foot and landed on the floor.

He pressed his lips to hers, laughing very softly, and then — while he still had the will to — released her.

He held her in the circle of his arm and reached down to retrieve the slipper from the floor.

Jiang Mi sat crimson-faced and watched Xiao Huaiyan put the slipper back on her foot.

He smoothed a strand of her hair aside. "Tangtan — I am willing to wait. I just do not want to wait too long."

He added, "The Dragon Boat Festival is coming in a few days. I will take you to watch the races — how does that sound?"

It was as though he would not let her go without her agreeing to at least one thing.

......
