Lady Liu came out of the imperial study covered in cold sweat. She walked back to the Lǎnyuè Pavilion in a daze.

She could not understand how the Emperor had refused her so cleanly, so utterly without any lingering feeling.

If Róu'er could not enter the palace — what respectable future was left for her?

Being the Emperor's woman was the highest position there was.

Her Róu'er had only ever wanted to marry His Majesty. Even with no favour — as long as she could see him sometimes, she would be content.

Lady Liu thought of the register the Emperor had shown her. That had been no list of names — it had been a draft edict of investiture.

She could not begin to understand why the Emperor would want to marry a girl from the Jiang family. Had he not previously shown no fondness for the Jiangs at all?

Was this his own wish? Or had the Empress Dowager, gravely ill and desperate, obtained his promise while she still could? Everyone knew that once the Empress Dowager was gone, the Jiang family would lose their only connection to the imperial house.

She had heard the Worthy Dowager Consort mention it before — that the Empress Dowager had long wanted to see her niece settled in the palace, but the Emperor had been rejecting the Board of Rites' petitions for investiture and so nothing had come of it.

And that Jiang girl seemed to have some ability of her own — she had used the merit of saving the Emperor's life to secure the betrothal to the Duke Zhen manor. Unfortunate, that the young lord had met his end at rebel hands and the engagement was dissolved.

By all conventional measure, such a woman could not possibly be elevated to Empress.

Could it be, as Shūróu had said — that the Emperor truly liked her?

The moment she entered the room she was met by Shūróu, who had been waiting anxiously. "Mother? How did it go? What position did His Majesty give me?"

Lady Liu could not bring herself to answer.

Shūróu clutched her sleeve and would not let go. "Mother — tell me."

Lady Liu said, "Róu'er — your mother will think of another way."

The smile on Shūróu's face slowly faded. She went frightened. "Mother — what does that mean? Did you not get to see Cousin?"

Lady Liu said, "I saw him. However, His Majesty said he was about to name an Empress and would not be taking consorts for the time being."

Shūróu was momentarily stunned. Then: "Then I can wait. After the Empress enters the palace, I will enter after."

She watched Lady Liu's face — and her mother's silence terrified her.

"Who is Cousin naming as Empress? Is it because of her that Cousin will not let me into the palace?"

Still Lady Liu said nothing. She did not know how to tell Shūróu.

But that silence told Shūróu everything.

She kept telling herself this should not be happening.

"Is it Jiang Mi?" The name came out before she could stop it. As she said it, the hostility she had felt from the first moment felt suddenly sharper — something closer to hatred.

Lady Liu saw Shūróu's expression and moved to calm her. "Not a word of this until the investiture edict has been proclaimed. Nothing is settled yet. Do not say these things carelessly."

Shūróu pushed Lady Liu away, shut herself in her room, and wept into her bed.

From the first moment she had seen Jiang Mi, something had been wrong inside her.

She had never met this person before — and yet the revulsion had risen from somewhere deep. That was why she had watched every word and movement, that was why she had noticed the prayer beads at once.

This was not how things were supposed to be. She did not know where it had gone wrong.

She cried herself to sleep, and dreamed she was standing in a room — the furnishings and arrangement looked like somewhere in the palace. Hanging on the wall inside was a portrait: a woman standing beneath a crabapple tree, reaching up on tiptoe to breathe in the scent of the blossoms.

The woman was barefoot. Around one ankle was a small bell of gold and jade, carved with beast markings.

Cousin's mark. Just as on those prayer beads — he always carved beast markings.

She looked at the woman's face in the portrait. It was Jiang Mi.

Shūróu went white with fury. She went forward to tear the portrait down — and found she could not move.

From somewhere a breeze arose, stirring the painting as though the woman in it might step out at any moment.

Shūróu grew more frantic. She reached out to grab it and drag it off the wall — but when she raised her arm, her sleeve was empty. There was nothing there.

Shūróu screamed and woke in terror.

Lady Liu pressed her down. "Róu'er — what is wrong? Did you have a nightmare?"

Shūróu stared at her mother. "Mother — Mother — my hand is gone! My hand is gone!"

Lady Liu held her. "Róu'er — calm down. You were dreaming. Your hands are perfectly fine. How could they be gone?"

Shūróu could not believe it and kept crying. Lady Liu pulled back the covers and took Shūróu's hands in hers. "Look — your hands are right here. I am going to find the Worthy Dowager Consort and ask her to call a physician for you."

Shūróu looked at the hands her mother was holding. She flexed her fingers.

Her hands were there. Both of them, still perfectly attached.

Lady Liu looked at Shūróu's state with a pain she could not put into words. She stroked Shūróu's forehead. "Róu'er — your mother will find a way."

chapters.title: Chapter 93
chapters.content:
Jiang Mi returned to the Ci'ning Palace. The Empress Dowager had been awake for some time.

Mama Cui was about to ask the palace maids to bring the evening meal.

Jiang Mi went to the bedside. "Aunt — are you feeling a little better?"

The Empress Dowager nodded. She looked at Jiang Mi's ear. "Tangtan — where is your left earring?"

Jiang Mi reached up to check. The lustrous glazed pearl earring was gone.

She thought back to the imperial study — there had been a brief warmth at her earlobe at some point while she was being held still. She had not noticed it in the moment.

Her earring had very likely ended up with Xiao Huaiyan.

She kept her expression neutral. "I must have dropped it somewhere. I will have Qiuyu help me look for it later."

The Empress Dowager did not inquire further.

After the evening meal with her aunt, and after helping her settle with her medicine, Jiang Mi called Mama Cui out to the corridor.

"Mama Cui — has anything come to light on the matter of Physician Wei?"

Mama Cui shook her head. "Nothing out of place with her background. Both parents are deceased. She learned medicine from an elderly physician for several years, then was recommended and made her way through successive selections to the imperial medical office. In recent days she has been well-behaved and has had no suspicious contacts."

"And the person who recommended her?"

"A Physician Huang who retired from the imperial medical office. He encountered Physician Wei in Luoyang and found her a promising student — he put forward the recommendation."

Jiang Mi frowned slightly. "Not a single irregularity?"

Mama Cui hesitated. "The person assigned to watch her did mention, in passing, that Physician Wei occasionally hums snatches of a Jiangnan folk song."

A Jiangnan folk song?

Jiang Mi thought for a moment. "Has she been anywhere near the Lǎnyuè Pavilion recently?"

Mama Cui looked startled. "How did Miss know? Word only just came — the Miss Shū staying at the Lǎnyuè Pavilion has fallen ill. The Worthy Dowager Consort called for a physician. Physician Liu, who was on duty, brought Physician Wei along with him."

"Mama Cui — please have the person watching her find out whether Physician Wei had any particular contact with anyone at the Lǎnyuè Pavilion. Whether anything was said."

Mama Cui nodded.

Jiang Mi returned to the side chamber, her mind somewhere else entirely. She very much wanted to know whether Physician Wei had any connection to Shūróu. In her last life, Shūróu had been someone who frequently used fragrant incense — and Physician Wei was skilled in precisely that area. It was natural to connect them. But if Physician Wei was Shūróu's person, why would she harm the Empress Dowager?

That evening Mama Cui came to the side chamber with a report. Physician Wei had had no significant interaction with Shūróu — she had simply stood beside Physician Liu while he worked. When the prescription was done, she went to prepare it. At the end of the visit, Lady Liu gave her and the other medical attendant who had come along a small gift.

Jiang Mi said nothing and asked Mama Cui to keep the watch going.

Several days passed. The Empress Dowager, with her new treatment, had improved enough to sit up and walk a little. She was still refusing visitors.

Jiang Mi had assumed that with Shūróu ill, she would rest and recover. Instead Shūróu came to the Ci'ning Palace every single day to pay her respects.

Each time Jiang Mi went out to excuse the visitors on her aunt's behalf, Shūróu's eyes made her uncomfortable in a way she could not name.

One evening after the meal, as Jiang Mi was sitting with the Empress Dowager, the calls of greeting outside announced the Emperor's arrival.

Jiang Mi had just risen when Xiao Huaiyan walked in, wearing apricot-yellow imperial robes.

Their eyes met the moment she looked up. He was already smiling faintly at the corner of his mouth. Before she could curtsey he said, "No need for formalities."

He sat down naturally in the chair Jiang Mi had just vacated, and said to the Empress Dowager, "Your Highness looks better than the other day."

The Empress Dowager, faced with the Emperor's attentions, felt a complicated unease. She managed a small smile. "I hear Your Majesty personally fed this Empress her medicine. With so many affairs of state pressing upon you, still you came to visit — Your Majesty is kind."

Xiao Huaiyan said, "Your Highness need not stand on ceremony. Coming to visit is only right."

He stayed a little while longer with easy, pleasant talk. He seemed genuinely to have come only for a brief visit.

When he rose to leave, he paused in his step as he passed Jiang Mi and murmured a few words.

Everyone else had their heads bowed and did not notice.

Jiang Mi went rigid and took her leave with the others.

A little later she excused herself on some pretext and slipped back to the side chamber.

Coming out of the Ci'ning Palace, she saw at once the apricot-yellow figure waiting ahead.

He had no attendants near him — he must have sent them all away.

She hesitated, then walked toward him. She stopped behind him and asked quietly, "Your Majesty — was there something you needed?"

Xiao Huaiyan turned. In the evening dark his phoenix eyes held steady on her. "Must there be something I need, to come and find you?"

He saw her eyes widen slightly, and a smile came to his lips. "You have something that was left at my residence."

His gaze dropped to her earlobe — small, pale, bare of any ornament.

Xiao Huaiyan raised his hand. A lustrous glazed pearl earring turned between his fingers.

Jiang Mi assumed he was giving it back and reached out to take it. Her thanks were not yet out of her mouth when he shifted it just beyond her reach.

"I will put it on for you."

Jiang Mi naturally wanted to protest.

But Xiao Huaiyan had already bent close — one hand cradling the side of her neck, the other pinching her earlobe.

He was suddenly that near. His warm breath made her shiver involuntarily, a tingling spreading through that whole side of her.

Jiang Mi held herself rigid. She could not help asking, "Your Majesty — is it done?"

Xiao Huaiyan said nothing. He gave the soft earlobe two additional slow pinches.

Feeling her gather herself to push him away, he said quietly, "Do not move."

Jiang Mi felt the urgency too — he had dismissed everyone, but who knew whether someone might pass along this palace corridor?

This was the first time Xiao Huaiyan had ever put an earring on a woman. The opening in her earlobe was very small. He steadied the earring and threaded it through with careful patience.

As he did, he heard a sharp intake of breath.

He stilled. "Did I hurt you?" He had barely applied any pressure at all.

Jiang Mi felt faintly exasperated. She did not know where this impulse of his had come from. Her sensitivity to pain was sharper than most — she had always been careful putting on her own earrings.

It was not quite pain. More of an odd, unfamiliar feeling.

She shook her head. The earring he had just put on swayed with the motion.

Xiao Huaiyan looked at her flushed earlobe, deep pink now as a dusted of rouge.

He turned his face and pressed a kiss to the blushing warmth.

Jiang Mi's face burned. She pushed him away in alarm. He let out a low, muffled laugh and straightened up.

He flicked the earring lightly with one finger. The pearl and the glaze rang softly against each other.

He felt a small, quiet pang. Not quite musical enough.

He took her hand. "Returned to its rightful owner. Come — I will walk you back."

Jiang Mi was startled. Was he not supposed to go back to the Qianqing Palace? Why did it turn into him walking her back?

Xiao Huaiyan read the question in her eyes. "If you walked me back, I might simply bring you along with me. So it is better that I walk you home."

The two figures grew small in the distance. A shape that had been concealed in the shadow stepped forward.

Shūróu stood in the moonlight, her face the colour of ash. She had bitten her own lip bloody.

Her eyes were full of jealousy and hatred both, a tide of rage surging through her.

How. How was it that woman who received Cousin's tenderness?

She had come to the Ci'ning Palace every day, hoping to catch even a glimpse of him, and had not managed it once. Then word reached her that Cousin had finally gone to the Ci'ning Palace — and she had come running.

Only to see that.

When had Cousin ever been this gentle with anyone?

He was warm to people, in his way — but there had always been a remove underneath, a distance that never quite closed.

When had he ever smiled like that? When had he ever allowed himself to be pushed away? How could he possibly put an earring on someone with his own hands?

Shūróu had never seen this version of Xiao Huaiyan.

Not when he was a prince, and even less imaginable now that he was Emperor.

She had never thought he could be like this. This was something she would not have dared dream.

If only she had not seen what she just saw — she could have gone on not knowing. But she had seen it, and now the hatred that had been flickering since the first moment she laid eyes on Jiang Mi was something that cut bone-deep.

She returned to the Lǎnyuè Pavilion. Lady Liu had also just come in.

Seeing Shūróu's lost, stricken look, she hurried over. "Róu'er — what is wrong? I told you to rest in the room. Why did you go out again?"

Shūróu seized her mother's sleeve. "Mother — please find a way to stop Jiang Mi from becoming Empress. Do not let her enter the palace. Please, Mother, I beg you."

If Cousin showed no special warmth toward anyone, she could perhaps bear it.

But she had seen what he was capable of — and she could not.

Jealousy burned through her until she felt she might collapse under the pain of it.

Lady Liu smiled and soothed her. "Do not say silly things. Becoming Empress is not so easily done."

If the Jiang family bore the name of having harmed the late Empress Yīzhēn, the Emperor — however much he might care for this Miss Jiang — could not tolerate it.

The thing she had been uncertain about before — she had made up her mind.

Shūróu did not quite understand her mother's meaning. "Princess An'yang said the investiture edict will come out after the Dragon Boat Festival. I am terrified Cousin will announce it that very day."

Lady Liu said, "Do not worry. I will make arrangements."

Her mother's calm did not comfort Shūróu at all. She was convinced she was only being humoured.

She lay awake in her bed. The Dragon Boat Festival was only a few days away. If nothing was done, and the edict was proclaimed for all the world to hear, nothing would matter anymore.

Shūróu thought of someone. Perhaps this person had the same goal as she did.

The next day, Shūróu invited Princess An'yang to meet her in the imperial garden.

An'yang had no great enthusiasm for walking in gardens, but was curious about what Shūróu had to say.

"You said you have a secret to tell me? What secret?"

Shūróu said haltingly, "This is something I heard from my mother — it concerns who His Majesty intends to name as Empress..."

An'yang's eyes lit up. Had Lady Liu learned the name from Xiao Huaiyan during her visit to the imperial study?

"Tell me — is it the Shen family or the Gu family?" She had heard her mother say those two families were the most likely candidates.

Shūróu shook her head.

An'yang frowned. "Could it be the daughter of the new Minister of War?"

Shūróu shook her head again. "None of those. It is — it is the Jiang family."

"What?" An'yang's voice shot up.

Shūróu grabbed her sleeve in a panic. "Your Highness — please keep your voice down."

An'yang could not believe it. "How is that possible? That cursed woman just killed off Young Lord Xue — how could Imperial Elder Brother bring her into the palace, let alone make her Empress?"

Shūróu saw the fury blazing in An'yang's face and knew she had found the right person.

"Your Highness — if my mother had not seen the edict herself, I could not have believed it either. He even refused to take consorts for her sake — I do not know if there is even a place left for me in the palace." Shūróu finished and burst into tears.

An'yang looked at Shūróu's distress and thought she was not lying.

An'yang's fury surged. Her cousin Xie Mingshan had been sent to a family temple for pushing Jiang Mi into the water and was now spending her days among the lamps and the sutras — the Xie family had never been able to lift their heads since. Her own mother and the Empress Dowager had always been at odds — if the Empress Dowager's niece became Empress, it would mean one more person pressed above her mother. And what she resented most of all was that the person she had been unable to stop thinking about had gone to Jiangnan with Jiang Mi and never come back. How could she make peace with that?

"Stop crying," she said. "Before the edict is proclaimed, we find a way to make sure she cannot enter the palace. With her looks, there are already men who have been setting their sights on her since the engagement dissolved. Find her a destitute household, and once it is done, she will have no choice but to marry him."

An'yang thought it over. "The difficulty with using medicine is that it leaves traces — it could be discovered and traced back, which would be troublesome. But for the moment, I cannot think of another approach."

Shūróu pressed her lips together and said quietly, "I happen to know of an incense. It resembles calming incense closely — it only makes the person sleep more deeply than usual. It generally leaves no trace."

chapters.title: Chapter 94
chapters.content:
After parting with Shūróu, An'yang went back to her own palace.

The moment she was inside, she sat down at her desk and began thinking over which destitute young nobleman to pick for Jiang Mi.

He needed to look passable enough on the surface, but be rotten through underneath — someone who would make Jiang Mi's married life a misery.

The fifth son of the Yǒngníng Earl's house? She had heard he spent all his time in the pleasure quarters, and had even bought a woman out of one of those establishments and set her up as an outside residence. Jiang Mi's looks would certainly appeal to someone like that — he would be more than happy to add her to his collection of women from the gutter.

An'yang shook her head. That was not enough.

She thought of another — the fourth son of the Zhōngqín Earl's house. She had heard from her Xie cousin that this one was fond of tormenting people. By the time he was finished with even the most beautiful of women, there was not an unscarred inch left on her body. The Xie cousin had said it was criminal — such a waste of a beauty.

An'yang continued running through possibilities. Jiang Mi's engagement to the Duke Zhen manor had been dissolved, and though she now had the name of one who brought ill-fortune to husbands, there were already several profligate young men from various families who had been taking note of her.

She was still lost in thought when a young palace maid with a pleasant face stepped forward to serve tea. The girl's hands were mottled blue and purple from old and new injuries — they shook faintly as she held the tray.

An'yang glanced at her. With a flick of her wrist she sent the scalding tea pouring over the girl's hands. The maid held in her cry of pain and knelt to beg forgiveness.

An'yang looked at the tears the girl was fighting to hold back. Her expression grew colder. "Yùhé — have you forgotten how to serve tea?"

The little maid Yùhé pleaded, "Your Highness — this servant knows she was wrong. This servant dares not do it again."

An'yang had a bellyful of anger with nowhere to put it. She picked up a whip and lashed out. "Did I give you permission to speak? And you dare look at me directly?"

A second crack of the whip followed.

Unable to hold back, the little maid cried out in pain.

An'yang, irritated by the sound, had her dragged out.

The maids standing outside caught sight of Yùhé being taken away and exchanged glances with one another.

When there was no one nearby, one of them asked in a low voice, "Why has Her Highness been taking it out on Yùhé these past few days?"

Another replied, "Who knows — Yùhé was never assigned to the front before. Somehow Her Highness noticed her once and said her eyes were too irritating to look at. She's been calling for her regularly ever since, and every time it ends in punishment."

One of them said, with a pity that was also resignation, "How unfortunate. Serving Her Highness like this — who knows how long she'll last."

Word of An'yang making trouble again reached the Worthy Dowager Consort. She gave instructions to her people: "Go and see what An'yang is up to this time. Tell her to keep a low profile. I am in the process of finding her a consort — once I have petitioned His Majesty for an edict of marriage, she cannot be causing scenes now."

A senior palace matron replied, "Yes, Dowager Consort."

......

The fifth of the fifth month arrived without warning — the Dragon Boat Festival.

A midday banquet had been set in the imperial garden. Officials' families, noble sons, and the daughters of prominent houses were all expected to attend.

Jiang Mi had woken early. She wore a pale lotus-pink brocade gown embroidered with cloud patterns, glazed pearl lotus-blossom earrings, and a crabapple jade-phoenix pin trembling in her pinned hair. Her movements were graceful as she walked. Her face, already beautiful as a blooming lotus, was given a pleasant balance between refined and vivid by the ensemble.

Jiang Mi sat at her dressing table and placed a bundle of five-coloured silk braids into a small wooden box.

Qiuyu came in carrying a small plate of green rice dumplings. "Miss — you wrapped these yourself and they just came off the steam. I have already sent a plate over to the Empress Dowager. This plate is for you to nibble on before we go."

"Set them aside for now."

Jiang Mi stood and carried the wooden box to Qiuyu. "Did you find out?"

"Yes, Miss. I asked — the women of the Duke Zhen manor will not be attending the Dragon Boat banquet today."

Jiang Mi handed her the box. "Then find a way to go out and deliver this to Ningzhu."

Qiuyu hesitated before nodding. "Miss — the Duke Zhen manor has been keeping its gates closed to all visitors. I am not sure I will be able to get this inside."

"Try anyway. Just say it is for Ningzhu."

Qiuyu was about to step away when someone came in through the screen.

Qiuyu dropped to her knees in a hurry.

Jiang Mi had not expected Xiao Huaiyan at this hour either. Had he not already gone to the imperial garden?

She was uncertain whether he had overheard her exchange with Qiuyu. She was uneasy about it. She had not dared ask too much about the Duke Zhen manor since returning from Jiangnan — she had not wanted to provoke him. But today was the Dragon Boat Festival. She had woven Ningzhu a bracelet of five-coloured silk threads, as a hope for the girl's safety and peace.

Xiao Huaiyan looked at Jiang Mi's tension and asked, with deliberate innocence, "What is that?"

"Silk thread bracelets, Your Majesty. This subject wove a few for the younger sisters in the family."

Xiao Huaiyan said nothing, and waved Qiuyu out of the room.

Just the two of them left in the room.

Xiao Huaiyan came toward her, his tone easy. "You keep quite a few people in your heart."

Jiang Mi was briefly lost for words.

She had only woven a few silk bracelets. It was a festival — she wanted the good fortune the colours were meant to carry.

Xiao Huaiyan drew an arm around that slender waist and looked down. "And what about me? Did you think of me today?"

Her lashes lowered. He was pressing closer and his presence was filling the air around her. She turned her head aside. "This subject made some dumplings, Your Majesty. If you would not find them too plain, you are welcome to try."

Xiao Huaiyan had been looking at the lip rouge on her mouth. He had no particular interest in dumplings.

But she was rarely the one to offer something first. He flexed his fingers and released that narrow waist, then took her hand and drew her to sit with him at the table.

The dumplings on the plate were small and dainty — one or two bites each — with honey set alongside.

For Xiao Huaiyan, they were more of a gesture than a meal.

The bamboo leaves were fresh, carrying a clean fragrance. He peeled one open and ate it. The dumpling was soft and slightly chewy, with nothing added beyond the grain — not too sweet, not heavy. The natural flavour of the filling had taken on the scent of the leaves. It suited his palate.

He noticed Jiang Mi sitting properly with her hands folded and not touching the food. He peeled open another and held it out to her. "You made them — are you not going to try one?"

He pushed the dish of honey toward her.

Unable to refuse, she quietly accepted the dumpling. She lifted it and took a small bite.

Xiao Huaiyan watched her eat in small, careful bites. His eyes moved briefly to her abdomen. He thought of the dumplings he had fed her once — just a few and she was already full. He could not understand how she could be so small.

He drank some tea. "Tangtan — would you like to know how the Duke Zhen manor's situation has been handled?"

Jiang Mi's hands went still. She swallowed what was in her mouth and looked up at him in surprise.

Of course she wanted to know. She had heard so much about his handling of those who had rebelled — so many people drawn in, so many ruined. She did not know what he would do to Ningzhu.

"Did you forget what I said to you?" Xiao Huaiyan calmly peeled another green dumpling and held it out to her.

He held her gaze. "I told you — if you have something on your mind, you can ask me directly. If you do not say it, how am I to know what you are thinking?"

Jiang Mi remembered. But she had not dared trust what he said.

"Will Your Majesty tell me?"

He smiled. "Eat this, and I will tell you."

Jiang Mi accepted the small green dumpling in silence, dipped it in honey, and put it in her mouth.

Xiao Huaiyan waited until she had finished. "The Grand Princess of Zhaoyang surrendered the iron voucher and immunity token. The Duke Zhen State has been stripped of his noble title and dismissed from his post. After the Dragon Boat Festival, she will take the household to Liangzhou and will not return to the capital."

Liangzhou — close to Yunzhou, where Xiao Huaiyan's trusted people held command. It was effectively house arrest.

Jiang Mi knew that to have their lives spared and the entire household intact was already more mercy than could have been expected.

And yet — she thought of the girl who was still so full of unclouded joy.

After a quiet moment she asked softly, "Your Majesty — when the time comes, might I be allowed to go and see Ningzhu off?"

He was not surprised.

Only — knowing her heart was tied up in others again made something in him restless. "You may," he said. "But I will come with you."

He rose. He had come here first, before setting out, simply to look in on her. The banquet with the officials was ahead, and after that there were still matters to attend to...

"I will go to the imperial garden first. After the banquet, I will take you to watch the dragon boats together."

Jiang Mi watched his retreating back, her thoughts in knots.

chapters.title: Chapter 95
chapters.content:
The sun blazed overhead, but the imperial garden was alive with noise and colour.

Officials' wives had dressed in their finest. Noble daughters held fragrant fans, sitting with composed dignity. Young men of good family were in high spirits, each hoping to come first in the dragon boat race.

Jiang Mi descended from the carriage, accepting a palace maid's hand. Though she had made a point of arriving late, she could still feel the light, barely concealed glances aimed at her from all sides.

She was used to being the subject of private talk. She followed the guiding maid toward the main hall.

Not far behind her, a young woman in a sunset-rose jacket started to call out — and was stopped by the young man at her side.

"Why will you not let me call out to her, Third Elder Brother?" Shen Yǎowēi said, smiling.

Shen Qiānxiū watched the distant figure. "Do not give her trouble."

"Poor Miss Jiang, when one thinks about it. Third Elder Brother — do you still think of her?"

Shen Qiānxiū said nothing.

Shen Yǎowēi said, "Perhaps after the banquet I can invite Miss Jiang to watch the dragon boats together — and Third Elder Brother, you can make a good impression."

Shen Qiānxiū hesitated. "If she does not wish to, do not press her."

Shen Yǎowēi covered her mouth with her handkerchief and laughed. "Third Elder Brother, you really are very considerate. And you have not even started, and already you are putting her feelings first. Though — Third Elder Brother, wanting Father to agree to this will not be easy."

Shen Qiānxiū knew that well enough.

The imperial examinations had been delayed because of the suppression campaign, and the results were not yet out. He was hoping to earn a good result first, then make his case to his father.

"All right — go on ahead to the Changle Hall. I have to get to the Wanhé Hall."

The moment Shen Qiānxiū was out of sight, the smile faded from Shen Yǎowēi's face.

......

Jiang Mi entered the hall and found the Marchioness of Cheng'en already seated.

She went over and sat beside her. "Aunt — where is Sister Yi?"

"Yì'er has had a touch of the summer heat — I did not bring her."

Jiang Mi nodded. "Then Sister Yi must rest and take good care of herself."

The Marchioness asked, "Tangtan — how is the Empress Dowager? Will she be attending today?"

"Her Highness has improved a little but is still very weak. She will not be attending."

The Marchioness looked quietly regretful. If the Empress Dowager was absent, the Worthy Dowager Consort would be the one holding court.

She remembered something and took a letter from her sleeve. "Your second aunt-in-law asked me to bring this for you."

Jiang Mi took the letter. She was fairly sure this was the reply from the Su family — she wanted very much to read it, but now was not the right moment.

She tucked the letter away and let her gaze sweep lightly over the room. Her eyes landed on a pleasant surprise.

Gu Xuan.

Sitting across from Jiang Mi, Gu Xuan had already spotted her and was nodding in greeting with a bright smile.

From outside, a eunuch announced, "The Worthy Dowager Consort has arrived! Princess An'yang has arrived!"

The hall grew quiet and everyone rose to bow.

The Worthy Dowager Consort took the seat of honour. She smiled and said, "Please — everyone be at ease. With the Empress Dowager unwell today, it falls to me to welcome all of you."

It had been a long time since the Worthy Dowager Consort had felt this free. She was hoping the Empress Dowager would simply not recover — ideally not survive at all — and then there would be no one in the inner palace to press above her.

She said a few words of welcome and received the expected flurry of responses.

The Worthy Dowager Consort raised her cup. "Today is the Dragon Boat Festival. We have prepared realgar wine and cornelian cherry wine for all our guests — please drink freely. I offer the first toast to everyone present."

Everyone in the hall drained their cups.

Jiang Mi set hers down. The realgar wine was sharp and burning — roughly the same calibre as what Gu Xuan had once brought to their drinking session.

She glanced over at Gu Xuan and saw she had already refilled.

Jiang Mi suppressed a smile. Gu Xuan really did have a taste for strong drink.

The dancing and music in the hall were in full swing when the Worthy Dowager Consort picked up her cup again. "There is one more person I want to toast individually."

She looked directly at Jiang Mi. "The third Miss Jiang has been tireless in nursing the Empress Dowager, and has brought about an improvement in Her Highness's condition. In my view, Miss Jiang has rendered a great service. Come — I raise my cup to you."

Jiang Mi was taken aback by the Worthy Dowager Consort's manner.

This cup she could not refuse.

She drank it.

Princess An'yang also rose. "Mother Consort is rarely moved to praise anyone. Miss Jiang has truly been diligent in her attendance at Her Highness's bedside. I also wish to toast Miss Jiang."

Jiang Mi frowned. What was happening today?

She said carefully, "Your Highness — this subject truly cannot hold much wine."

An'yang said, "Miss Jiang drank from Mother Consort's cup — surely she can drink from mine. There is no room for declining."

Jiang Mi smiled and said, "This subject attends the Empress Dowager as any junior member of the family should — it is no more than duty. Worthy Dowager Consort and Your Highness are too generous. It seems to this subject that the Worthy Dowager Consort herself deserves great credit — she has gone to such lengths to host and prepare for this Dragon Boat banquet. It should be this subject who toasts the Worthy Dowager Consort — but as this subject has always had a weak constitution and little head for wine, she will offer tea in place of wine, with apologies to the Worthy Dowager Consort and Her Highness. Please, do as you wish."

She raised her teacup and offered the substitute toast in their direction.

By the time she had finished speaking, to press the matter any further would make the attempts seem distinctly deliberate.

The Worthy Dowager Consort had not anticipated the ball being kicked back to her.

An'yang's eyes flashed with irritation, but she had little choice but to let it go.

At that moment Gu Xuan rose with her cup. "Miss Jiang makes a fair point. This Dragon Boat Festival — the Worthy Dowager Consort has laid out fine wine, fine food, and magnificent entertainment for all of us. That is considerable effort indeed. We should be the ones toasting the Worthy Dowager Consort."

With that, several wives and daughters of military families joined in, lifting their cups to the Worthy Dowager Consort.

The Worthy Dowager Consort knew full well that the Loyal and Brave Marquess's house was one of the Emperor's most trusted households, and that this eldest daughter Gu Xuan had followed the Emperor at Yunzhou for years — whether she eventually entered the palace as a consort or served in another capacity, she would be the Emperor's person. She could not afford to refuse the toast.

And having accepted, she could not stop what followed.

Once Gu Xuan's enthusiasm for drinking caught fire, she found a new excuse to pour at every turn — toasting the Worthy Dowager Consort, then An'yang, then Lady Liu and Shūróu in succession.

She and the other military wives worked the atmosphere until everyone was swept up in the spirit of it.

The Worthy Dowager Consort found it a distinct headache.

An'yang, refusing to be outdone, had also drunk more than intended — she began to compete quietly with Gu Xuan in a private contest of wills.

Jiang Mi's side of the room remained relatively quiet.

Two cups of strong liquor were not going to make her properly drunk, but the heat from them was rising and she felt the faintest dizziness setting in.

The Marchioness leaned over. "Realgar wine is strong to begin with, and you drank too quickly. Eat something to soak it up."

She helped Jiang Mi to a few dishes. Jiang Mi managed a little, then found she had no appetite.

Across the table, the Worthy Dowager Consort had not bargained on Gu Xuan's remarkable capacity — after making the rounds, the woman was still steady and bright-eyed, showing no signs of slowing.

The Worthy Dowager Consort was thinking about the dragon boat viewing to come in the afternoon — the Emperor would be there as well, and she could not appear with the smell of wine still on her. She needed to recover.

She excused herself from the table to rest.

Lady Liu also rose before long, murmuring a few words to Shūróu before she left.

Shūróu did not know what her mother was going to do. But inside she was tense with nervous anticipation. Princess An'yang had made her arrangements. They were only waiting for the prey to walk into the net.

Once it was done — no matter how much Cousin cared for her — he could not name her Empress. And Jiang Mi's only paths would be to take her own life or marry the man who had dishonoured her.

The ladies and daughters in the hall, seeing the Worthy Dowager Consort had departed, began drifting off one by one to the resting rooms the palace had arranged, waiting for the dragon boat race and the chance to catch a glimpse of the Emperor.

The Marchioness looked at Jiang Mi, who had barely touched her food. "Tangtan — would you like to go and rest for a while? I will come and find you when it is time to go to the Wàngyún Terrace."

Jiang Mi nodded and rose.

Before she left she glanced over at Gu Xuan, who was still very much engaged in drinking with An'yang. She went ahead with the guiding maid.

The maid leading her was a pleasant-looking girl who walked with her head down and said nothing.

It was the height of noon. The sun was fierce — enough to make one squint.

For Jiang Mi, rest was secondary. She really wanted somewhere quiet to read the letter.

Just then, Chengzhong appeared ahead and came trotting over. He smiled broadly. "This servant greets Miss Jiang."

Jiang Mi felt her brow involuntarily furrow. From the unctuous quality of Chengzhong's smile, she could already guess what his next words would be: His Majesty requests your presence.

Chengzhong's appearance flustered the guiding maid. She said quietly, "Eunuch — I am to bring Miss Jiang to her rest."

Chengzhong barely glanced at her. "You are not needed here. You may go."

The maid opened her mouth, then closed it, seeing Chengzhong's warning look. She stepped back in silence.

Chengzhong turned to Jiang Mi. "Miss — His Majesty has sent this servant to escort you to the dragon boat viewing."

"Does it not begin after noon?"

"Quite right, quite right. His Majesty simply thought you would be more comfortable resting at his pavilion in the meantime. When the banquet is over he would still have a moment to speak with you. If you would rather not, of course — perhaps His Majesty will simply come and find you himself later..."

Jiang Mi's head was already aching faintly from the wine. He was doing this on purpose.

She stepped into the palanquin Chengzhong had waiting.

The maid who should have departed lingered in the shadows. When she stepped back out, her face was drained of colour and her whole body was shaking.

She had let the target walk away from her. What was she supposed to do? She couldn't very well have stopped Chengzhong — but the Princess was going to be furious. Would the Princess beat her to death?

She was still trembling when she looked up and saw, not far ahead, two familiar palace maids standing with their backs to her, speaking quietly.

"Yùhé must have delivered the person by now, yes?"

"I have been watching. I saw that Miss Jiang walking off with Yùhé."

"Yùhé is unlucky. With Her Highness already despising her so, sending her to do this is as good as sending her to her death. Whatever follows will be blamed on her — she might as well be gone sooner rather than later."

"Shush — let us hurry. We need to take the sobering broth. Her Highness is waiting in the pavilion."

After the two maids moved away, the maid who had been standing frozen in the shadows felt the reality of what she had nearly done settle over her.

She had known, vaguely, that something bad was going to happen. She had known the Princess would push her out as a scapegoat. But she had had no choice.

Her body was damp through with sweat. The blazing sun gave her no warmth.

It was death on every side. She looked at the new and old bruises on her hands, and the burn marks that had never fully healed.

She was as insignificant as an ant. But even an ant, scrambling desperately, was only trying to stay alive. Why could no one give her a way to live?

Yùhé went quiet. She turned and walked back in the direction of the main hall, and saw Princess An'yang ahead, reclining against the railing of a pavilion.

An'yang squinted at her and let out a small burp from the wine. "Come here."

Yùhé walked over. An'yang looked at her and said, "You are back? Is there a problem?"

Yùhé shook her head. "This servant came to report — the lady has retired to rest."

An'yang swayed to her feet. "Good. Come and support me — I am going back to rest and let this wine settle. I want to be sharp for the entertainment ahead."

Yùhé stepped forward to take her arm and guided An'yang away by a different route.

......

The Wàngyún Terrace stood beside the Qūsōng Pavilion — a three-storey structure that offered the finest view of all the surroundings. Jiang Mi followed Chengzhong up to the third floor, where she looked out over the railing. Not far below, a broad river filled her field of vision.

At least eight dragon boats sat waiting on the water. On the opposite bank, crowds of ordinary citizens had already gathered to watch.

Chengzhong said, "Miss — you may rest inside for a while. His Majesty should be back very soon."

The room inside was appointed with nothing less than perfect care.

After serving tea, Chengzhong quietly withdrew.

Jiang Mi settled on the daybed and took out the letter.

She unfolded it and read carefully.

Just as she had guessed: the events of the tenth year of Yongshun had all been buried under silence. The fragrance physician had been traced, some partial details recovered — but that physician had died in the sixteenth year of Yongshun. His wife had taken their newborn daughter and left Xuzhou.

Jiang Mi stared at the letter. Something flickered through her mind, elusive. Then, without quite knowing why, she thought of what Mama Cui had told her — that Physician Wei occasionally hummed snatches of a Jiangnan folk song.

She estimated the ages. An unsteady thought surfaced.

Physician Wei's age was similar to what the physician's daughter's age would be now. Could that physician be the same one her great-uncle had silenced? Could Physician Wei be his daughter?

Jiang Mi stood up sharply. She walked quickly toward the door.

And walked directly into someone coming in.

Before she could step back she was caught at the waist, and a low, somewhat rough voice said, "What is the hurry?"

Jiang Mi looked up. Xiao Huaiyan's eyes were faintly reddened at the corners. There was a hint of wine on him — he had clearly been drinking at the banquet.

"Your Majesty — this subject would like to return to the Ci'ning Palace."

Xiao Huaiyan rubbed his brow, one arm still loosely around her, and walked her back into the room. "There is no rush. You promised to watch the dragon boats with me."

Jiang Mi's mind was elsewhere entirely — full of the letter and Physician Wei and what it might mean. She wanted to speak with her aunt. Though she was not sure what her aunt would do with the information.

"Just half a day's company — you cannot spare even that?"

Her expression was complicated.

At that moment someone on the far bank flew a kite out across the river.

On the kite, painted in a colour like blood, was a single large character: INJUSTICE.

Jiang Mi had been looking out the window. The moment the kite swept past, an arrow shot it out of the sky.

Xiao Huaiyan had seen it too. His voice went cool. "There is always someone who insists on choosing a day like today for this sort of thing."

He spoke to the outside. "Go and have Pei Chi look into it."

Jiang Mi did not know why her heart was beating faster. She felt, without being able to say why, that something was about to happen.

Xiao Huaiyan turned back to her with easy unconcern. "Did you have enough to eat at the banquet? Shall I have something brought for you?"

"No need, Your Majesty. This subject is not hungry."

Before long, attendants brought in dishes of imperial food, steaming and fragrant.

Xiao Huaiyan ladled her a bowl of soup. "Not hungry — just keep me company and eat a little more, then."

He set food in her bowl without haste, watched her eat a few bites, and put his chopsticks down.

Then Pei Chi's voice came from the doorway. "Your Majesty — the person has been apprehended. She claims to be one of the late Empress Yīzhēn's old attendants. She says she carries a grievance and wishes to petition Your Majesty directly. The matter concerns the sixteenth year of Yongshun — and the allegation that Empress Yīzhēn was murdered."

Jiang Mi's spoon nearly slipped from her hand. Her face went white.

In the last life it had been the fifth year of Yuanxi when someone had brought accusations against the Jiang family for their role in the death of Consort Jin — the posthumously elevated Empress Yīzhēn — in the sixteenth year of Yongshun.

Why had the accuser appeared now?

She did not dare look at Xiao Huaiyan's face.

Consort Jin was his most protected wound. What would happen to her aunt — to the Jiang family?

In this life — what would Xiao Huaiyan do to the Jiang family?

Xiao Huaiyan looked at Jiang Mi, her head bowed low. He asked, "Have you finished eating? If so — come with me and meet this old attendant."

Jiang Mi looked up, unable to quite believe what she had heard.

Her heart was filled with dread and fear — and yet she wanted to go. She wanted to hear it for herself. She wanted to know what this woman had to say, and how it differed from what her aunt had told her.

Her aunt was still alive. There was still someone who could speak in the Jiang family's defence.

Whatever guilt fell on the Jiang family — let it at least be understood plainly.

......

Jiang Mi went with Xiao Huaiyan, but she did not show herself. She sat behind a screen.

Through the latticed opening, she watched a woman in her mid-thirties be brought in.

The woman's face bore a long, deep knife scar. She prostrated herself before Xiao Huaiyan with great care, then raised her head. "Your Majesty — do you still recognise this servant? I am Wénpíng, who served at Consort Jin's side."

Xiao Huaiyan said, "I have a vague impression of you. You do resemble the Wénpíng I remember — but to confirm your identity, there is someone who will know more clearly than I do." He turned to Li Fu. "Go and summon Lady Liu."

Li Fu said, "By your command."

The woman seemed unconcerned. "Your Majesty was young at the time — not knowing this servant's face is entirely natural. Any old hand from the palace, or Lady Liu, can confirm who I am."

Xiao Huaiyan said, "If I recall correctly, the two senior maids who attended my mother both died in Xuzhou. Wénpíng was one of them."

The woman's eyes filled with tears. "This servant was lucky — barely lucky enough. They tried to silence her and left her for dead at an unmarked burial ground, but she did not die. She crawled out from among the corpses. All these years this servant has been hiding and running, clinging to this worthless life — only for the day she might come before you and tell you: the person who harmed Consort Jin is still alive, still deceiving you."

Xiao Huaiyan said, "Who had you silenced?"

The woman said, "This servant and Wénlíng had taken the incense to a physician for verification. The physician found the incense was wrong — and then we were hunted down by the Marquess of Cheng'en. And that incense had been given to Consort Jin by the current Empress Dowager Jiang."

chapters.title: Chapter 96
chapters.content:
Behind the screen, every drop of blood in Jiang Mi's body seemed to turn to ice.

So it had come to this — aimed at her aunt, aimed at the Jiang family.

Afraid the Emperor would not believe her, Wénpíng pressed on. "Every word this servant speaks is true. Before Consort Jin set out on the southern tour, she could not sleep well at night. Knowing that the Empress — now the Empress Dowager — had long relied on calming incense to aid sleep, she went and asked for some. But it was precisely that incense that put Consort Jin in danger. Her Highness took her own life to prove her innocence — and the incense could have been used to prove that what she said was true, that the late Emperor should have believed she was innocent. Yet the Marquess of Cheng'en silenced everyone who knew. He prevented this servant and the others from bringing the evidence before the late Emperor. The Jiang family's intentions were murderous indeed!"

Wénpíng finished and prostrated herself, waiting for imperial fury.

The room was absolutely still.

Jiang Mi held her breath. The blade that had been suspended over her head for so long had finally fallen.

Xiao Huaiyan's voice gave nothing away. "Summon the Empress Dowager and the Marquess of Cheng'en."

Jiang Mi's back went cold with sweat.

After a moment, Li Fu came in escorting Lady Liu.

Lady Liu had barely finished her greeting when Xiao Huaiyan pointed at Wénpíng. "Aunt — do you recognise her?"

Lady Liu looked carefully at the kneeling woman. The puzzlement on her face shifted to shock. "You — you are Wénpíng? You are the personal maid who served my elder sister?"

Wénpíng knocked her head to the floor before Lady Liu. "Wénpíng greets the Second Miss." She called Lady Liu by the family rank she had held before her marriage.

Lady Liu went to her and took her hands, unable to believe what she was seeing. "You — were you not said to have died in service to your mistress?"

Wénpíng gripped Lady Liu's hands, visibly overcome. "Heaven had mercy and kept this servant alive — so that she would not let a single person who harmed Consort Jin escape."

Lady Liu looked shaken. "Can it be that there was more to what happened then?"

Xiao Huaiyan's eyes passed over the two of them. "Since Aunt is also someone with knowledge of what happened, she may remain and listen."

Jiang Mi watched Lady Liu take a seat. She herself could not sit still.

She paced back and forth behind the screen, barely able to endure the wait.

Before long, she saw an attendant come in to report.

"Your Majesty — there has been an incident with the Marquess of Cheng'en."

Xiao Huaiyan looked up. "What happened?"

The attendant's head was bent, his voice careful. "The Marquess was just attacked. A physician from the imperial medical office suddenly drew a blade and stabbed him."

Xiao Huaiyan's brow lowered. He set down his teacup. "Is the injury serious?"

"The Marquess managed to avoid the vital points. He sustained surface wounds."

Xiao Huaiyan's tone was even. "If he can walk, then bring them both here."

The attendant withdrew.

Before long Jiang Mi saw her great-uncle Jiang Qingdé being helped inside, and behind him — held by guards — was Physician Wei.

Jiang Qingdé saw who sat at the head of the room and knelt in spite of his wounds. "This minister pays his respects to Your Majesty."

Xiao Huaiyan, as though the events of the last hour had not touched him, asked with perfect composure, "Marquess — how did you come to be injured?"

Jiang Qingdé answered truthfully. "This minister does not know. I was walking to the Wàngyún Terrace with colleagues when this physician drew a blade at me while ostensibly delivering medicine."

The physician being held by guards suddenly erupted, pulling frantically against her captors. "Your Majesty — this subject acted to avenge her father. This subject's father discovered that the calming incense had been laced with angel's trumpet — and the Marquess had him killed for it. This subject has been wronged!"

Jiang Qingdé's eyelid gave a violent twitch. He shouted, "Utter nonsense. I ask Your Majesty to judge clearly."

The woman kneeling nearby raised her head. "Lord Marquess — you say this physician speaks nonsense. Then does this servant's testimony hold true?"

Jiang Qingdé looked at her. When he made out her face, his heart lurched.

Her eyes held old hatred. "Lord Marquess — did you expect this servant to still be alive and able to stand before the Emperor and expose the evils your family committed?"

The veins in Jiang Qingdé's forehead stood out. His hands were shaking, but he forced himself to compose and knelt toward the man at the head of the room. "Your Majesty — this minister does not know what she is speaking of. I ask Your Majesty to investigate clearly."

A sound came from behind the screen. Xiao Huaiyan glanced that way.

Everyone kneeling in the hall waited for the Emperor's reaction.

Lady Liu was anxious too. His response was not what she had imagined — too contained, too steady.

Was he waiting to hear the Empress Dowager's account first?

Her thoughts were burning when the eunuch outside announced: "Her Highness the Empress Dowager has arrived."

All eyes turned toward the door.

Empress Dowager Jiang entered slowly, one hand resting on a young woman's arm.

Jiang Mi walked beside the Empress Dowager and curtseyed toward Xiao Huaiyan.

She could not remain behind the screen forever. She had seen her aunt's procession from the window and had slipped out through the side door to meet her.

The Jiang family could not avoid this reckoning. She could only face it.

Xiao Huaiyan's gaze was unfathomable. His eyes moved from Jiang Mi and away.

Once the Empress Dowager was seated, with Jiang Mi's help, she looked over everyone kneeling in the hall and asked Xiao Huaiyan, "What is it Your Majesty wished to ask this Empress?"

Xiao Huaiyan's expression gave nothing away. "There is an old matter I would like to ask you about."

The Empress Dowager had been preparing herself on the way here. She said with quiet steadiness, "Your Majesty, please speak."

Xiao Huaiyan did not soften his words. "In the tenth year of Yongshun, before the late Emperor departed on his southern tour — did my mother come to the Empress Dowager to ask for calming incense?"

The Empress Dowager felt a plunge in her chest. She gripped her prayer beads. "That did happen. Consort Jin was worried she would not sleep well during the journey and asked this Empress for some calming incense. This Empress thought it a small matter and said no more of it."

"Your Highness, of course you would not dare say more. The incense you gave my mistress cost her life." Wénpíng could not hold herself back when she saw the Empress Dowager still keeping up appearances.

The Empress Dowager narrowed her eyes at the kneeling woman. "You are Wénpíng?"

"Yes. This servant accompanied Consort Jin to your palace to collect that incense."

The Empress Dowager looked at Xiao Huaiyan. She did not know whether he would believe her — but she had to make her position clear. "Your Majesty — this Empress had no intention of harming Consort Jin. Some of that calming incense remains in this Empress's possession. I am willing to have it submitted to the imperial physicians for examination."

Wénpíng thought of the imperial physician's finding all those years ago, and was afraid of being deceived again. She said urgently, "After so many years, who knows whether the incense in Your Highness's hands has not long been replaced. The only incense that truly matters is the one taken from our mistress."

Jiang Mi, standing to one side, saw this woman who had served Consort Jin casting doubt on her aunt again and again, and could not keep silent. "Those who are skilled in fragrance can determine the age of an incense — whether it is freshly made or old. This lady surely wants the truth. Would it not be best to let the imperial physicians make a thorough examination?"

Wénpíng pressed her head hard to the floor. "Your Majesty — the imperial physicians have examined this incense before. At the time the late Emperor had it checked by a Physician Hé, who said the incense was without fault. But this servant took what remained and brought it to a local physician skilled in fragrances, who gave an entirely different verdict. That physician said the incense contained a small quantity of angel's trumpet mixed in — enough to make the user fall into an unusually deep sleep and lose vitality. Over time the cumulative effect could easily cause a miscarriage."

Wénpíng drew something carefully wrapped from her chest and opened it — a few fragments of incense. "The incense from that time was destroyed. This servant saved only this much. If Your Majesty wishes to examine it, please do — and see whether what this servant has said is true."

After Wénpíng finished, Physician Wei spoke, her voice flat. "This subject also has half a stick of incense. Her mother found it clutched in her father's hands after his death. When her mother passed, she left it to this subject. This is what her father had verified — and what cost him his life."

Xiao Huaiyan's face settled into still water. His voice went cold. "Summon Chief Physician Gu."

......

The hour of the dragon boat race was approaching. Ladies who had been resting after the banquet began emerging in twos and threes, making their way toward the Wàngyún Terrace.

Shen Yǎowēi asked a palace maid for the room where Jiang Mi was resting and started toward it. Halfway there she saw the Worthy Dowager Consort accompanied by a number of ladies and daughters, also moving in that direction.

Shen Yǎowēi followed and saw the Marchioness of Cheng'en standing at the door, trying to block the Worthy Dowager Consort from entering.

The Marchioness was straining to keep her expression neutral. "Dowager Consort — please allow this subject to go in first. Tangtan may simply have overslept."

The Worthy Dowager Consort smiled. "We are all family elders — what does it matter who goes in first? This seat is worried the wine we pressed on Miss Jiang may have upset her. Let me go and look."

Before the Marchioness could object, the Worthy Dowager Consort's senior matron had already pushed her aside.

Shūróu followed behind the Worthy Dowager Consort. She had been waiting a long time for this moment.

An'yang would be too drunk to witness it — Shūróu would simply have to describe the scene for her in detail afterward.

The group entered the room. The smell inside made several of the ladies' expressions go strange.

A few of them pulled their daughters back, not letting them in.

The Marchioness, in a panic, rushed forward trying to stop what was coming.

Someone exclaimed, "There are men's garments on the floor."

The Marchioness, forgetting all decorum, planted herself in front of the bed canopy. "Dowager Consort — I beg you..."

The Worthy Dowager Consort had her attendants haul the Marchioness aside. She smiled a smile that did not reach her eyes. "I am rather curious what is inside."

With that she had someone yank the bed curtains aside.

On the bed lay a man and a woman, clothing in disarray, tangled together.

When those standing behind the Worthy Dowager Consort made out who it was, they all drew a sharp collective breath.

The Worthy Dowager Consort's expression froze. She blinked, unable to trust what she was seeing.

Shūróu also went rigid. She stumbled back several steps.

The Marchioness let out a private breath of relief — though she dared not show it.

The Worthy Dowager Consort let out a sharp cry, "Get out — get out! Everyone get out!"

The figure on the bed seemed completely unaware. She turned over, muttering drowsily, "Mother Consort, you are so loud..."

That voice — everyone still in the doorway heard it.

Was that not Princess An'yang's voice?

How had Princess An'yang come to be in the room prepared for the Jiang miss — and in such a state, with a man no less?

Had not the Worthy Dowager Consort been in the process of selecting a husband for her?

Several families that had previously shown interest promptly abandoned the idea entirely.

The ladies who had followed the Worthy Dowager Consort inside exchanged looks and filed out quickly. They had seen the man's face — was that not the fourth son of the Zhōngqín Earl's house? His reputation was widely known. No family with daughters to protect would ever consider such a match. The Zhōngqín Earl's wife had been fretting over his marriage prospects — well, it seemed that problem had resolved itself.

But what puzzled everyone was: this room had supposedly been prepared for the Empress Dowager's niece. How had An'yang ended up here, in this state, with a man?

......

In the Qūsōng Pavilion, several imperial physicians were verifying the incense.

Li Fu came in at a brisk pace and murmured something in Xiao Huaiyan's ear.

Xiao Huaiyan's expression darkened with undisguised contempt. His voice came out cold. "It really is quite a lively day. Send Pei Chi — have the Embroidered Guard take over and give me a thorough investigation."

Li Fu took his leave.

Jiang Mi stole a glance at Xiao Huaiyan. Something had happened — whatever it was, his expression had grown more forbidding than before.

Xiao Huaiyan sensed her looking, and when he raised his eyes, Jiang Mi caught that dark gaze and looked away quickly in the other direction.

Everyone waited while Chief Physician Gu and several colleagues conducted repeated comparisons of the three samples of incense.

After some time, Chief Physician Gu bowed toward the seat of honour. "This minister reports to Your Majesty. The incense samples are of comparable age. The sample provided by the Empress Dowager is ordinary calming incense — nothing unusual was found. The other two samples contain angel's trumpet mixed in, which can cause hallucinations and heavy drowsiness. Over time its toxicity poses a danger to unborn children."

Wénpíng could barely contain herself. "Your Majesty — you have heard. Consort Jin was given that incense containing angel's trumpet, and it was because of it that she fell into so deep a sleep that the Noble Consort's scheme succeeded. The Empress Dowager was their accomplice!"

The Empress Dowager slapped the table and rose. "Preposterous! How could this Empress possibly want to harm Consort Jin?"

Having now had the verification confirmed, Wénpíng pressed harder. "If Your Highness has nothing to hide and fear, why did you have the Marquess silence those who knew? The greatest harm that incense could cause was to an unborn child. Your Highness — will you dare claim you had no designs on the child in Consort Jin's womb?"

The Empress Dowager, still fragile from her long illness, could barely breathe from the agitation. She gasped in desperate, sharp breaths.

Jiang Mi pressed a hand against her aunt's back and tried to help her find calm.

Her heart sank. Her aunt could not prove the incense had nothing to do with her. And the most fatal point remained: her great-uncle had genuinely killed people.

Would Xiao Huaiyan believe what they said?

Jiang Qingdé knew there was no room left for luck. The Emperor was clearly conducting a thorough investigation into what had happened.

There was no escaping it. Jiang Qingdé removed his official cap and knelt. "Your Majesty — what happened then was entirely this minister's mistake, a moment of poor judgment. It had nothing to do with the Empress Dowager. At the time the Noble Consort and Virtuous Consort were watching for any weakness in the Empress Dowager's position, waiting for a chance to bring her down. This minister feared she would be implicated and committed a grave error. The Empress Dowager truly had no intention of harming Consort Jin."

Lady Liu, who had been silent throughout, felt her heart surge with hope. Though Jiang Qingdé was still defending the Empress Dowager, he had confessed. The Jiang family could not recover from that.

Once the Emperor formally assigned the guilt, the Jiang girl could forget about the Empress's position. The Jiang family was finished.

At that moment, hurried footsteps came from outside. A voice arrived before its owner: "Your Majesty, Your Majesty — you must do right by An'yang!"

The Worthy Dowager Consort walked in and found, unexpectedly, a hall full of people — even the Empress Dowager was present.

She saw Jiang Mi standing beside the Empress Dowager and pointed at her. "Why are you here?"

Jiang Mi was genuinely baffled.

The Empress Dowager said in a hoarse voice, "Tangtan is accompanying this Empress — why should she not be here?"

The Worthy Dowager Consort choked on her words. Her informants had told her a man had entered the room where Jiang Mi was resting. She had been quite satisfied to let it play out — she knew there were men who had been taking notice of Jiang Mi since the engagement was dissolved, and that someone was probably seizing the opportunity. If it succeeded, the shock might well push the Empress Dowager straight into the afterlife. She had certainly had no intention of intervening, had in fact wanted the whole affair loudly witnessed. She could not imagine how it had gone so wrong. The disgrace that should have fallen on Jiang Mi had somehow landed on her own An'yang.

She swallowed her mortification and appealed to Xiao Huaiyan. "Your Majesty..."

Xiao Huaiyan raised a hand. "I already know. Pei Chi has been sent to investigate. A result will come quickly. Dowager Consort may return and wait for news."

The Worthy Dowager Consort had come partly to ask for justice and partly to secure the Emperor's protection for An'yang. With what had happened, a princess of the imperial house could not possibly be made to marry a man like that. She had heard his reputation — it was utterly unacceptable. The best outcome would be for the man to quietly expire and for no one to speak of this again, and then perhaps the Emperor, out of pity for An'yang, would grant her a decent marriage.

She looked at the scene in the hall, and at the Empress Dowager's wretched colour, and at the Marquess of Cheng'en kneeling on the floor. Was the Jiang family being called to account? She found she was not quite ready to leave.

But the Emperor had told her to go, and she could not very well stay. The Worthy Dowager Consort walked out unwillingly — and came face to face with the Embroidered Guard commander Pei Chi, coming in with his men.

She saw three palace maids being escorted under guard. There was also a censer being carried by someone. She thought she recognised it.

Her heart gave a jolt. She stopped.

Pei Chi entered and bowed toward the man at the head of the room. "Your Majesty — this minister noticed something suspicious about the censer in the room prepared for Miss Jiang in the South Garden, and would request Chief Physician Gu to examine it."

Jiang Mi frowned. She had not gone to the South Garden at all — she had followed Chengzhong here instead, and had never gone to rest in the prepared room.

Could something have happened there?

Xiao Huaiyan glanced at the censer and had Chief Physician Gu brought back in.

Gu Tanghai was waiting next door and came at once. He opened the censer, removed the remaining half-stick of incense, crumbled a piece, and smelled it. His expression changed.

"Your Majesty — this incense — it is identical to the angel's trumpet blend."

At those words Lady Liu nearly dropped her teacup.

Wénpíng and Physician Wei also looked startled. Why would this poisonous incense appear in a Jiang family member's room?

Was the Empress Dowager trying to harm her own niece?

Xiao Huaiyan gave a short laugh — the kind that held no warmth, only cold. "Whose incense is this?"

Pei Chi raised a hand. Guards stepped forward with a palace maid, soaking wet. "Your Majesty — this maid was found attempting to drown herself in the lake. This minister had her pulled out and questioned."

The maid knelt on the ground, not daring to look up at the Emperor. She was shaking badly. "Th — this servant was ordered by Princess An'yang to lead Miss Jiang to the room to rest. The incense was also given to this servant by Princess An'yang, with strict instructions to light it."

The Worthy Dowager Consort, still standing in the doorway, went white. She came back inside and cried out, "Wretched girl — how dare you make false accusations."

The little maid wept and shook. "This servant speaks only the truth. The Princess instructed this servant to lead Miss Jiang to that room, and others were to bring the fourth son of the Zhōngqín Earl there as well. The Princess said the incense would make Miss Jiang sleep deeply without knowing, so no one would notice."

At those words, the expressions throughout the room shifted in all directions.

The Empress Dowager said furiously, "This is monstrous behaviour. Have you no decency? Worthy Dowager Consort — is this the daughter you raised?"

Xiao Huaiyan tapped his fingers on the table. His voice was oddly calm. "I am rather curious — how did An'yang come to have that incense? Could it be the Worthy Dowager Consort was also involved in the events of the tenth year of Yongshun? Does Dowager Consort know anything about this incense?"

The Worthy Dowager Consort was thoroughly lost, but she knew that any connection to the tenth year of Yongshun would mean nothing good. She denied it emphatically. "I know nothing. I had no idea. An'yang could not have had any such incense. She must have been taken advantage of by someone else."

Xiao Huaiyan's eyes carried a deep chill. "Whether that is so — summon her and ask."

......

The drums outside had started. The dragon boat race had begun. Cheering carried faintly on the air.

But in the Qūsōng Pavilion, there was only silence.

Jiang Mi was tense. She knew now that An'yang's incense might be the key that unlocked everything. If the source of her incense could be traced, her aunt's name could be cleared.

She watched her aunt sitting with eyes closed, conserving what strength she had. To have held together this long in her condition was already remarkable.

Her great-uncle was still kneeling. Blood was seeping from his wound again. Both she and her aunt knew — they could not speak a word in his defence.

Wénpíng sat with her head bowed, lost in some private thought. Physician Wei stared blankly ahead.

Lady Liu, seated below, seemed preoccupied. The handkerchief in her hands had been wrung into a twist.

Jiang Mi dared not look at Xiao Huaiyan.

When the drums outside sounded a second round, An'yang walked in weeping. "Imperial Elder Brother — you must do right by me!"

Behind An'yang came Shūróu, her face clearly frightened, and bearing the vivid red mark of a slap.

Lady Liu started up and went to Shūróu. "Róu'er — what happened to you? Who did this?"

Shūróu was wretched with humiliation, but she dared not say. She did not understand how things had gone so wrong — how what should have happened to Jiang Mi had instead fallen on Princess An'yang.

When An'yang had woken and learned what had happened, she had turned her rage on Shūróu and struck her across the face.

Shūróu did not dare complain. She shook her head at her mother. She had not wanted to come, but An'yang had insisted she come too.

In this state — how could she face Cousin?

Shūróu had kept her head down through the entire greeting.

An'yang had just begun to work herself up to her grievances when she looked around and saw, among the maids kneeling under guard, two of her own — beaten, barely conscious — and Yùhé soaking wet and shivering.

Before she could make sense of it, the Worthy Dowager Consort snapped at her: "An'yang — where did you get that incense? Tell your imperial elder brother this instant."

The Worthy Dowager Consort signalled urgently with her eyes. The Embroidered Guard had found everything out. An'yang could not escape responsibility for what she had done to Jiang Mi — the only hope now was to distance herself from the incense itself.

An'yang had never seen anything like this. She looked up at her imperial elder brother — and found the face that was usually mild now set in an expression that made her stomach drop.

An'yang hesitated.

"Tell him," the Worthy Dowager Consort urged sharply.

An'yang was frightened. She pointed: "It — it was Shūróu who gave it to me. She said she'd seen her mother use it on a concubine. She said it was similar to calming incense, but with one thing added — it made people very drowsy, and if used long enough it would damage the womb. She said her mother had used it to make a concubine who was with child lose the baby without anyone noticing. And she said physicians generally wouldn't find anything."

That torrent of words hit Lady Liu with no warning at all.

She felt her heartbeat nearly stop. She looked at Shūróu in disbelief.

Shūróu kept her head down, avoiding her mother's eyes.

She was shaking uncontrollably. "No — no, I didn't. Mother — I didn't."

Lady Liu pulled Shūróu down to her knees before the Emperor. Her expression was one of pain. "Your Majesty — my Róu'er understands nothing of all this. To impose a crime, one need only fabricate a pretext. Princess An'yang, in her desperation for a scapegoat, should not be pointing at my daughter."

The Worthy Dowager Consort tried to cut herself free. "Lady Liu — I thought Shūróu was a good girl, and encouraged An'yang to spend time with her. Who could have known that all these filthy schemes came from your daughter!"

Xiao Huaiyan rubbed his brow. Something like impatience showed briefly in his expression.

He rose. "One drama after another. I am beginning to find it tiring."

Every step he took drew the room taut.

As he passed Wénpíng he said quietly, "Who instructed you to fly that kite and call for justice first — to draw my attention?"

Wénpíng went rigid.

He stopped beside Physician Wei. "And who told you to wait for noon and attack the Marquess at that particular moment?"

The physician, who had been motionless until now, lost what little colour she had left.

Xiao Huaiyan gave a short, soft laugh. "The timing was rather precise."

He turned to Pei Chi. "Bring them in."

Pei Chi complied. Within moments the Embroidered Guard escorted in an elderly matron and a woman in her mid-thirties.

Xiao Huaiyan said, "Aunt — do you recognise them?"

Lady Liu's lips were trembling. The warmth had drained from her back. The strength seemed to leave her all at once.

Of course she knew them. The first was Mama Zhang, who had been at her side for years. The other was her personal maidservant — who, when Lady Liu had come of age, had been married off to the manager of one of her shops, becoming a shop manager's wife, but had gone on working for Lady Liu in secret.

These two knew everything she had ever done.

A terrible thought rose in Lady Liu's mind: had the Emperor already learned the truth?

chapters.title: Chapter 97
chapters.content:
Lady Liu felt as though she had been thrown into an ice cellar. Fear was swallowing up what little composure she had left.

She opened her mouth, struggled several times before a sound came out. "Your — Your Majesty — what crime have these two servants of mine committed?"

People cornered beyond all hope will always cling to one last thread of chance.

Xiao Huaiyan returned to the seat of honour. His tone was mild. "It seems Aunt's memory is not very good. Perhaps it would be better to let them speak first — about that incense."

Mama Zhang, prostrated on the ground, reached into her robe with shaking hands and produced an oil-paper parcel. A guard took it, opened it: incense, inside.

Mama Zhang's courage was failing her. She could not look at Lady Liu, and dared not look at the man at the head of the room.

Her voice was barely above a whisper. "This servant has always kept this incense for the Lady. The Lady enjoys blending fragrances, and once came to know a western merchant who dealt in fragrant spices. At the time the Lady was greatly troubled by a concubine in the household who had fallen pregnant, and this merchant described this incense to her. He said it resembled ordinary calming incense, but with one thing added — a substance that caused the user to become drowsy and sluggish, and after prolonged exposure, any child in the womb would not survive. The damage to the body afterward would make it difficult to conceive again. At the time the Lady had not yet become pregnant herself, and could not bear to have a concubine's child take precedence. So she used this incense on the concubine. Just as the western merchant had promised — the concubine began to sleep constantly, had no energy, and after some time lost the child in her womb. Everyone said the concubine simply had poor fortune. No one suspected the incense. Afterward the concubine, her body ruined, lost the master's favour."

"That was the first time the Lady used this incense — and she achieved exactly what she wanted. She valued it and feared it both, and had this servant seal it away. Then came the tenth year of Yongshun, and the Lady used it again. A thing like this, once you have touched it, is not so easily put down..."

Mama Zhang's voice died to a rough, low murmur. When she finished speaking, every person in the hall was struck cold with horror.

The looks directed at Lady Liu were like pointed blades.

Lady Liu suddenly lunged at Mama Zhang, her face contorted. "Lies — all lies! You wretched old woman — who has paid you to frame me!"

She clawed toward Mama Zhang's throat with both hands.

Pei Chi moved like lightning, seizing Lady Liu and throwing her to the ground. His blades-pring sword came to rest against her shoulder. "Lady Liu — you are in the Emperor's presence. You may not harm anyone here."

Mama Zhang clutched her throat, coughing, her body in spasms.

She knew she would not survive this. But she had a son, grandchildren — and for their sake, she had to speak everything she knew.

"Continue."

Jiang Mi glanced at Xiao Huaiyan. His face appeared calm — but behind those phoenix eyes, a chill that went to the bone was being held in restraint.

Mama Zhang dared not conceal anything. "In the tenth year of Yongshun, the late Emperor's procession stopped at Xuzhou. The eldest Miss — Consort Jin — had not seen family in a long time, and invited the Lady to come and spend time with her. Before long, the Lady had this servant fetch the incense. The Lady gave it to Zhúhuì."

Zhúhuì, kneeling at Mama Zhang's side, flinched when she heard her own name. She spoke in a trembling voice. "Consort Jin's incense was ordinarily kept by Sister Wénpíng. The Lady had me befriend Sister Wénpíng, and when she was not looking, I swapped it for the incense laced with angel's trumpet."

Zhúhuì swallowed hard.
