"After Consort Jin met her end, the Lady learned that Sister Wénpíng and the others were taking the incense to have it verified by a physician, and was afraid something would be discovered. She had people follow them, with orders to silence them the moment anything unusual was confirmed. But by coincidence, someone else had already moved first. Afterward, the Lady gave a sum of money to the widow of the physician who had died wrongly, and told her to take her child and leave Xuzhou. In the years that followed, a sum of money would be sent each year — to Luoyang."

Lady Liu closed her eyes and sank to the floor.

If looks could kill, the eyes in that room would have cut Lady Liu to pieces.

Wénpíng's composure shattered. All these years she had hidden and run, always afraid of being found by the Noble Consort, the Virtuous Consort, or the Jiang family. She had endured until the Emperor finally ascended the throne and come all the way to the capital. With no way of getting an audience and afraid of being found out, she had first gone to Lady Liu, hoping to use her connection to seek an audience and expose the Jiang family.

And now, the very person she had trusted completely turned out to be the one who had caused Consort Jin's ruin.

Wénpíng was overwhelmed with grief. "Why — why? Consort Jin treated you well. She was your own blood sister!"

That question spoke for everyone in the room.

The Empress Dowager could never have imagined that all the years of her own anguish and dread had been caused by Lady Liu from beginning to end.

The Worthy Dowager Consort, having heard these secrets, was frightened beyond measure. If she had heard things the Emperor wished kept hidden — would there be a reckoning later?

Lady Liu, knowing there was no way out, listened without resistance to Wénpíng's denunciation.

A low, strange laugh came from her. Her voice was hoarse and broken. She slowly opened her eyes.

"Why... I also want to ask why. Why could my sister become a beloved consort and live in splendour, while I could only marry a fifth-rank official and endure him bringing women into the household one after another? Why could my sister and I be equally beautiful and end up in such entirely different lives? Why was it my sister who was sent to the imperial selection, and not me? Why did my sister let me see with my own eyes what it meant to have the Emperor's love — to have everything, to be flattered by everyone? Why did the late Emperor have to give me hope by mistaking me for my sister — and plant a seed of desire in me?"

Lady Liu raised her head and looked at the young Emperor in the seat of honour.

Xiao Huaiyan was younger than the late Emperor had been, and more handsome. In his hands lay the power of life and death over all the realm.

Even at terrible risk, she had wanted to put Shūróu in the palace — at the Emperor's side.

She had simply not foreseen that this would lead only to a dead end.

"Your Majesty," Lady Liu said. "I admit that I was seized by greed. But I never wished for my sister's death. I only — I only wanted her to sleep a little more deeply, so that when the late Emperor came she would have a little more time with him. I never intended it. I never meant for it to go this far. I could never have imagined that the Noble Consort and Virtuous Consort would plot against her so viciously. My sister's death brought me no benefit at all. It was a moment of weakness — I only wanted to return to the palace with her. How could I have wanted her life?"

"Silence!" the Empress Dowager said sharply.

"Liu Shi — you say again and again that you had no intention. How could you not know that incense was harmful to a woman with child? How dare you claim you had no malice toward the child in Consort Jin's womb? In this Empress's view, you wanted Consort Jin's child to miscarry quietly, and then while she was weakened and grieving, you planned to reveal your own connection to the late Emperor, hoping Consort Jin would speak to him on your behalf and bring you back to the palace."

The Empress Dowager had witnessed far too many such schemes in her years in the inner court. Lady Liu's intentions were transparent.

Consort Jin had died by the Noble Consort and Virtuous Consort's trap — but what Lady Liu had done to Consort Jin was also a wicked act, and it could not be dismissed with a single claim of having meant no harm. Because of Lady Liu's exchange of the incense, the Jiang family had been forced into a position of complicity in a death. That guilt had weighed on the Jiang family ever since. Under the name of suspected involvement in the Emperor's own mother's death, the Jiang family had no path forward. For this matter, she herself had nearly sacrificed her own life, and had forced Tangtan to enter the palace and seek favour for the family's sake — at such cost.

And now this serpent-hearted woman had wanted to pin the blame of the incense exchange on the Jiang family. There were no words vile enough for her.

Lady Liu, having been seen through completely, fell silent.

She knew there was nothing more to say.

Lady Liu looked at Xiao Huaiyan with pleading eyes, hoping he might remember some small warmth she had shown him in his childhood and deal with her leniently.

Shūróu, sitting nearby, felt the world collapsing around her. She knelt beside her mother, her face blank. How had it come to this? She had been going to be a palace consort. How in a single moment had her mother become the person who had harmed her mother's own sister? Cousin's expression was terrifying.

Xiao Huaiyan let his eyes pass over everyone kneeling before him. His voice went cold. "Take them away. Put them in the imperial prison."

Pei Chi obeyed. The Embroidered Guard moved to seize all parties.

Jiang Mi watched the fierce soldiers clamp their hands over Lady Liu and Shūróu's mouths. Their pleas and weeping barely had time to begin before they were dragged away.

Her great-uncle Jiang Qingdé rose as well and went with the Embroidered Guard. She saw something in his face that looked almost like relief. That matter had pressed on his heart too long. At last it had settled.

All those with any part in the events of that time were to await their sentence.

The hall that had been packed with people was suddenly emptied.

The Worthy Dowager Consort very much wanted to leave with Princess An'yang, but the Emperor had not spoken and she did not dare move.

Xiao Huaiyan seemed to remember the Worthy Dowager Consort and An'yang only then. "Since An'yang chose this match herself, I will grant her a marriage edict. Dowager Consort, you will keep An'yang under close supervision — she is not to set foot outside the Changchun Palace until her wedding."

An'yang startled. At first she did not understand — and then the meaning sank in and terror seized her. She collapsed to her knees. "Imperial Elder Brother — no — I do not want to marry into the Zhōngqín Earl's house. Please, Elder Brother. I know I was wrong. I will never do it again."

If it was an imperial edict, even petitioning for divorce would be impossible.

The Worthy Dowager Consort's face went the colour of ash. She too knelt. "Your Majesty — An'yang cannot marry that man. Please, I beg you. I will discipline her properly. She will truly repent. Your Majesty — please take back this command."

Xiao Huaiyan pressed his aching forehead and lifted one eyelid. "When An'yang marries, Dowager Consort will go to the travelling palace."

Not one crack of softness in those words.

The Worthy Dowager Consort thought of Lady Liu being dragged away just now. The courage to plead a second time left her entirely.

Her throat tightened. She could only accept. "By Your Majesty's command."

The Empress Dowager watched the Worthy Dowager Consort and Princess An'yang depart. She looked at Xiao Huaiyan, and felt something like apprehension — she herself had barely survived today's upheaval. She could only imagine what it had cost Xiao Huaiyan.

The Empress Dowager said, "Your Majesty — the Jiang family accepts the consequences of what was done."

Having spoken those words, the Empress Dowager felt a weight that had sat on her chest finally lift. The outcome today was so much better than anything she had dared imagine.

Xiao Huaiyan said nothing. His dark eyes rested on Jiang Mi.

Jiang Mi lowered her head, took her aunt's arm, and left with her.

Xiao Huaiyan watched her retreating figure. He pressed a hand to his brow, his expression hidden in shadow.

On the way back to the Ci'ning Palace, the Empress Dowager fell asleep in the palanquin.

Jiang Mi's mind was still running over everything that had just happened, dread and relief tangled together.

From the moment she had left the Changle Hall, there had been scheme after scheme waiting for her. One wrong step and she would have been trapped.

She thought about it for a moment, then told Mama Cui to look after her aunt, and slipped off the palanquin on some pretext.

Jiang Mi went back to the Qūsōng Pavilion.

The attendants and maids around it had all been sent away.

The slanting light of dusk stretched long shadows across the ground. She walked inside.

The man in the seat of honour opened those narrow eyes. He looked at the figure coming toward him through the last of the sunset and was not sure, for a moment, whether he was dreaming.

Xiao Huaiyan said, his voice rough, "Why did you come back?"

Jiang Mi pressed her lips together. "This subject had promised Your Majesty she would watch the dragon boats."

chapters.title: Chapter 98
chapters.content:
Xiao Huaiyan went very still for a moment, not entirely sure he had heard correctly.

Was this truly not an illusion?

When the Empress Dowager had spoken, he had been looking at Jiang Mi. He had wanted to say something to make her stay.

But her eyes had been full of resistance and evasion — even fear. She had still refused to let him be seen in the open, had not wanted the Empress Dowager to know he wanted her.

He had given her his word and would keep it. Much as he did not want to, he had watched her leave with the Empress Dowager.

He had started to wonder whether he had drunk too much and was imagining things.

Had his Tangtan come back?

The figure standing in the last light of the sun seemed too unreal to touch.

He was afraid that if he moved toward her, she would disappear.

Jiang Mi stood where she was, her feelings not yet settled.

The impulse had come over her when she stepped down from the palanquin. Her mind had been in chaos. She had not known whether it was right or wrong, whether she should or she should not.

She thought of that quiet, desolate figure. The deep, still look in those eyes.

He had kept his promise. She could keep one of hers.

Following that thought, she had walked back. She had half-expected Xiao Huaiyan to have already gone by the time she arrived.

Now the room was unlit. His entire figure was swathed in shadow. He had asked only one question and then fixed her with those hawk-like eyes, and Jiang Mi felt her heart give an unsteady beat.

She caught the smell of wine. An empty wine jar had rolled to Xiao Huaiyan's feet.

Consort Jin's truth had always been Xiao Huaiyan's most protected wound. The truth itself had been brutal enough — and what Lady Liu had done made it worse still. He had no one left on his mother's side of the family now. At a time like this, he probably needed most of all to be alone.

Jiang Mi was not sure whether coming back had been the right thing.

She looked down. "This subject was impulsive."

She curtseyed and turned to go.

Xiao Huaiyan surged to his feet. He crossed the room in a few strides and stood before her, his eyes holding something that looked like disbelief and joy colliding.

He pulled her into his arms. "Tangtan."

Jiang Mi was pressed against him. His breath was warm at her ear. She could smell the faint trace of wine on him.

Xiao Huaiyan breathed in the sweetness of her — and the anger that had been building slowly in his chest began to ease.

He looked at the sky, now darkening. The river banks were bare and empty. The race had ended long ago. The officials, the noble families, the ladies — they had all gone.

But she had remembered his invitation. She had been willing to come back.

Xiao Huaiyan loosened his hold a little, giving her room to breathe. His voice was rough. "The dragon boats are gone now. Will you keep me company for a while?"

Jiang Mi let out a long, quiet breath.

She let Xiao Huaiyan take her hand and lead her down from the Qūsōng Pavilion.

They sat in a dragon boat, drifting in the middle of the river.

Above them, the stars were thick and bright. From the reeds along the banks came the distant sound of frogs and insects.

Only the two of them in the dragon boat.

It was not wide. Jiang Mi sat on a bamboo stool. Xiao Huaiyan stood at the prow, hands clasped behind his back, letting the boat drift where the current took it.

A slow river breeze came in carrying threads of coolness.

Jiang Mi watched Xiao Huaiyan pour what remained in his wine jar into the water.

He had stood there for a long time now. The breeze lifted his sleeves.

She thought of the day he had taken her to release river lanterns in Xuzhou. He had stood at the river's edge the same way, pouring jar after jar of plum wine into the current.

He was thinking of Consort Jin.

Jiang Mi sat quietly.

Xiao Huaiyan spoke at last. "Were you frightened today?"

She had been. The ruthlessness of the inner palace, the darkness in people's hearts. She had not anticipated that after the Changle Hall banquet there would be yet more waiting for her — a trap laid by An'yang and Shūróu together. If Xiao Huaiyan had not had people divert her from the path, would she have escaped unharmed?

And then Lady Liu had arrived with her people and tried to press the name of Consort Jin's murderer onto the Jiang family, step by calculated step.

If Shūróu had not accidentally produced that incense, which led the Worthy Dowager Consort to take the matter to the Emperor — if Mama Zhang and Zhúhuì had not been questioned and brought in — then Wénpíng and Physician Wei's testimony alone would have left the Jiang family as trapped as they had been in the last life.

Even thinking of it now left her cold.

But what confused Jiang Mi was this: in the last life, the accusation against the Jiang family had not come until the fifth year of Yuanxi, and Lady Liu's attendants had never been found at all. So in this life — how had Xiao Huaiyan managed to trace them? When had he first begun to suspect?

"This subject is all right," Jiang Mi said. "This subject thanks Your Majesty."

Xiao Huaiyan heard the tension she was trying to conceal. He said gently, "You are thanking me again. Is there nothing you want to ask me?"

She had questions — but did not know whether she was permitted to ask, or whether she should.

Her silence told him what he had already guessed. She was still remembering what he had said in their last life, and still did not dare step out of line.

"You have forgotten again," Xiao Huaiyan said, turning to face her. "I told you — you can ask me anything, say anything. Not in front of me."

She did not know whether it was something in his voice, or whether the weight in her chest was simply less than it used to be.

She looked up. "When did Your Majesty start looking into this?"

She would ask what she wanted to know. But she did not dare ask about the fate of her great-uncle.

Xiao Huaiyan walked toward her. With each step the small boat rocked, and Jiang Mi lost her balance — she reached out and caught not anything solid, but a pair of warm hands.

"Careful." Xiao Huaiyan steadied her.

Nearly half of her had fallen against him.

He looked down at her and answered her question. "When I took you to Xuzhou to pay respects to my mother — that is when I began investigating again."

So early, she thought.

Then she realised — when Xiao Huaiyan had taken her ashore to visit Consort Jin's memorial in Xuzhou, had he gone specifically for that purpose?

And then — had he known all along that Lady Liu and Shūróu were coming to stay in the palace? Had he let them come?

She steadied herself and frowned. "Your Majesty deliberately refused Lady Liu's request to have Shūróu enter the palace, and then let her know you intended to name a Jiang woman as Empress?"

Xiao Huaiyan did not release her hand. "Wanting to name you as Empress is the truth — she would have found out sooner or later. Human greed is unpredictable."

Jiang Mi was quiet for a long time. She pulled her hand back twice; Xiao Huaiyan let her take it.

After a pause she said carefully, "Does Your Majesty want to hear what this subject truly thinks?"

"This subject is not suited to the inner palace. She is not clever enough, does not have the cunning for the kind of scheming it requires. She wearies of navigating all the hidden currents. She does not want a life spent perpetually reading the intentions in every face — that is an exhausting way to live. And her nature is too narrow. She could never be the Empress who presides with dignity over the realm."

Xiao Huaiyan looked at her — the slight anxiety in her expression as she laid out her honest thoughts, voice soft.

Even still not willing to relent. But it was a beginning of sorts.

His face gave nothing away. Jiang Mi was uneasy.

He said, "Tangtan — I said I would not let go. If you refuse to enter the palace, refuse to be Empress — are you content to stay at my side with no name and no standing?"

Jiang Mi shook her head, again and again.

She bit her lip, her voice going soft. "This subject — this subject could retire to a family temple and pray for Your Majesty's health and prosperity."

Xiao Huaiyan felt something like a wound opening from the inside. He had done everything — cleared every obstacle — for the purpose of giving her time to slowly let go of her fears. And this was what she proposed: prayers at a temple?

His brow lowered in that dangerous, almost-smiling way. "Such a beautiful little novice — I would be even less at ease."

Xiao Huaiyan reached out and caught her to him. "When I had you in the imperial study to hear my exchange with Lady Liu — did you consider that there might be another meaning besides my intention to name you Empress?"

He saw the blankness on her face and guessed she had not thought about it at all.

"Jiang Mi — have you not considered that my inner palace will have no one in it but you?"

"The Empress is my wife. I want to marry you as my wife."

Jiang Mi looked at the expression on his face — that barely leashed intensity — and did not dare think it. No Emperor in Da Wei's history had ever had only one Empress.

She even wondered whether he was deceiving her again.

His eyes right now were darker than the night itself. Like a predator that had been starving for a very long time.

He bit down on those red lips with controlled force, holding himself in restraint.

His arms circled her. Her hands tried to push him away and found themselves held tighter and tighter. The boat swayed and dipped. She could not breathe; the motion was making her dizzy.

She felt where his hands had drifted to, and a thread of fear crept in — from what she knew of Xiao Huaiyan in the last life, he would probably take what he wanted right here on this boat...

Jiang Mi let out a small, muffled sound, her eyes reddening.

Xiao Huaiyan released her at once. She gasped, pulling in air.

"Your Majesty — I want to go back."

Something cleared in Xiao Huaiyan's eyes. He pressed a light kiss to the centre of her forehead and lifted her into his arms. "All right. I will take you back."

He carried her back to the Ci'ning Palace on the imperial palanquin. He was composed throughout the journey.

Jiang Mi sat with her teacup and did not look at him.

Xiao Huaiyan knew he had frightened her. He had thought he was showing considerable restraint.

Afraid she would pull away again, he took the teacup from her hands and made her look at him. "Tangtan — I will not hurt you."

She knew he had stopped. She could feel his care in the way he held back. But for one instant she had been overtaken by a sensation of the Xiao Huaiyan from the last life and the Xiao Huaiyan of this life collapsing into one.

Things were different this life. Why did it still happen?

Xiao Huaiyan knew this could not be rushed. He would simply have to be patient.

He only needed Jiang Mi to stop running.

Before she descended from the palanquin, he said, "Since I promised you time, I will keep my word."

She heard the concession in it — and heard too, beneath the words, that his patience was not without limit.

Jiang Mi returned to the Ci'ning Palace and was told her aunt had already gone to sleep. She returned to her own side chamber.

Too much had happened today. The moment her composure eased, exhaustion flooded in.

She was asleep almost before she touched the pillow.

......

The next morning, she woke late.

She dressed and went to pay her respects to her aunt.

This time her aunt had woken before her and was having the morning meal with Qingxue's help.

The Empress Dowager saw Jiang Mi arrive and urged her to sit and eat.

She asked, in passing, "Where did you go yesterday evening, Tangtan?"

Jiang Mi gave the answer she had prepared. "I went to find Miss Gu of the Loyal and Brave Marquess's house, Aunt."

The Empress Dowager nodded. "Keeping close to the Loyal and Brave Marquess's family is good. This Empress is feeling somewhat better now — you have been busy long enough. It is time to let you rest."

Jiang Mi was taken aback. Was her aunt saying she could leave the palace?

The Empress Dowager said, "You really do show everything on your face. The danger to the Jiang family has largely passed now. I will not push you toward things you are unwilling to do any longer. If there is someone you have come to care for yourself — tell me, and I will help you look into it. There is no need to keep hiding it from me."

Jiang Mi's feelings were too complicated to name. She nodded quietly.

The Empress Dowager saw Jiang Mi's eyes going red and laughed softly. "Now you are crying? Your aunt knows you have been waiting to hear this for a long time. As long as you do not resent me for it, that is all I need."

The Empress Dowager too felt as though a stone had been lifted from her chest.

She knew Tangtan had suffered a great deal. From now on, she would make it up to her.

Just then Mama Cui came in hurriedly and said in a low voice, "Your Highness — Lady Liu was given poison wine last night in the imperial prison."

The Empress Dowager put down her chopsticks. "And the others?"

"All those of Lady Liu's household who knew and participated have been put to death. The rest of the Liu family has been banished to Lingnan. Miss Shū witnessed Lady Liu drinking the poison and was so frightened she lost her wits. She was put on the road last night under escort."

The Empress Dowager's main concern was the Jiang family. Mama Cui, knowing this, had led with the others first — to give Her Highness a moment to brace herself.

"As for the First Master," Mama Cui said, "he will likely lose his title of nobility."

The Empress Dowager was prepared for this. "And the official post? Has that been stripped as well? Is he to be exiled?"

Mama Cui shook her head. "The First Master has been demoted to Yizhou."

chapters.title: Chapter 99
chapters.content:
With the Empress Dowager and Jiang Mi watching in anxious relief, Mama Cui continued. "Your Highness — the First Master has been demoted to Prefect of Yizhou. In a few years, he may yet be recalled to the capital."

From Assistant Minister of the Board of Rites, demoted to Prefect of Yizhou.

The Empress Dowager gripped her prayer beads. Tears rose in her clouded eyes.

Relief. Gratitude. And something deeper she could not name.

She dared not feel even a trace of grievance. This was already an extraordinary mercy from the Emperor.

Jiang Mi offered a cloth to wipe her aunt's eyes. She herself was surprised.

She and her aunt had assumed her great-uncle would likely lose his title and his post and be exiled to some distant borderland.

To keep his life had seemed the most they could hope for. But to still hold an official position — that she had not imagined.

The Empress Dowager said, "Yizhou is a hardship posting, but this is already the best outcome possible."

Jiang Mi was quiet. Yes — it was already the best possible outcome.

The Empress Dowager patted Jiang Mi's hand. "Tangtan — the Jiang family is in the middle of a great change. Go back on my behalf and see how things are. I do not know whether your great-aunt and the others will be able to hold together. Tell them also — this Empress is still here in the palace, though the title of Marquessate is gone. Tell them to stand firm and not lose their composure. Every thunderclap and every mercy comes from the Emperor. The Jiang family is to receive it and be grateful."

Jiang Mi's throat felt tight. "I understand, Aunt. You must take your medicine on time and try to eat something even when you have no appetite."

The Empress Dowager managed a smile. "I will. Do not worry."

At that moment Qingxue came in and curtseyed. "Your Highness — Li Fu from the Qianqing Palace has come and asks for an audience."

The Empress Dowager was puzzled — what could require Li Fu to come in person?

"Show him in."

Li Fu came in with a smile and bowed respectfully. "Your Highness — His Majesty wishes to know your wishes regarding the disposal of Physician Wei."

Jiang Mi looked at Li Fu. Li Fu smiled and nodded at her.

Both Jiang Mi and the Empress Dowager knew that Physician Wei had tampered with the incense used in the Ci'ning Palace. But they also now knew that the physician her great-uncle had silenced — the one whose evidence was destroyed all those years ago — had been her father.

The Empress Dowager turned her prayer beads. She considered for a moment and said slowly, "Send her back to Xuzhou. Forbid her from ever handling any incense or fragrance again — then release her."

Li Fu was mildly surprised. He bowed. "As Your Highness commands. This servant will convey the message."

After Li Fu left, the Empress Dowager said, "I am a little tired."

Jiang Mi brought the medicine and helped her drink it, then helped her settle in bed.

When the Empress Dowager was asleep, Jiang Mi walked out of the sleeping chamber, her mind turning over what her aunt had just decided about Physician Wei.

When Li Fu had come to ask, she had already guessed what her aunt would say.

Firstly — her great-uncle had killed Physician Wei's father. Whatever the reason, the Jiang family bore a genuine fault.

Secondly — it was a gesture her aunt was making for the Emperor's benefit. The Emperor had shown leniency to the Jiang family, allowing her great-uncle to go to Yizhou with an official post. The Empress Dowager did not wish to do things to excess.

Everything was settling now. The shadows that had hung over the last life were lifting. From here, the Jiang family's road would be more stable.

Jiang Mi thought to seek out Physician Duan before leaving the palace — to ask how the toxicity in her aunt's body was progressing.

She walked toward the rooms assigned to Physician Duan. The corridors were quiet.

She stood before the half-open door, about to push it, when voices inside made her pause.

"You saved us a great deal of effort by coming here when you did, young relative. Without you, this old man might not have noticed in time that it was cinnabar poisoning."

Physician Duan's voice: "Uncle Gu flatters me. I had planned to travel south to Diǎnnán in search of medicinal herbs, but the Emperor's command was not to be refused, so I came to the capital first. Fortunately, the toxicity had not yet penetrated the vital organs — had it gone any deeper, even the most skilled physician would have had nothing to offer."

Chief Physician Gu said thoughtfully, "In your assessment, how much of the Empress Dowager's constitution can be recovered?"

Physician Duan shook his head. "Hard to say. The foundation has been damaged. Let us begin with a careful course of treatment and observe. Uncle — what do you think of adding this herb to the new formula?"

Jiang Mi stood in the corridor with a look of confusion. The Su family had found Physician Duan — so why would he say the Emperor had commanded him to come? And how was he on such familiar terms with Chief Physician Gu?

Could it be that Physician Duan's arrival in the capital to treat her aunt had been Xiao Huaiyan's arrangement all along?

She waited a little while longer before pushing the door open.

Both physicians looked up in mild surprise.

Chief Physician Gu said, "Miss Jiang — is something wrong with Her Highness again?"

Jiang Mi curtseyed. "My aunt has taken her medicine and gone to sleep. I came to ask about her recovery."

The two physicians exchanged a glance. Physician Duan said, "Miss Jiang — Her Highness is improving, but the foundation has been damaged and she will need a long period of rest and care. But you need not worry — both Physician Gu and I will do everything in our power for Her Highness."

Jiang Mi thanked them with sincere gratitude.

Both physicians said in unison that she was far too kind.

......

Jiang Mi returned home toward evening.

The plaque that had read 'Cheng'en Marquessate' had already been taken down. In its place: Jiang Residence.

Her great-uncle had not yet returned. The edict had arrived before him.

Jiang Mi was taken to the main hall of the first branch of the family. She walked in to find her father, Su-shi, her great-aunt, and her cousins Jiang Hóng and Jiang Wǎn all present.

The former Marchioness, Madam Chen, saw Jiang Mi and asked urgently, "Tangtan — has the Empress Dowager sent any message?"

Jiang Mi nodded. "My aunt says — the Jiang family must hold firm. Whatever happens, there is still a Empress Dowager in the palace. And: every thunderclap and every mercy comes from the Emperor. The Jiang family is to receive it and be grateful."

Madam Chen slumped back into her seat. "Is there truly no room to appeal?"

An entire night's fall from grace — the title stripped, the post demoted — it was more than Madam Chen could absorb.

Jiang Wǎn tried to comfort her mother.

From Su-shi, Jiang Mi had learned that the imperial edict had made no mention of Jiang Qingdé's involvement in the events of the sixteenth year of Yongshun — only that he had committed a serious error in carrying out his duties and was being demoted accordingly.

Before long a manservant came running: "Madam — the First Master is back."

Everyone in the hall rose.

Jiang Qingdé walked in, supported by a servant. His face was ashen. He moved slowly.

Madam Chen cried out in alarm, thinking he had been subjected to punishment. She ran to him in tears. "Husband — husband, what has happened to you?"

Jiang Qingdé sent all the servants from the room.

He turned to Madam Chen. "I am all right. I have something to say to everyone."

He looked at Jiang Qingxuān of the second branch and at Jiang Mi. There was guilt in his face. "Second younger brother — I have wronged you all."

Bearing the pain of the stab wound, Jiang Qingdé told them the truth: the rash killing of Consort Jin's maidservants and the physician who had verified the incense.

Everyone in the room was shaken.

Jiang Qingxuān understood at last why his elder sister and his elder brother had kept this secret so closely guarded.

It truly was a disaster that could have wiped the Jiang family from existence.

Madam Chen had gone the colour of chalk, too frightened to speak another word. The First Master had been demoted to Yizhou — and that was the Emperor's mercy.

No wonder the Empress Dowager had sent Tangtan back with a message saying the Jiang family had no grounds to feel wronged.

Madam Chen sat with the bitter weight of something she could not put into words.

For the Jiang family to have survived this, though by the Emperor's lenient hand — the loss of imperial favour was real. The First Master was going to Yizhou. The Second Branch could remain in the capital, and the Empress Dowager was still in the palace. But once the Empress Dowager was gone, the Jiang family's chances of recovery would be slim. And her Yì'er — the engagement just arranged — was probably now dissolved.

......

Jiang Mi walked back from the first branch's rooms to the Yuanzhǐ Courtyard.

Her mood was heavy. She could feel the mixture of gratitude and fear in her great-uncle's reaction to the Emperor's decision.

Her father was probably wrestling with his own worries. He had never been given much weight in the Board of Works to begin with. Her great-uncle's demotion would affect him too.

And even now, though the Marquessate residence had not been confiscated, no one knew how much longer they could remain.

Perhaps the family would be divided before long.

She was still thinking when a small, thin sound reached her ears.

Not Mianmian's voice.

Jiang Mi saw Chunhuí hurrying toward her. "Mianmian — has she had her kittens?"

Chunhuí nodded vigorously. "Three kittens, Miss! They are all in their nest."

Jiang Mi went and looked. Mianmian was lying on her side, and curled against her were three round little bundles. One was pure white, just like Mianmian. The other two had yellow markings.

Mianmian saw Jiang Mi and gave a gentle meow. She shifted a paw and nudged one of the fumbling kittens gently, as though showing them off.

Jiang Mi crouched down and stroked Mianmian's head. "You worked hard, Mianmian. They are all lovely."

Mianmian extended her tongue and licked Jiang Mi's hand.

The three kittens still had their eyes closed but were lively and wriggling. Jiang Mi did not dare touch them — they were so tiny, she was afraid of misjudging her strength.

Jiang Mi said to Mianmian, "You rest well. I will have Chunhuí bring you extra nourishing food so the little ones can grow quickly."

The kittens changed a little each day. Slowly their eyes began to open.

Jiang Yì visited the Yuanzhǐ Courtyard constantly, coming to see the kittens.

"Tangtan, give me one," she said one day. "I will take good care of it."

Jiang Mi smiled. "Ask Mianmian. If she is willing, I will allow it."

Jiang Yì huffed. "Can Mianmian understand you? Just say if you do not want to, Tangtan."

Jiang Mi took Jiang Yì by the hand, crouched in front of Mianmian, and swayed their joined hands. "Mianmian — she wants one of your kittens. Are you willing?"

Mianmian went on licking her own paws. She reached out a paw and dragged a kitten that had been about to wander off back to her side.

Jiang Yì said, "You see — she is not even looking at you. She cannot understand."

Jiang Mi picked up a small bamboo ball and turned it in front of Mianmian. "Mianmian — do you remember Ningzhu? The little girl who liked you so much? She sent this bamboo ball for you. She may be going very far away now, and she will be very lonely. Would you let one of your little ones go keep her company?"

Jiang Yì turned to look at Jiang Mi. "Is Xue Ningzhu leaving the capital?"

Jiang Mi nodded without a word.

Jiang Yì also fell quiet.

The two sisters, seeing Mianmian lie still, both prepared to stand. It had only been playful talk.

Then Mianmian turned over, took the white kitten gently by the scruff, and carried it toward Jiang Mi.

She set it down. The tiny white kitten lay softly on the toe of Jiang Mi's embroidered slipper.

Jiang Mi did not dare move, afraid to knock the kitten over.

Jiang Yì's eyes went wide. "Did she actually understand — or is she just playing with you?"

Jiang Yì turned back to Mianmian. "Mianmian — what about mine?"

Mianmian turned away, settled back into her nest, tucked the other two kittens close, and began washing them.

Jiang Yì was absolutely indignant. "Tangtan — look at your Mianmian! How can she be so partial! Fine — I am claiming one from the next litter. I am absolutely decided."

Jiang Mi was busy very carefully lifting the little creature from her slipper and cupping it in her palms.

Just then Jiang Yì's maid came in hurriedly. "Miss — a caller has come from the Zhang family. Madam asks you to come back."

Jiang Yì's brow creased. She sat down in the nearest chair. "I am not going. If it is just a broken engagement, then so be it. I am not going."

The maid was urgent. "Miss — you really should go. Both the Madam from the Zhang family and the Second Young Master have come."

Jiang Yì was irritated. "What are they coming for, if they are going to break the engagement."

Jiang Mi set the kitten gently back beside Mianmian. "Sister Yi — if Great-Aunt has sent specifically for you, there must be something important. Why not go and see?"

Jiang Yì could not really sit still either. She grabbed Jiang Mi's wrist. "Come with me, Tangtan."

Unable to refuse, Jiang Mi went with her.

Both of them hid behind the flower hall screen and listened.

From Madam Chen's laughter, Jiang Mi could tell — this did not sound like a broken engagement at all.

Jiang Yì also wore a puzzled expression.

They heard a woman's voice, a little lower: "Then it is settled. The Board of Astronomy says the twenty-first of next month is an auspicious day. Though it is rather soon, we thought — since First Master Jiang will be departing for his post, it would be best if he could see Second Miss married before he goes. That is why we have moved the date forward."

Madam Chen was genuinely moved. "Thank you so much for your consideration."

A young man's voice said, "Aunt — please be at ease. I will take good care of Second Miss."

Neither Madam Chen nor the Minister's wife had expected the Zhang Second Young Master to speak up like that. Both of them began to laugh.

Behind the screen, Jiang Mi pressed her lips together to hold in a smile, looking sideways at Jiang Yì.

Jiang Yì's whole face was red. She covered it with both hands.

Madam Chen rose to see the Minister's wife and the Second Young Master out.

Jiang Mi said to Jiang Yì, "Congratulations, Second Sister."

Jiang Yì stamped her foot and reached over to tickle Jiang Mi.

When Madam Chen returned and found the two of them in a tangle, she shook her head with a helpless laugh.

This, at least, was a happy thing amid everything. The Zhang family had not broken the engagement at all — they had moved the date forward. She would never have imagined it.

chapters.title: Chapter 100
chapters.content:
Two days passed. Jiang Mi had promised Jiang Yì to help her choose the embroidery pattern for her wedding veil, and was sorting through designs when Qiuyu came in with a visitor.

Jiang Mi looked up. It was Chengzhong.

Chengzhong bowed. "Miss Jiang — someone you hold dear is setting out on a long journey. His Majesty has sent this servant to escort you."

Jiang Mi was quiet for a moment. "Please wait a moment, Eunuch Cheng."

She gathered what she had already prepared, then went to find Mianmian. Mianmian saw her coming and once again picked up the white kitten by the scruff and carried it toward her.

Whether Mianmian truly understood, Jiang Mi could not say — but ever since she had spoken to her that day, each time Jiang Mi appeared, Mianmian brought out the little white kitten.

This time Jiang Mi accepted it and cupped it in her hands. She stroked Mianmian's head. "This time it is for real, Mianmian."

Mianmian gave a small meow and bumped her cheek against Jiang Mi's palm.

......

Chengzhong saw Jiang Mi emerge carrying a bamboo basket lined with soft silk, covered over.

He moved to take it from her helpfully. Jiang Mi stepped aside. "I will manage it, Eunuch Cheng."

Chengzhong fell into line and led the way.

The carriage waiting at the side gate was a little different from the usual ones. Jiang Mi's mind was elsewhere and she did not notice.

She stepped up on the mounting block and climbed inside.

Chengzhong was just dropping the curtain, preparing to drive, when Qiuyu called out behind him: "Eunuch Cheng — Eunuch Cheng — our Miss said this must come with her."

Chengzhong turned to look. Qiuyu was leading a nanny goat.

He was baffled. But since it was Miss Jiang's instruction, he could not refuse, and called on the attendants following behind to bring the goat along.

The moment Jiang Mi stepped inside, she caught the faint scent of dragon's blood incense.

She looked up and found a man already seated in the carriage.

He wore plain white brocade robes with subtle embroidered patterns, a white jade crown — refined and striking.

Jiang Mi could only murmur, "Your Majesty."

Xiao Huaiyan was brewing tea. He poured a cup and held it toward her. "You slipped out of the palace without a word — and now you are being formal with me again? I have not forgotten any of the promises I made you."

Jiang Mi felt a small inward sigh. Of course she knew. But she still had not figured out how she was supposed to be with him.

She sat down, set the basket beside her, and accepted the cup with both hands. "Thank you, Your Majesty."

She had barely taken a sip when he asked, "What have you got there?"

Jiang Mi paused, then lifted one corner of the cover to show him.

Xiao Huaiyan was mildly surprised. A kitten — pure white all over.

He raised an eyebrow. "One of Mianmian's?"

Jiang Mi nodded.

Xiao Huaiyan laughed softly. "Fast work."

His gaze lingered on Jiang Mi's slender waist, her flat abdomen. Something in his eyes deepened.

Jiang Mi saw the little creature in the basket beginning to push at her hand, wanting out. She lifted it onto her lap and let it tumble and play.

Xiao Huaiyan watched her eyes soften and her expression grow peaceful as she patiently played with the kitten. He looked at her for a long time without quite realising it.

......

On the road out of the city, from inside a heavily guarded procession, the Grand Princess of Zhaoyang saw a carriage approaching in the distance.

A figure stepped down. When she made out who it was, the Grand Princess accepted her maid's arm and walked toward her.

Jiang Mi walked toward her in turn.

The Grand Princess narrowed her eyes. "I did not expect anyone to see us off."

Jiang Mi curtseyed. "This subject greets the Grand Princess."

The Grand Princess said, "At a time like this, what use is courtesy? That you came at all is more than this Princess expected." The great families, whatever they knew or did not know about what had happened to the Xue household, had seen the title surrendered and the voluntary departure to distant Liangzhou — and had been quick to cut their ties.

"Your Highness — may I see Ningzhu?"

"Ningzhu is asleep."

The Grand Princess saw Jiang Mi's face fall. "You should not have come, really," she said.

Then she sighed and said, "Jìnglín put you in danger. Have you ever hated him for it?"

Jiang Mi was silent.

The Grand Princess gave a rueful smile. "It is this Princess's fault too. If I had not let him discover the truth of his birth, perhaps he would have been content to be the Duke Zhen heir. You may be wondering why he chose such a road with no return."

The Grand Princess looked at the young woman before her, whose expression had turned to one of surprise, and continued. "The fault lies with the late Emperor — for his moral failure in a drunken moment, when he wronged this Princess's daughter-in-law. And with this Princess — for a single moment of weakness in letting the child live. And it should never have happened that Jìnglín found out — and once he knew, his unwillingness could never be settled. He was a prince by blood, and yet he could only be a ducal heir, a companion and subject to princes. If there had been no war of succession, if he had not watched this Emperor ascend to the throne successfully — perhaps the restlessness in him would have stayed buried. But he was consumed by his obsession. One misstep and he was beyond saving."

"Do you know why this Princess chose to tell you these things? Because this Princess knew you would have a great fortune. I wanted you to give Ningzhu your shelter. When this Princess is gone — watch over her."

The Grand Princess had been waiting, ever since she received Xue Jinglin's coffin and learned the true account from the Embroidered Guard, for the edict that would order the execution of the entire clan. Rebellion was a crime that extended to all nine degrees of kinship — not even imperial blood was exempt.

Yet when the Emperor returned to the capital, the word outside was that Jìnglín had died at rebel hands. At first she could not make sense of it. Gradually, she understood.

Confinement in Liangzhou was the best outcome the Xue line could have hoped for.

But she was old. And Ningzhu's mind had always stayed at the age of nine or so. She was afraid that when she was gone, there would be no one left to protect her.

Jiang Mi's head was still buzzing. She had had no idea the Grand Princess would tell her any of this. She could never have imagined that Young Lord Xue's origins would have another layer of secrecy.

She drew a slow breath. "Grand Princess — I think of Ningzhu as my own younger sister. I will do whatever I can to look after her." She held out the basket. "This is for Ningzhu. Will Your Highness pass it to her?"

The Grand Princess said, "Miss Jiang — this Princess believes that the truest thing she has done in her life was to bring Ningzhu into the palace on the day of the Longevity Banquet."

Jiang Mi watched the Grand Princess return to her carriage. The procession began to move.

She was just turning away when the curtain of the carriage was pushed aside. Xue Ningzhu leaned half her body out, crying, "Sister Jiang — I will miss you. I will take good care of it."

Ningzhu's voice was carried back on the wind: "Sister Jiang — I will miss you."

Jiang Mi raised her hand and waved. "I will miss you too, Ningzhu."

She watched the procession grow small in the distance, a hollow ache settling in her chest.

She walked back slowly to the carriage.

Chengzhong held the curtain aside with great attentiveness.

He said quietly, "Miss — that nanny goat you asked for has been sent ahead to join the procession. Please do not worry." He had worked out the purpose of the goat the moment he saw the kitten.

Jiang Mi gave a small nod.

She climbed back into the carriage, aware that Xiao Huaiyan was watching her.

But just now she did not want to speak. She only wanted to be quiet for a little while.

Xiao Huaiyan had a chess board out. He said to her, "Come — keep me company for a game."

Jiang Mi was startled. She looked at the board and asked, "Does Your Majesty prefer black or white?"

"You choose first."

Jiang Mi picked white.

Xiao Huaiyan took black.

The game went on for a long time. Neither of them spoke much.

Jiang Mi looked at the board and thought through each move, letting the game gradually absorb the grief she had been carrying.

She was no longer the way she used to be — in a hurry to lose quickly. She pressed against his pieces and held her ground.

For a long stretch, the outcome was genuinely unclear.

Then she laid down a move she had thought through carefully. The situation on the board shifted quickly. She saw a winning line opening up.

One more exchange. Xiao Huaiyan put down his piece, a slight smile at the corner of his mouth. "Tangtan — you have won."

Jiang Mi studied the board. She shook her head.

She looked up. "Your Majesty let me win."

Xiao Huaiyan looked back at her. His voice was low, the last syllable slightly rough.

"I am not always the one who calculates everything ahead of time. I lose sometimes too."

His eyes were like a still lake in shadow — quiet, unhurried, drawing her in without making a sound.

Jiang Mi's face grew warm under that gaze.

In everything she remembered of him, Xiao Huaiyan had always moved through the world with mastery, without being caught off guard. He had never lost.

This version of him — she did not know quite what to do with. He felt unfamiliar. And that unfamiliarity made him feel, strangely, less far away.

Xiao Huaiyan reached over and took her hand. "Tangtan — do you blame me?"

Jiang Mi was not sure whether he meant the way her great-uncle had been handled, or the way the Duke Zhen manor had been handled.

But his voice carried a kind of bleak, quiet sorrow that landed somewhere tender without warning.

Jiang Mi looked down and pressed her own fingertips together. She said softly, "This subject does not know."

The hand at his side clenched suddenly. "You may blame me if you wish."

She should blame him. She should resent him.

Before she had fully absorbed those words, Xiao Huaiyan pulled her into his arms.

Her hands came up against his chest.

She could feel his heartbeat.

"Are you not hot, Your Majesty?" Jiang Mi said, slightly muffled.

The weather was growing warm. Being held like this made her vaguely flustered.

Xiao Huaiyan heard that and the darkness in his eyes dissolved into laughter. He pressed his lips to her earlobe. "I am... quite warm."

But holding her — soft, cool, with that sweet fragrance — he was not willing to let go.

Xiao Huaiyan captured her hand, guiding her fingertip to trace across his face.

Jiang Mi watched her own finger move along his jaw, across those fine-edged lips, his straight nose...

Those long narrow phoenix eyes — with a warmth like flame.

The flush spread from her face all the way down her neck. She turned her head aside, but the warmth still lingered around her.

Xiao Huaiyan looked at the pale, smooth curve of her neck and bent toward it.

His hand traced slowly along that narrow waist.

The carriage rolled on, unhurried. When dusk fell it came to rest again at the back gate of the Jiang residence.

Jiang Mi pushed him away, straightened her skirts, and was about to lift the curtain.

Xiao Huaiyan said, "Tangtan."

She paused. She looked back and met his eyes. He said, "I do not want to wait much longer."

Jiang Mi released the curtain in silence and stepped down from the carriage.

......

The Jiang family was now focused on two things at once.

On one hand, preparing for Jiang Yì's wedding. On the other, sorting through what Jiang Qingdé would need for his journey to take up his new post in Yizhou.

As for the spring examinations — Jiang Hóng had sat them, without great confidence in his chances, and sent a manservant to check the results more out of habit than hope.

The manservant came sprinting back, overjoyed. The eldest young master's name was on the board — ranked one hundred and thirty-fourth.

The entire Jiang household erupted with happiness. Madam Chen distributed generous tips to the messenger on the spot, and everyone in the residence received a bonus.

For the Jiang family at this time, it was a true and welcome cause for celebration.

Jiang Qingdé and Jiang Qingxuān were both deeply relieved. The ranking was not high — but it was a degree, and that mattered.

Jiang Mi and her sisters all went to Jiang Hóng's courtyard to congratulate him.

He was beaming. He looked at these sisters of his — each one lovely — and thought at last he could do something to help them.

Listening to his sisters ask about the examinations, he said with a smile, "I have to say — much of the credit goes to my friend Shen. His guidance and insights along the way were invaluable."

Jiang Yì said, puzzled, "Shen? Could that be the third son of Grand Secretary Shen's family?"

Jiang Hóng nodded. "Qiānxiū — he took first place this session. After the palace examination, he will certainly be named first rank."

Jiang Mi set her teacup down quietly. That matched what she knew.

In the last life, her elder cousin had failed this examination. It seemed Shen Qiānxiū was truly gifted — even spending time with him had benefited her cousin enormously.

Ten days later, the palace examination confirmed it. Shen Qiānxiū was named top scholar. Jiang Hóng was granted the title of presented scholar.

The parade through the city in honour of the new top scholar — Jiang Mi did not go to watch.

Jiang Yì urgently needed help choosing the embroidery for her veil, and Jiang Mi stayed home with her.

As she sorted through the silk thread colours she said, teasing, "Your dark charcoal young master also passed his examination — are you not curious to go and see?"

Jiang Yì shot her a look and reached for her waist. Jiang Mi dodged away, laughing.

Jiang Yì said with mock irritation, "He was not in the top three, there is nothing to see. Besides — I heard the new top scholar was pelted with handkerchiefs and silk pouches and flowers and fruit all down the street. He is a Grand Secretary's son on top of that, and now first-ranked scholar — every noble young lady in the capital will be fighting over him."

Jiang Mi pressed her lips together and smiled.

Jiang Yì looked at Jiang Mi's face for a moment, then pulled her arm. "Tangtan — what are you thinking now? Has Second Uncle taken any steps about your marriage yet? Do you have any thoughts?" She hesitated. "Actually — at the hunt at the Fèngchí travelling palace, if Young Lord Xue had not been there, I thought you and Shen Qiānxiū were rather well-suited. Only now that he is such a prize, with everyone after him — if you have any such inclination, you might ask Aunt to arrange a marriage directly, claim him before someone else does..."

Jiang Mi's eyes went wide. She reached out and covered Jiang Yì's mouth. "Sister Yi — please do not say such things." The word 'arrange' made her heart stutter.

Jiang Yì, caught off guard, deflated a little. She pulled Jiang Mi's hand away and sighed. "I am only talking. I know Grand Secretary Shen's family has real influence and is close to the Emperor — even Aunt's word might not be enough there. What I really mean, Tangtan, is — do not lose heart. Your marriage will come right. Aunt and Second Uncle will both be paying attention now."

Jiang Mi knew Jiang Yì was trying to look out for her. Her own marriage — she did not know whether she should accept what was being offered. She could feel that his patience was nearly at its limit.

She smiled at Jiang Yì. "I understand, Sister Yi. Now come and look at this peony design — do you like it?"

Jiang Yì saw she was deflecting, but said no more. She leaned over to look at the design in Jiang Mi's hands.

......

Madam Chen had always believed that Jiang Yì's marriage going smoothly and Jiang Hóng's examination success were the Buddha's way of watching over them. She resolved to take the Jiang sisters and Jiang Hóng all together to the Qiānshuāng Temple to give thanks.

Even Jiang Mi was drawn along by Jiang Yì.

The Qiānshuāng Temple always had abundant incense offerings. Jiang Mi followed Madam Chen to the main hall to worship. Along the way she saw many ladies from official families who had come to pray for auspicious marriages for their daughters.

Most of these ladies behaved as though they did not see Madam Chen — where before they might have exchanged a few polite words, now they kept their distance.

Madam Chen led the Jiang sisters with her chin lifted, eyes forward. She knew she would have to grow used to this difference sooner or later.

Then there was a small commotion ahead. A group of people moved through the crowd like a tide parting around them.

The Jiang family glanced over. At the centre was the wife and daughters of Grand Secretary Shen's house.

All the nearby ladies were smiling broadly and making way for the Shen matriarch.

Madam Chen gave a quiet sound and led the Jiang sisters into the Guānyīn Hall.

Madam Chen asked Jiang Mi and Jiang Wǎn to draw lots first, whispering to the bodhisattva: "May the Buddha grant good marriages and keep everyone safe and well."

Jiang Mi and Jiang Wǎn exchanged a glance and each suppressed a smile.

Both pressed their palms together and breathed their private hopes, then picked up the lot-drawing tubes and began to shake.

A bamboo slip dropped from Jiang Mi's tube after a few shakes.

She picked it up. Lot number nine.

Madam Chen brightened at once. "Tangtan — go quickly and have the interpreting monk read your lot."

Jiang Yì, who had just finished her offering of thanks, came over and saw the lot in Jiang Mi's hand. "Come — I will go with you."

Jiang Mi had no choice but to go along. She came to the lot-reading table, where an elderly monk sat half-dozing. Each pilgrim who came would hand him a lot, he would announce which number it was, and hand over the written interpretation.

Jiang Mi held out her bamboo slip. The old monk accepted it as he always did.

Then the eyes he had been keeping half-closed opened wide. "A great auspicious lot!"

He raised his head and studied the young woman before him with genuine attention. "Miss has a karmic affinity with the Buddha — to draw a great auspicious lot! Of the lots in this temple dedicated to the Guānyīn, there are only three of this kind. Whatever lies in miss's heart, all of it shall come to pass as she hopes."

Jiang Yì was delighted. "Tangtan — it is the great auspicious lot!"

Jiang Mi was a little surprised herself.

Before the old monk had finished speaking, the Shen family came up beside them.

The Shen matriarch and Shen Yǎowēi both heard what the monk had said.

Shen Yǎowēi squeezed the bamboo slip in her own hand, something uneasy in her.

She stepped forward with her mother and offered her slip.

The old monk resumed his drowsy expression. He glanced at it. "Lowest lot. Would you like the reading?"

The Shen matriarch startled. "Surely you have not made a mistake, Venerable Master?"

The monk recited without hesitation: "Do not heed idle words of right or wrong; morning and evening let the name of Amitābha be your guide. If you take idle imaginings for truth, how can a painted cake ever fill the hunger?" He finished and glanced at Shen Yǎowēi, then repeated the last line. "How can a painted cake ever fill the hunger?"

Shen Yǎowēi felt a flush of indignation rising up through her. She took her mother's arm. "Mother — I do not want an interpretation. What is the point of this sort of thing anyway?"

The Shen matriarch was startled by her words and hurried to steer her away. "Āwēi — you must not speak like that."

She was also made uncomfortable by the verse the monk had read — Yǎowēi had been praying about a marriage, so why had it come out as lowest lot with painted cakes and an empty belly?

Shen Yǎowēi said, "Mother — I am going to find Third Elder Brother."

Walking away, Shen Yǎowēi's mind was still on what the monk had said to Jiang Mi just now. The Jiang family was in trouble — title stripped, position demoted, clearly no longer in favour. How could a great auspicious lot possibly make sense for them? And how could all of it come to pass as hoped?

......

Jiang Mi came out of the Guānyīn Hall. Madam Chen had spotted the Madam of the Minister of Revenue's family — Jiang Yì's future mother-in-law — and the Second Young Master was there as well. Madam Chen led Jiang Yì off to speak with them. Jiang Wǎn and Jiang Hóng had gone to the Mañjuśrī Hall.

Jiang Mi thought of the prayer tree she had seen last time with its wishes tied in red silk.

Following her memory, she walked in that direction.

Before long, she saw the great tree.

Jiang Mi walked to its base and looked up at the ribbons of red silk crowding every branch, each one carrying a wish. There was something peaceful about it.

Looking more closely, the tree seemed a little different from the time she had come before to tie her own ribbon.

A little shorter, perhaps.

She was still puzzling over this when footsteps came from behind.

She turned. A young man in blue-grey robes stood not far away.

He gave Jiang Mi a bow with clasped hands and a smile. "I thought it might be you, Miss Jiang. Forgive me for approaching unannounced."

Shen Qiānxiū.

Jiang Mi returned the courtesy. "Shen Gōngzǐ."

Shen Qiānxiū looked up at the tree and said, "Have you come to make a wish again, Miss Jiang?"

She had no red silk with her and had written nothing. She had only come on a whim to look at the tree.

He continued, "Did the wish you made last time come true?"

Jiang Mi paused, then turned the question back. "And yours, Gōngzǐ?"

Shen Qiānxiū smiled with easy pleasure. "Heaven and the bodhisattva have been generous — more than half of it has come true."

Jiang Mi nodded. "Congratulations, Gōngzǐ."

Shen Qiānxiū said, "The other half requires me to ask the Miss a question."

Jiang Mi looked at him in puzzlement.

Shen Qiānxiū drew a slow breath. He wanted to use this rare chance of finding her here. He stepped forward. "Miss Jiang — I wonder if this Shen now has standing to come and propose to your family?"

chapters.title: Chapter 101
chapters.content:
Having said the words, Shen Qiānxiū's heart was unsteady. He thought he might not have been this nervous even at the palace examination.

He looked quietly at the young woman standing beneath the tree. A breeze stirred her skirts — she was like a living painting of the Goddess of the Luo River. He had gone slightly absent from himself.

Then he saw Jiang Mi take a step back. He collected himself and said quickly, "Miss Jiang — I know this was sudden. Please do not be angry. I could not help myself when I saw you here. I simply wanted to ask you first."

His words genuinely surprised her. In the early days she had once considered Shen Qiānxiū as a possible patron for the family — then gradually set the idea aside. The Shen family had shown no particular regard for the Jiangs, and she did not know why he would say such a thing now. If anyone overheard, it could cause trouble. The Jiang family in its current state could not weather fresh gossip.

Jiang Mi said quietly, "Master Shen — matters of marriage are decided by parents and arranged through a matchmaker. Your honoured mother will find you a good match. I must be going."

Shen Qiānxiū stopped short. He knew what he had said was improper. If he were serious, the right way was to seek his parents' approval first, then have a go-between approach the Jiang family elders. To speak to her directly like this was presumptuous.

He had not gone about it well.

Before he could say anything more, a bright voice came from behind him. "Third Elder Brother — there you are. I have been looking everywhere for you."

He turned. Shen Yǎowēi, in a pale green dress, came toward them with a smile.

She held her handkerchief and feigned surprise. "Oh — Miss Jiang is here too."

Jiang Mi looked at her. She said with an easy smile, "The prayer tree at the Qiānshuāng Temple has always been famous. I came especially to have a look. Miss Shen — here to make a wish as well?"

Shen Yǎowēi's eyes moved between Jiang Mi and her brother. Her smile went a little stiff. "Yes — yes, the prayer tree here is very efficacious. I heard about it and came to see. Although I understand this tree was newly planted — I wonder if it is still as effective as the old one..."

Shen Qiānxiū frowned. He was plainly displeased by the interruption.

He cut her off. "Āwēi — what did you want?"

Shen Yǎowēi could tell her brother was impatient. "Mother is waiting for you in the meditation hall. You should go quickly, Third Elder Brother."

Shen Qiānxiū did not want to leave, but this was not the moment. He would need to speak openly to his mother first, then have her send a go-between to sound out the Jiang family's wishes, and only afterward have a formal matchmaker call.

He looked at Jiang Mi for a long moment, bowed, and said, "Miss Jiang — I must take my leave."

After Shen Qiānxiū left, Jiang Mi had no wish to remain alone with Shen Yǎowēi and prepared to go as well.

Shen Yǎowēi called after her. "Miss Jiang."

She came toward her, smiling. "Actually — I heard what my third brother just said."

Jiang Mi stopped. She looked at Shen Yǎowēi.

Shen Yǎowēi offered a faintly apologetic smile. "I will be honest with you, Miss Jiang — my mother has been looking at a young lady from the Duke Ningguo's house for my third brother. She called him over just now so both families' elders could have a look."

Jiang Mi thought she should have gone with Wǎn-jiě to the Mañjuśrī Hall. Then she would not have walked into any of this. Whatever Shen Qiānxiū did with his marriage was no concern of hers.

Jiang Mi smiled. "That is indeed a happy occasion."

Shen Yǎowēi had expected to see Jiang Mi look pained. How was she still smiling with such perfect composure? Should she not be unhappy, or at least wistful?

Shen Yǎowēi said, "I believe this is the second time we have run into each other here at the Qiānshuāng Temple. What a coincidence. Miss Jiang — do you know that our Shen family has kept a spirit lamp burning here for years?"

Jiang Mi nodded. "I have heard something of it."

"It is for my sister Shen Yǎoróng — once the betrothed of the current Emperor."

Shen Yǎowēi looked at Jiang Mi's bright face and continued, "My sister died for the Emperor's sake. His Majesty has always shown the Shen family great favour. The fact that he has not yet established an Empress means that position is being kept for our family. Miss Jiang — I am nearly of age." Though she tried to contain it, the boastfulness in her tone was impossible to hide.

Jiang Mi understood the implication — that when Shen Yǎowēi came of age, that would be the moment Xiao Huaiyan named an Empress.

But even in the last life, Xiao Huaiyan had not named an Empress after Shen Yǎowēi came of age. Later the Shen family matriarch passed away, Grand Secretary Shen observed mourning, and Shen Yǎowēi was in mourning alongside.

Jiang Mi understood what Shen Yǎowēi was really saying: don't set your sights on my brother. The Shen family's future glory would be beyond anything she could hope to aspire to.

Jiang Mi found it faintly amusing. For someone so young, Shen Yǎowēi had quite an intricate set of schemes.

She smiled. "Then let me offer my congratulations in advance, Miss Shen."

Jiang Mi walked past her and away. She was tired and wanted only to find her great-aunt and go home.

Shen Yǎowēi watched her go, feeling exactly as if she had swung a fist into a mass of cotton — unsatisfying in every way. Jiang Mi was supposed to feel dejected and envious. Why was she so entirely unmoved?

......

On her way back to the main temple, Jiang Mi found herself turning over what Shen Yǎowēi had just said — that her sister had died for the Emperor's sake. In everything Jiang Mi knew, the Shen family's eldest legitimate daughter had died of sudden illness. Had something else happened?

Lost in thought, she looked up and saw a grey-robed elderly monk walking toward her. She stepped left to make way.

The old monk stopped. He pressed his palms together and said to Jiang Mi, "Amitābha. Benefactress, please wait a moment."

Jiang Mi stopped. "Venerable Master — what is it?"

The old monk studied her for a moment and said, with an air of meaning, "Benefactress has a deep affinity with the Buddha."

She found this a little odd. This was the second time today someone had told her she had an affinity with the Buddha. Was the temple simply hoping the Jiang family would make a larger donation?

But the elderly monk before her had a gentle and wise appearance, the bearing of someone of genuine virtue. He did not seem to be angling for anything.

She could not help asking, "Why do you say so, Venerable Master?"

The grey-robed monk looked toward a tall pagoda to the south. He said unhurriedly, "Does the benefactress know what is enshrined in that pagoda?"

Jiang Mi shook her head. "I do not." She was unfamiliar with the Qiānshuāng Temple and did not know the history of the pagoda.

The old monk returned his gaze to her. "For a hundred years, the pagoda has housed the sacred relic of an eminent monk. According to legend, this golden relic possesses the power to restore life. Using the blood of the one who petitions as the catalyst, and burning through the years remaining to them, it can call the petitioner back in a future life."

Jiang Mi's heart lurched. She murmured, "Could such a thing truly exist?"

The monk said, "This monk cannot say whether the legend is true. Nor would it be possible for anyone to verify it now. That golden relic, on an unremarkable day last year in the ninth month, dissolved into dust without warning and was scattered by the wind into the heavens and earth."

Jiang Mi quietly clenched her hands inside her sleeves. Her palms were damp.

The grey-robed monk smiled gently. "Do not be troubled, benefactress. This monk only spoke at such length because he saw that your affinity with the Buddha is profound."

He pressed his palms together, recited the Buddha's name, and went on his way.

Jiang Mi stood where she was, eyes on the distant pagoda, the monk's words still ringing in her ears.

The golden relic — could it truly have called a person back in a future life?

She carried that thought with her as she rejoined the Jiang family.

On the carriage home, Jiang Yì saw her looking downcast and said, "What is the matter, Tangtan? You drew the great auspicious lot — why the long face?"

Both Madam Chen and Jiang Wǎn looked over at Jiang Mi.

Jiang Mi shook her head. "I am all right. Just a little sleepy, Sister Yi. Let me rest against you."

Jiang Yì generously let Jiang Mi lie with her head on her lap.

Jiang Mi lay with her eyes closed, hovering between sleep and waking, as images flickered past too quickly to catch.

Back in the Yuanzhǐ Courtyard, she felt as if she had not quite woken, and continued to lie in bed in a drowsy haze.

She slept more deeply than she had in the carriage.

She knew when she had slipped into a dream.

She was walking through the imperial palace — but she felt at once that this dream was unlike any she had had before. It was not the last life she knew.

The palace was empty. She walked for a long time and saw not a single court attendant.

It was very quiet. Even birdsong and insects were absent.

White mourning cloth drifted everywhere. The whole palace seemed drained of all colour, grey and dim.

She saw the Héngwú Hall — the hall she had once lived in.

Something pulled her inside.

When she stepped through the threshold, she saw the first spot of colour.

A butterfly kite, brilliant with paint, hung from the branch of a tree.

The further she walked, the more kites appeared — every kind imaginable, placed in the grass, on the ground, on the tables, filling the courtyard until there was scarcely room to move.

At the far end of all those kites, a figure sat at a table with his back to her, apparently painting.

He was dressed entirely in white. Every one of those kites had been made by his hand.

A gust of wind rose. A string of bells rang out.

The figure turned.

It was Xiao Huaiyan.

That same handsome face — yet his expression was cold and shadowed, nothing like the warm, composed manner she knew. And where his hair had been dark as ink, white had crept in at both temples.

Jiang Mi stood frozen. She was directly in front of him, yet he seemed not to see her at all. His eyes moved toward where the bells had rung.

Jiang Mi followed his gaze and saw it — the gold-and-jade bell anklet.

Xiao Huaiyan gave a short, self-mocking laugh, his voice low and rough. "It is not you."

A wrench of grief rose in Jiang Mi's chest. She tried to walk toward him and found she could not move.

The scene before her blurred. Then darkness.

......

A peal of thunder rolled through the gathering clouds. Lightning cut across the sky in coiling arcs, and the rain that had been building for so long came down in a deluge, hammering against the windows.

Jiang Mi opened her eyes slowly. She sat up and touched the dried traces of tears on her face.

She put on a thin outer robe and climbed out of bed. The rain had already let up somewhat.

The shower had cooled the air a little.

Jiang Mi pushed open the lattice window and breathed in the smell of wet grass and rain.

She looked at the flowers and plants beaten down by the rain, her thoughts adrift.

Then a figure appeared in her line of sight.

Jiang Mi startled, and before she could collect herself the figure had already walked in.

Xiao Huaiyan was in a dark everyday robe, and the rain had soaked one shoulder through.

He came toward the woman sitting by the window, his gaze somewhat heavy. He saw the faint confusion on her face.

He softened his expression. "Where did you go?"

Jiang Mi looked up at him and pressed her lips together. "Your Majesty already knows, does he not?"

Otherwise he would not be here.

Xiao Huaiyan lifted her and sat her on his knee. Jiang Mi's hands rested loosely on his shoulder.

She looked at the wet patch on his clothing and lowered her eyes.

Xiao Huaiyan tilted her chin up and bent to kiss her.

He was always the most tormenting when he kissed her. She breathed in ragged bursts, half-numb, and pressed urgently against his hand.

Xiao Huaiyan's eyes darkened. He tugged loose his own collar and the tension in his chest eased somewhat.

He said, his voice mild, "Today the Prince of Píngnán came to ask me to arrange a marriage for Princess Shūyí. I think the new top scholar would be rather suitable. Tangtan — what do you think?"

So he had heard about what Shen Qiānxiū said at the Qiānshuāng Temple.

Jiang Mi sighed. "Your Majesty should not be matchmaking for people at random."

Xiao Huaiyan said, "Are you reluctant?"

Seeing his brow tighten, Jiang Mi found that, for some reason, she was not as afraid as she used to be.

She pinched her own fingertips together, lashes flickering, and said quietly, "Is Your Majesty not reluctant to give the Shen family's daughter away then?"

Xiao Huaiyan's expression went slightly strange. He had never heard Jiang Mi ask him something like that.

He took hold of her pale wrist and folded her soft hand inside his. "What Shen daughter?"

Jiang Mi looked up at him. "Has Your Majesty never considered giving the Empress's position to the Shen family? Grand Secretary Shen is a pillar of the court — his daughter would be far more suited to the Empress's role."

Xiao Huaiyan looked at her steadily. "I have never considered it. My Empress's position is reserved for the one I myself have chosen."

chapters.title: Chapter 102
chapters.content:
Her almond eyes were naturally beautiful — full and glistening, enough to draw sympathy from anyone who looked. And now her lips were a deep and vivid red, the corners of her eyes flushed, a sweetness in her beauty that turned to something warmer.

The scent of her kept drifting into Xiao Huaiyan's breath.

He looked at her looking at him like that, and his eyes darkened.

He wound a loose strand of her hair around his finger. "The one I have chosen — you know better than anyone who that is. Why do you still think I would give the Empress's position to the Shen family?"

Jiang Mi looked away from him. After hesitating a moment, she asked: "Does Your Majesty not wish to make it up to the Shen family?"

Xiao Huaiyan's brow lifted slightly. A faint smile appeared. That she could ask this directly was a good sign.

He had no intention of hiding it. "It seems you have heard some things. The late Emperor once arranged a match between myself and a daughter of the Shen family. At that time Shen Chānghéng had not yet entered the Grand Secretariat. But the Prince of Jin and the Prince of Qí were still unwilling to see me form a connection with the Shen family. That eldest Shen daughter met with misfortune on an outing one day. To protect her family and to protect my name, she took her own life."

"The Shen family suppressed the matter and told the world she had died of sudden illness. I felt guilt over it and treated the Shen family generously — my people worked to clear the path for Shen Chānghéng's entry into the Grand Secretariat. The Shen family's covert support of my cause was something they had no choice but to offer: the late Emperor's engagement edict made their position inevitable. If someone else had claimed the throne, the Shen family would have fared no better. They backed the right side — and I will naturally give them a clear path upward. What need has that of an Empress as recompense?"

Jiang Mi was very still.

In the last life, Xiao Huaiyan had delayed naming an Empress for so long that everyone had assumed he was waiting for Shen Yǎowēi to come of age. Yet what he had just said meant he had never once considered giving the Shen family that position?

In the last life, Noble Consort Duān had been a cover. Consort Róu's favour had been performance. And taking a Shen as Empress had never been on his mind.

Jiang Mi thought of the monk's words about the golden relic. She thought of the man in the dream, white at his temples, in an empty palace.

There was no escaping it. No hiding from it.

Xiao Huaiyan... can I truly try again with you? Can I trust you one more time?

Xiao Huaiyan saw her go quiet. He pressed a kiss to the corner of her lips. "That you would ask these things — does it mean you have started to care about me a little?"

Jiang Mi made no sound. She did not know how to answer.

Xiao Huaiyan turned her face toward him so she could not look away. "Tangtan — I will not permit you to dwell on anyone who does not concern me. You are mine!"

Jiang Mi exhaled quietly, and at last let her eyes close. She let the kiss hold her — long, burning, unwilling to release — and could not help a small trembling.

Xiao Huaiyan rose with her in his arms and carried her to the bed. Jiang Mi's embroidered slippers were slipped from her feet.

Silk-stockinged feet curled inward. A gentle press, and she sank into the quilted bedding.

Xiao Huaiyan stood tall at the bedside, his gaze lowering steadily toward Jiang Mi, his hand moving to his waist sash as though to undo it.

Seeing the motion, Jiang Mi shrank back against the bed, a flicker of apprehension in her eyes.

Xiao Huaiyan leaned down over her. "Do not be afraid. I will not hurt you..."

Jiang Mi knew that in the moment she had accepted, this could no longer be avoided. From what she understood of Xiao Huaiyan, he had run out of patience...

A soft, broken sound came from behind the bed hangings. A snow-pale hand reached out and gripped the curtain, fingertips whitening with force.

Then another arm covered it, drawing the hand back inside.

After a time, Xiao Huaiyan stepped down from the bed. He went to the table and poured a cup of water. He pulled back the hangings and helped the person inside — now soft as warm silk — to sit up.

Jiang Mi's face was flushed. She looked at Xiao Huaiyan's fingers on the teacup and turned her head away.

He laughed low, held out the water. "Are you not thirsty?"

Jiang Mi glanced at his lips, thought of what had just been done, and wanted to pull the quilt over her head and not come out.

Xiao Huaiyan sat on the edge of the bed, and since she seemed unwilling to take the cup, placed it in her hands and let her drink on her own.

He steadied his own breathing. His gaze rested on her pale, smooth skin, and his throat moved.

He reached over and smoothed her disordered hair back from her face. His voice was low. "Tangtan — I will wait until our wedding night."

Jiang Mi was in the middle of drinking. At those sudden words she choked, pressing her hand to her mouth and coughing softly.

She had assumed Xiao Huaiyan would take everything tonight. He had not gone to the end — but he had not spared her entirely either.

Her expression shifted. She heard what he meant: he did not want to wait any longer. He intended to name her Empress and hold the wedding.

She would be entering the palace again very soon.

Though this life was different from the last, her heart was still uncertain — she had nothing in her hands to hold on to.
