It was only in taking from her, again and again, feeling her warmth and her presence, that his arid inner world found any peace.

chapters.title: After the Wedding, Part Three
chapters.content:
Sunlight filtered through the window and fell on Jiang Mi, wrapping her in a soft golden warmth.

As she read on, she found herself drawn into the landscape and customs described in the text. At one passage she stopped and asked with a small laugh: "When Your Majesty passed through that place where a girl on an embroidered-ball tower was choosing a husband — did she toss the ball toward Your Majesty's direction?"

Xiao Huaiyan opened his eyes, his voice very quiet. "Guess." He was faintly surprised — he had barely mentioned it in passing, and she had asked about it specifically.

Jiang Mi glanced down and met the burning steadiness of his gaze. That face of his — even stripped of his imperial status — would be striking enough to draw anyone.

Needless to say, the ball had been thrown at him.

She murmured under her breath: "Your Majesty is blessed with quite remarkable romantic fortune."

Xiao Huaiyan's eyes moved with a glint of amusement. "That remark is not wrong."

Jiang Mi snorted inwardly and chose not to respond.

She returned to the manuscript and turned to the next page to continue.

Xiao Huaiyan listened quietly, and the oppressive feeling that had been pressing in on him from inside seemed to be soothed a little.

Soft sounds have a way of making the mind drift.

Just as Jiang Mi sank again into the text and its wonders of distant places, her voice changed — becoming hesitant, with a faint catch of breath.

A tint of rose had risen in her face and the sunlight passing through made it all the more mesmerising.

Without her noticing, her sash had been untied and her collar had come slightly open.

Jiang Mi pressed against the hand that had slipped inside. "No — this won't do."

His eyes darkened. His palm closed around her hand. "I did not tell you to stop. Keep reading."

In these days of living with Xiao Huaiyan, he had been almost entirely accommodating — only rather frequent in this particular area — and had never refused what she asked for. She had been testing his limits in their dealings, and this was the first time his tone had been this firm.

Jiang Mi was pressed further into the couch until her back was against the wall, half-reclining there, her dress worked open, her legs pale and long.

Xiao Huaiyan shifted positions, pressing against those slender legs. He looked up at her. "Why have you stopped reading?"

In this situation, how was she supposed to read anything? She watched Xiao Huaiyan bend his head.

She shrank back in alarm, but there was nowhere left to retreat.

She could feel that his grip was strong; no amount of struggling pulled her free.

In this open daylight, even the little moles on her most private skin were entirely visible.

Jiang Mi's face blazed so hot she thought she would combust. Shame washed over her.

She trembled helplessly, raised the manuscript to cover her own face, and wept in a small voice: "Wuu — Your Majesty is bullying me. If you want it read, read it yourself."

Xiao Huaiyan lifted his head. He looked at her flustered, aggrieved expression, and smiled slowly. "Very well — since you don't like that one, shall I read you something else?"

"Suddenly coming upon a grove of peach blossoms, lining both banks for hundreds of steps, with no other trees among them, the grass below fresh and fair, petals falling in drifts..."

"The clouds above grow blue as if to rain, the waters stretch on and on into mist..."

Jiang Mi heard him recite the well-known lines and felt both shame and indignation. Travel writing passages sounded utterly strange coming from Xiao Huaiyan's low voice — he was doing it deliberately to torment her.

She was mortified. She had never seen him so entirely without shame.

She threw the manuscript at him. "Stop, stop reading! Your Majesty only knows how to bully me, Your Majesty is nothing but a liar..."

Xiao Huaiyan paused. The smile at his mouth deepened. He propped himself and leaned in to kiss her.

Jiang Mi turned her head to dodge his lips, both hands against his chest.

She refused.

Xiao Huaiyan, seeing that, laughed aloud for some reason. He turned her face and tipped her chin. "I bullied you? Where exactly did I bully you?"

He bit her lightly. "Here?"

"Or here?"

Jiang Mi's almond eyes were wide and hazy with shock before she had even recovered.

He continued: "I am afraid to use too much force in case you call it painful, and afraid to use too little in case it is not enough — where exactly would I dare bully you?"

His voice was low with a trace of roughness.

Jiang Mi's mind went blank. Her first instinct was to cover his mouth with her hand.

But her palm touching his lips — burning, suggestive. She snatched it back immediately and covered her own scalding ears instead. Those wanton, shameless words — they were entirely too much to bear.

Xiao Huaiyan's high, straight nose brushed the back of her hand. Knowing she could still hear: "Tangtan — there is no use in hiding. And this is not bullying — this is what is natural between a husband and wife."

"Because I want to be close to you. I want more."

He pressed a kiss to her lips, and those thin lips traced their way down to her slender, fragile neck.

Jiang Mi's whole body trembled. His breath came against her ear, the faint scent of ambergris enveloping her.

Her breathing gradually grew heavier. Afraid of making an embarrassing sound, she wanted again to bite down on her own fingers.

Xiao Huaiyan caught her wrist once more. "Do not bite yourself. Tangtan — your voice is pretty. Do not hold it in."

Jiang Mi was drenched in perspiration, her hair-pins crooked, her hair coming down. She slumped boneless against him, eyes unfocused.

Xiao Huaiyan carried her to the bathhouse.

In the warm water she recovered a little.

She lay quietly against the side of the pool — but then Xiao Huaiyan was pressing close again, and she had no strength left to deal with him. She hooked an arm around his neck and raised her leg...

Xiao Huaiyan's expression changed. He gave her a light smack. "Who taught you that."

Jiang Mi pressed her lips together, slightly nervous. "Was it not Your Majesty?"

Xiao Huaiyan's brow lifted. "You have made progress!"

Seeing this, she immediately turned her voice soft. "Your Majesty — I cannot anymore... I am too tired."

She had been trying to move things along, and it had had precisely the opposite effect.

This particular urgency of his was not simply what he claimed. He had made her read those travel manuscripts, then recited a few lines himself. She thought of the Sōngxún book that had disappeared from the table and understood it perfectly now.

She thought for a moment and asked: "Your Majesty — were you angry today?"

Xiao Huaiyan smiled as he looked at her. "Why would you ask that?"

"Was Your Majesty displeased by the book this concubine was reading?"

Xiao Huaiyan saw she had understood his meaning, so he said directly: "It is not the book — it is the person. Tangtan — you may read any book, and I will find you whatever you want. But you must not dwell on someone who is no concern of mine."

Jiang Mi rarely spoke to Xiao Huaiyan this plainly. She was quiet for a beat and then said: "And what of Your Majesty? There was Miss Xiè, Cousin Liǔ, Miss Shěn — and the women in Yúnzhōu, the friends made during study travels. Has this concubine asked about any of them even once? I was only reading a book. The person has nothing to do with it."

Whatever Xiao Huaiyan thought, she still needed to make herself clear.

Xiao Huaiyan frowned. "What a collection of random people — none of those have anything to do with me either."

And then, as if remembering something, he pulled her into his arms and said quietly against her hair: "My romantic fortune — only you."

chapters.title: After the Wedding, Part Four
chapters.content:
Jiang Mi — had she any strength left — would very much have liked to scratch Xiao Huaiyan.

What on earth was he saying!

She looked up at him. His long phoenix eyes were curved with laughter, his beautiful face entirely too capable of leading people astray.

Inwardly she thought: he is coaxing me again, surely.

She leaned against him and watched the wavering patterns on the water, and felt her own heart go a little unsteady along with them.

The following day she slept until the sun was high. Xiao Huaiyan had long since left for court.

Jiang Mi sat up with the quilt around her, head in her hand, and thought vaguely that she was becoming more and more lax.

When they had first been married, she had still held herself to a small watchfulness — tired as she was, she had not dared to sleep too deeply, had woken when Xiao Huaiyan rose in the morning and attended him as he dressed and saw him out.

But since Xiao Huaiyan started pressing her back down to keep sleeping, she had given in more deeply each time.

At first she had been able to sense when he was getting up. Now she slept straight through and knew nothing at all.

She had barely finished her morning meal when Qiuyu came in hurriedly and curtseyed. "Your Highness — the Empress Dowager has changed her departure date for Wǔtái Mountain. She is leaving today."

Jiang Mi's heart lurched.

Was her aunt not supposed to leave in three days?

Why the sudden change?

She rode the phoenix palanquin to the Ci'ning Palace in haste and found palace maids carrying trunk after trunk out to the carriages.

The Empress Dowager stood nearby, leaning on Matron Cuī's arm.

Jiang Mi hurried forward. "Aunt!"

In her agitation she used the title from before her marriage.

The Empress Dowager beckoned to her. "Tangtan — do not rush. Mind your footing."

She had thought she had a few more days. She had not imagined it would be so sudden. She took the Empress Dowager's hand. "Empress Mother — why was the date moved forward? Why did you not tell me sooner?"

The Empress Dowager said with a smile: "The weather looked fine today. I was afraid it might rain in a few days and make the road difficult."

Jiang Mi heard the excuse at once. "Then wait for the rain to stop and find another good day."

The Empress Dowager shook her head. She tapped the tip of Jiang Mi's nose with one finger. "If we do that, I may never reach Wǔtái Mountain at all. I know you are reluctant to let me go — so this is better, leaving on a day like today without warning."

A pang of grief went through Jiang Mi. Once her aunt left, the inner palace would feel very empty.

Not wanting her aunt to worry, she made herself smile naturally. "Since you have made up your mind, take everything Tangtan prepared for you — I already had Official Sun's people bring it over."

The Empress Dowager nodded with a smile, then could not resist adding one more reminder: "Remember well what I told you earlier."

She glanced pointedly at Jiang Mi's abdomen as she said it.

While the two were still talking, the imperial palanquin arrived from the other direction.

Xiao Huaiyan had heard the Empress Dowager was leaving that day and had come to see her off.

In all outward forms the Empress Dowager was his adoptive mother — and more importantly, she was Tangtan's closest family.

He needed to be here.

He looked at Jiang Mi, who was visibly downcast, and came to stand beside her. He said warmly to the Empress Dowager: "Empress Mother — the road to Wǔtái Mountain is long. Take good care of yourself."

The Empress Dowager said: "With the imperial guard the Emperor has sent as escort, I have nothing to worry about. I only feel a little uneasy about Tangtan. I hope the Emperor will take good care of her."

Xiao Huaiyan smiled. "Your Highness may rest easy."

The Empress Dowager, afraid that saying too much would become tiresome, patted Jiang Mi on the shoulder, then took Matron Cuī's arm and got into the carriage.

Jiang Mi stood beside Xiao Huaiyan and watched the imperial guards escort that carriage slowly through the palace gates.

Xiao Huaiyan took her hand. Seeing her look of surprise, he said simply: "Walk with me a while."

The palace maids and eunuchs followed at a distance, not daring to come too close.

Jiang Mi walked beside Xiao Huaiyan at a leisurely pace, and before long they had reached the lakeside.

The lotus flowers were in full bloom, and the breeze carried their faint sweet scent.

They walked into the pavilion by the lake and sat in the cool wind, looking out over the water.

Jiang Mi gazed at the green jade of those lotus leaves stretching to the horizon, the flowers standing clean and upright, and the melancholy from her aunt's departure eased a little.

This was not her walking with Xiao Huaiyan — this was Xiao Huaiyan walking with her.

She said quietly: "Thank you, Your Majesty."

Xiao Huaiyan smiled. "That is all the thanks I get?"

The attendants at a distance saw the Emperor and Empress settle into the pavilion and rushed to bring tea and a tray of refreshments.

Chéngzhōng led palace maids carrying everything over, and as they all prepared to step back again —

Xiao Huaiyan called him back. "Bring brush and ink. I wish to paint."

Jiang Mi had not expected him to be in that kind of mood.

But with scenery this beautiful, it was worth commemorating in paint.

In truth she was a little curious about his painting. In the last life she had borrowed many master works from him to copy, but never seen one of his own. From the occasional hints he had given her and the way he held a brush, she had guessed he was no amateur.

That gave her something to look forward to.

Before long Chéngzhōng had everything laid out.

Xiao Huaiyan spread the paper flat, and when Jiang Mi made to stand, said: "Stay where you are. Do not move."

She stopped. She had thought he was going to paint the lotus flowers.

She had even been thinking she would go stand beside him and watch.

Xiao Huaiyan saw her confusion and said with a smile: "I intend to paint a beauty."

Jiang Mi stiffened. How had this become a portrait of her?

She gripped her handkerchief tight, suddenly tense.

She opened her mouth to say something, but saw that Xiao Huaiyan standing at the table had already put brush to paper and begun.

She sat back down. She supposed that was that.

Jiang Mi sat with her toes raised, embroidered slippers touching the ground, and had been sitting properly for quite a while.

Xiao Huaiyan changed brushes. His gaze had not left her once.

With that focused attention upon her, her heart beat a little fast.

He could see her constraint. But that very compliance made her all the more pitiable.

"Tangtan — change your position, it is all right."

She pressed her lips together and asked: "Is Your Majesty nearly finished?"

Xiao Huaiyan looked down at his painting, brought the last stroke down, and looked back at Jiang Mi, as if comparing and assessing. He smiled. "There is still one thing that is not quite right — but you may come and see first."

She was curious. She rose and walked toward him.

When Jiang Mi saw the painting, her pupils contracted slightly.

The woman in it looked exactly like her. What Xiao Huaiyan had called "not quite right" was clearly nothing to do with the likeness.

But the woman was not sitting in the pavilion — she was sitting in a small boat on the lake, shoes and silk stockings removed, her pale jade legs trailing in the water, stirring up little splashes as she played, her expression languid and her eyes beguiling. Behind her, lotus leaves and flowers filled the frame, and against those the woman was as radiant as a lotus herself — and altogether more enchanting.

Jiang Mi's face went warm. She did not need a mirror to know she was flushed.

Xiao Huaiyan came to stand behind her, arms braced on either side to encircle her. "Tangtan — can you see what is different?"

She said with embarrassed exasperation: "Your Majesty is bullying me again. How could you paint it like this? This — the person in this painting is definitely not me."

Xiao Huaiyan gave her earlobe a bite.

He lifted her and sat her on the stone table.

His hand rested on her leg. "Tangtan — look once more and find the difference. If you find it, I will let you down."

She panicked. She was afraid Xiao Huaiyan would act without restraint, as in the last life...

Jiang Mi looked again at the painting.

She saw it — at the ankle of the woman in the painting, a half-open lotus had been sketched, its stamens trembling softly.

She had just opened her mouth to speak when she felt her embroidered slipper being removed, and a pale bare foot taken in someone's hand.

Xiao Huaiyan held a brush, his voice very low. "Tangtan — I am only painting. Nothing else."

How could she possibly not worry?

Even if the attendants had all withdrawn, out here in the open by the lake, she could not trust his words.

"Your Majesty may paint by yourself — this concubine needs to return to the Kūnníng Palace. Please put this concubine down at once."

Xiao Huaiyan heard the irritation in her voice and said agreeably: "All right. Once I fill in this last missing detail, we will go back together."

Even as he spoke, she felt a strange sensation at her ankle.

She looked down and watched Xiao Huaiyan trace a brush tip inked in vermilion across her ankle — and quickly, a lotus flower took shape there, petals unfurling, half-opened, shy and not yet in full bloom.

Like a young woman's blush; and yet coiled through with a flirtatious grace.

When he finished, he looked up at her frozen expression and asked: "Is it lovely?"

In all honesty — Jiang Mi looked at the flower, and it was indeed lovely.

But painted on her ankle, it had something disconcerting about it.

Xiao Huaiyan was also staring at it, his gaze burning.

Jiang Mi curled her foot and gave a low cough and pulled at Xiao Huaiyan's sleeve. "Your Majesty — we should go back."

He looked at that nervous expression of hers and laughed low.

He bent down and kissed her lips, then helped her put her slipper back on.

Jiang Mi had just climbed down from the stone table when she realised he seemed to intend to simply walk back with her and leave the painting there. She said quickly: "The painting — it cannot be left in the pavilion." A picture like that could not be seen by anyone else.

Xiao Huaiyan rolled the painting up with one hand and placed it in hers. "Are you at ease now?"

She heard the playfulness in his voice and said nothing. She was already working out what to do with this painting once they were back.

Xiao Huaiyan read her small scheme and said lightly: "Do not worry about the painting being damaged. I can make more."

Jiang Mi's eyes went wide. She was not afraid of it being damaged — she wanted to destroy it the moment he was out of sight!

Xiao Huaiyan saw her puffed-up expression and could not resist provoking her further. "If you are not satisfied with this one, tell me what you would prefer and I will paint it until you are happy. Shall I?"

She suspected this had a trap in it — no telling what Xiao Huaiyan was planning.

She saw the phoenix palanquin being brought over and tried to head toward it, but Xiao Huaiyan pulled her onto the imperial palanquin.

He delivered her to the Kūnníng Palace. "I will not come in with you — there are still matters in the imperial study. I will be back for the evening meal."

Jiang Mi felt a small breath of relief.

She went back, put the painting into a box and pressed the lid firmly shut, then went to the washroom to try to scrub the lotus flower from her ankle. But whatever pigment Xiao Huaiyan had used, nothing would shift it.

She gave up.

In the commotion of all that, the small cloud of melancholy from her aunt's departure had been chased away to almost nothing.

At the evening meal, Xiao Huaiyan came back in the dark.

They ate together as usual. Then Xiao Huaiyan said out of nowhere: "Your birthday is in half a month — your first Thousand Autumns celebration since entering the palace. How do you wish to observe it?"

Jiang Mi paused. She had nearly forgotten her own birthday.

Her birth had cost her mother her life, and she had always passed her birthdays quietly.

She was still for a moment. "Something simple, Your Majesty."

To Xiao Huaiyan, this was the first birthday she would observe as Empress. He had no intention of keeping it simple.

chapters.title: After the Wedding, Part Five
chapters.content:
Xiao Huaiyan came back to the sleeping chamber after his bath to find Jiang Mi, who had been playing with the cats, already bundled in the bed.

He untied his belt and sat on the edge of the bed. "So early to sleep? No travel books tonight?"

Jiang Mi watched him take off his outer robe. He hadn't even come close yet and she could already feel the warmth radiating from him.

She inched further in, shifting her legs uncomfortably. She had been thinking of the lotus flower he had painted on her ankle this afternoon and was fairly certain she was in for more of the same tonight.

But she wasn't sure if it was the departure of her aunt or the sudden mention of her birthday, but her mood was low today, and she had been hoping to fall asleep quickly and slip past it all.

Now Xiao Huaiyan had come back too quickly, and the more she rushed the less she could sleep.

When he mentioned the travel books again, Jiang Mi felt a headache coming on. Now that she thought about it, any time she opened a travel book she seemed to hear Xiao Huaiyan reciting in that low, faintly rough voice. The memory alone made her face and ears burn. It would probably be a very long time before she wanted to look at anything travel-related again.

A few moments later Xiao Huaiyan's arm reached across, about to lift the quilt.

Jiang Mi pressed her lips together and said quietly: "My monthly cycle has come. I am a little tired..."

Xiao Huaiyan's hand paused. He settled back against the bedside, eyes carrying a faint smile. "A shame — I was just thinking of enjoying a flower by lamplight."

Jiang Mi heard his insinuation at once. She gave a large yawn in the manner of someone deeply drowsy, turned over to face away from him, exposing a length of creamy nape.

His fingers reached over and ran lightly across it — soft and fragrant and warm.

She felt the tickle and could not escape it. "Your Majesty — do stop."

He did. Then he said, in an easy voice: "I believe your cycle is not usually this date. You seem to be early by quite a few days. Should I summon the physician?"

Jiang Mi went rigid. She had never imagined he kept track of that.

She heard him apparently calling for Li Fu to fetch the physician, and turned from the quilt to grab his sleeve. "Your Majesty — there is no need to trouble anyone. I..."

She was debating whether to come up with an excuse or simply tell the truth, when she looked up and met his phoenix eyes — and his expression showed clearly that he had already seen through her.

Jiang Mi's face flushed with embarrassment. The words she had been about to say would not come.

Xiao Huaiyan raised a hand and cupped her chin. "If you genuinely don't want to, tell me. I will not eat you."

She was not entirely sure whether to believe that. In every other matter he had indeed given her what she asked for. But in this, he had always taken the lead, and she had generally gone along with it — except when her cycle came.

Xiao Huaiyan bent down and pressed a kiss to her lips. "Every other day I cannot tell whether you truly don't want to, or whether you are too shy, or simply feeling lazy. Tangtan — while you are working out what I am thinking, I am working out what you are thinking too."

"Are you missing the Empress Dowager? Would you also like to go out and see the world?"

Jiang Mi's eyes widened slightly. Even her surprise was soft and endearing, and Xiao Huaiyan could not help pulling her close.

He still remembered it — on the road to the south, the way Jiang Mi had greeted every new place with curiosity and discovery. Her love of travel books. Her longing, looking out at all that scenery and customs from the page.

Her reluctance to see her aunt go was real — but so, too, was the envy beneath it.

Xiao Huaiyan stroked her hair gently. "Tangtan — I may not be able to grant your wish very soon, but there will come a day when I take you to see the great rivers and mountains of Great Wei."

Jiang Mi's heart contracted. Her pulse quickened.

She looked up at him, something shining in her eyes. Her voice was as light as a feather. "I will wait for you, Your Majesty."

He said: "I will not make you wait too long. I can't take you just yet — but I can tell you about the places I visited when I was travelling and the amusing things that happened. Would you like that?"

Jiang Mi shifted closer against him in his arms. "Yes. But Your Majesty is not allowed to tease me again."

Xiao Huaiyan laughed. Those phoenix eyes lifted faintly.

Jiang Mi's face went pink.

She rested a hand on his chest and felt his warmth and his heartbeat and listened to his voice, and for a moment she lost herself entirely.

Beyond the bed hangings, a candle guttered and swayed. Now and then there drifted a soft, happy laugh, and the warmth of the room was like early spring.

......

Jiang Mi had imagined the palace would feel lonely once her aunt left.

On one side, Xiao Huaiyan had her come over to the Qiánqīng Palace to read and paint while he worked, and when he was done they would eat together. Some nights she stayed over there.

On the other, women of the imperial clan — elderly royal consorts — came calling at the palace now and then, wanting to talk and share domestic news about this family and that.

From those visits Jiang Mi gradually came to know the imperial relatives a little better.

After a few of those visits, she also began to hear something underlying them.

They would work in a casual question about whether there had been any news from her belly, or mention marriage prospects in the Jiang family.

Jiang Mi understood: though she had only just entered the palace, many people were already watching her womb.

Her eldest and second male cousins on the Jiang side had not yet taken wives.

Her younger sisters were still young, but old enough for matchmaking to begin.

The Jiang family's marriages — both in taking wives and giving daughters — would need careful consideration now.

What she hoped was that her brothers and sisters would all follow their own hearts.

Especially A-Róng. In this life, A-Róng would marry a man she loved and become his legitimate wife.

She wondered if her father and Su-shi had begun looking for matches for her yet.

As an imperial in-law family now, she also did not know what Xiao Huaiyan's view was on the Jiang family's marriages.

She gave it some thought, and decided she ought to go and speak to Xiao Huaiyan.

She went to the Qiánqīng Palace. Li Fu hurried out to welcome her, bowing. "This servant greets Her Highness the Empress."

"Where is the Emperor?"

"Minister Xuē, Young General Gù, and Minister Pei have matters to report, and the Emperor has gone to the imperial study first."

Jiang Mi nodded. "Then I will read a while and wait for the Emperor."

Li Fu brought tea with eager attentiveness. "The Emperor is sure to be very pleased to know the Empress has come."

Li Fu thought to himself that the Emperor had added many books and paintings to the shelves here, obtained specifically for the Empress, so she would not find it dull.

Jiang Mi browsed the bookshelves in the sleeping chamber — nothing there she particularly wanted. She walked to the other side and reached up for a book placed slightly higher than the rest, and accidentally knocked a rosewood box in the adjacent shelf to the floor.

It landed on the carpet and made no sound.

She picked it up. Something inside moved with a clear, familiar ring.

She opened the box, curious.

The expression on her face slowly solidified.

Inside were two objects.

One was a gold-and-jade bell anklet. The other was a length of red silk.

Jiang Mi looked at the beast-pattern carved into the gold-and-jade bell anklet.

It was identical to the one from her last life.

Why would this anklet still exist?

And the red silk — she recognised that too.

She hesitated, then took out the red silk and unfolded it.

Written on it in fine, neat characters was: "Peace and good fortune — may I find a worthy husband."

The tips of her fingers trembled.

This was the wish she had written on her very first visit to the Qiānshuāng Temple — hanging it on the prayer tree. She had been wishing for her family's safety and her own good fortune, hoping to find a match who could protect them.

How had this piece of red silk come to be in Xiao Huaiyan's possession?

Jiang Mi thought back over her encounter with Xiao Huaiyan at the Qiānshuāng Temple — he had invited her to play chess and given her a chess manual. When she left, there had been a vague sound of something falling, and afterward the temple had replaced the prayer tree with a new one.

Xiao Huaiyan could not have gone so far as to have the tree cut down just to retrieve her wish-ribbon.

But then why had he been at the Qiānshuāng Temple in the first place?

Jiang Mi quietly put the red silk back in the rosewood box alongside the gold-and-jade bell.

She steadied herself, chose a book at random, and came to sit on the day-couch.

Li Fu was just then leading palace maids carrying fresh-made coconut cup cakes, mandarin duck rolls, steamed sweet curd, luck cakes, and preserved green plums in from the imperial kitchen.

He smiled. "Your Highness — do taste these and see if they are to your liking."

Jiang Mi took a piece of luck cake. "Thank you for the trouble."

Li Fu bowed. "Your Highness must not say such things."

Jiang Mi ate a bite and sipped her tea. "This luck cake tastes almost exactly like the one I had at the Qiānshuāng Temple."

Li Fu said: "Your Highness — you are right. This recipe was actually obtained from the Qiānshuāng Temple."

She smiled. "What a coincidence. I happened to encounter the Emperor at the Qiānshuāng Temple once — I never knew why he was there."

Li Fu thought it over. The Emperor's regard for the Empress was plain for all to see. There seemed no harm in letting her know — and perhaps she could even be one more voice to advise him.

"Your Highness — the Emperor goes to the Qiānshuāng Temple to see Master Xuánmíng for treatment of his head-sickness."

She remembered the rumour that a once-famous physician had taken holy orders at the Qiānshuāng Temple, and that the medicine slips obtained there were remarkably effective. That physician must be Master Xuánmíng.

Something clicked into place in her mind. "Master Xuánmíng — is he a grey-robed monk, with a red mole above his left eyebrow?"

Li Fu said: "He is."

"Is the Emperor's head-sickness very serious?"

Li Fu considered a moment and nodded. "But since the Empress entered the palace, the Emperor's attacks have been very infrequent."

Jiang Mi's mind was in disorder.

Xiao Huaiyan had told her his head-sickness had been with him since childhood.

Master Xuánmíng was the same grey-robed elderly monk who had told her about the golden relic in the pagoda.

He and Xiao Huaiyan knew each other.

Then — did Xiao Huaiyan also know about the legend of the golden relic?

Her heart was beating very fast, her head aching in waves. Without reason she thought of that dream — the empty, silent palace, the courtyard full of kites, and Xiao Huaiyan, young-faced but white at the temples...

chapters.title: After the Wedding, Part Six
chapters.content:
Thoughts came crashing in on all sides. Jiang Mi's heart was in turmoil.

When Li Fu came to refill her tea, she stood up. "Eunuch Li — since the Emperor is occupied with state affairs, I will return first."

Li Fu was taken aback. One moment she had been perfectly comfortable and the next she wanted to leave?

He tried to dissuade her. "Your Highness — the Emperor should be back quite soon. Will you not sit a little longer? Or I could go and check at the imperial study?"

Jiang Mi shook her head. "No need to trouble yourself."

Seeing the Empress was determined to go, Li Fu had no choice but to see her out of the Qiánqīng Palace and watch her board the phoenix palanquin.

He stood watching the palanquin go until it had disappeared from view, then turned back.

He thought to himself: if the Emperor came back and found out the Empress had come and gone without anyone keeping her, would he be blamed for poor attendance?

About half an hour later, Xiao Huaiyan came out of the imperial study. Li Fu reported that the Empress had come to the Qiánqīng Palace and sat for a short time before leaving.

Xiao Huaiyan went into the sleeping chamber and looked around, then asked: "Did she say what she had come for?"

"Your Highness did not say. She had been looking at the books for a while, then ate a piece or two of pastry and left."

Li Fu saw the Emperor's brow furrow and — thinking of something — added brightly: "The Empress also specially asked about Your Majesty's head-sickness. She is very much concerned about Your Majesty's health."

A trace of warmth passed through Xiao Huaiyan's eyes. He walked to the bookshelf and swept a glance over it — then his gaze stopped abruptly on a rosewood box.

His expression changed. He looked at Li Fu. "What did you tell her?"

Li Fu was frightened by the cold sharpness in his voice and answered honestly: "This servant told the Empress that Your Majesty goes to the Qiānshuāng Temple to seek Master Xuánmíng's treatment for the head-sickness, and that since the Empress entered the palace the attacks have been very infrequent."

Li Fu thought: that could not have been wrong, surely.

Xiao Huaiyan walked outside at a fast pace. Li Fu followed close behind, watching his direction — the Kūnníng Palace.

......

In the Kūnníng Palace.

Jiang Mi had come back and sat on the day-couch in a daze, memory after memory surfacing, the more she thought the more her heart raced.

This life was supposed to be so different from the last.

Then why did the gold-and-jade bell anklet still exist in Xiao Huaiyan's possession?

In the last life it had been given to her as a forfeit when she lost a chess game. Was it not?

And her wish-ribbon — what had Xiao Huaiyan meant, taking it down?

He was becoming impossible to read again.

She tried to piece together the changes between the last life and this one. Apart from the entanglement between herself and Xiao Huaiyan, the rebel uprising and the Jiang family's disaster had both occurred earlier. Even the original sequence — rebel conspirators joining with the hostile nation, leading to an invasion — had become Xiao Huaiyan uncovering the spies and choosing to strike first.

Nothing was as it had been.

How had Xiao Huaiyan come to know all of this in advance?

For one instant Jiang Mi wondered: was Xiao Huaiyan reborn, as she had been?

But the thought dissolved almost immediately.

From the moment she had returned the hangover broth to him on that first morning, Xiao Huaiyan had not seemed to carry any memory of the last life.

If he had truly remembered, he would not have agreed to her conditions when she asked him to intervene on her behalf for the engagement. He would have brought her into the palace far earlier.

And the Xiao Huaiyan of the last life had not had this kind of patience.

Yet there were far too many things that did not add up.

Her own rebirth was extraordinary enough on its own. Could another person have experienced the same?

She had also never truly asked herself why she had come back — why she had been given a second life.

Master Xuánmíng's words came back to her. The legend of the golden relic: using the blood of the one who petitioned as the catalyst, burning through their remaining years of life, to call them back in a future life.

Was the legend true? Was that dream real?

The more she tried to reason through it, the larger the uncertainty became.

Jiang Mi rubbed at her temples. She did not know how to face Xiao Huaiyan.

At that moment she heard the greeting sounds from palace maids outside: "His Majesty is well."

Jiang Mi's expression went still. He was back already?

A few moments later, a figure in imperial yellow came around the screen.

Jiang Mi gripped her handkerchief and stood up from the couch. "Your Majesty."

Xiao Huaiyan read her expression as composed and ordinary. He smiled lightly. "Why did you leave without waiting for me?"

Jiang Mi smiled. "I had a small matter I wanted to ask about, but seeing how busy Your Majesty was, I didn't want to disturb."

He sat down in an armchair. "What was it?"

She hesitated. "These past few days, the Qìng Dowager Consort has been talking to me about matters among the imperial relatives, and mentioned that her youngest grandson is not yet married and asked me to help her look among the capital's noble families. She also raised the question of whether my cousins and younger sisters had found matches yet..."

She trailed off, unsure how to ask directly whether the Jiang family's marriages would be constrained. The late Emperor had disliked her aunt choosing Jiang daughters to marry into households with great military or political power; the Jiang sons had all married below their rank as well. She did not know if Xiao Huaiyan would have concerns along those lines. Even if the Jiang family's children did not necessarily aim to marry high, she still wanted to test the ground first.

Xiao Huaiyan's brow lifted slightly. He reached out and drew her onto his lap, settling her into his arms. He breathed in the delicate scent of her.

"The Qìng royal line was already a line of idle princes under the late Emperor — all unremarkable in ability and talent, and their descendants have not amounted to much. The Dowager Consort's youngest grandson runs with a crowd of good-for-nothings. Imperial clan or not, he is not a good match. You need not pay her any attention."

He met those surprised almond eyes, and his smile deepened. "Do not worry about those few relatives of higher seniority using their rank to press you. No matter how many generations back their seniority goes, it cannot rank above you. You are my Empress. If you are in a good mood, listen to their chatter. If you are not, simply decline to see them. They come here to be seen, to be remembered by you, and to feel that they have not lost their favour and standing. That is all."

Jiang Mi had only been testing the waters with that question — she had not expected him to speak so openly, and his words carried the weight of guidance for her.

"The Jiang family's marriages — you decide entirely, as you wish. Their happiness is what matters."

Jiang Mi looked up. Their eyes met. Her heart moved. Xiao Huaiyan had understood what she had not been able to say. He was answering the unspoken question.

Her lips parted — the word of thanks had barely formed when it was sealed away by a burning kiss.

Her hair came slightly undone, her collar loosened. She braced against his shoulder and caught her breath, and a warmth pressed against her ear. "If you want to thank me, give me something worth having. Can I admire the lotus flower now?"

It was phrased as a question, but her ankle was already being taken in hand, an embroidered slipper slipping off, and against the snow-white skin the painted lotus trembled open — shy and beguiling as its bearer.

His burning palm made her bite down on her lip.

Xiao Huaiyan pressed close to her mouth and guided her to look together at the lotus flower. He said deliberately: "What do you think of my painting?"

Jiang Mi turned her head and ignored him. Xiao Huaiyan laughed once, gathered her up, and carried her to the bed.

Jiang Mi closed her eyes. She could not say why — perhaps it was seeing the gold-and-jade bell anklet — but she felt a faint disorientation, as though the thing painted on her ankle were not the lotus flower but that anklet itself.

She had never thought so carefully about it before, but now it was vivid and clear: Xiao Huaiyan's mannerisms and habits were the same as they had been in the last life.

But — this was the same person. No matter how much he changed, his habits and nature were rooted in him to the bone.

Jiang Mi bit down on his shoulder. She trembled, her mind slightly elsewhere.

Xiao Huaiyan's eyes were very dark. He lifted her chin and kissed the corner of her lips, a low laugh. "Tangtan — you are especially... today..."

The words were swallowed between lips and teeth.

Jiang Mi was limp with exhaustion and nearly asleep. She thought she heard Xiao Huaiyan say something again about her birthday.

In her drowsing, a fragment of memory suddenly surfaced.

In the last life, the day before her birthday there had been an incident in the palace. The Chǔxiù Palace had suddenly caught fire — it had been the bedchambers of Consort Jin while she was alive. Xiao Huaiyan had been furious, and everyone in the palace walked on glass. Even Noble Consort Duān had been punished. And so the next day her birthday had passed quietly, with no one knowing and no one celebrating. She had boiled herself a bowl of noodles, and spent her seventeenth birthday that way.

At home, too, her birthdays had always been quiet. Had Xiao Huaiyan not kept bringing it up, she might have truly forgotten.

She worked out the date. Was the Chǔxiù Palace fire in the last life not tonight?

The thought came to her: if she wanted to test a certain suspicion, perhaps this could be a way to verify a little.

Jiang Mi lay in Xiao Huaiyan's arms and turned restlessly, and before long he woke.

He touched her forehead — no fever. "Tangtan — what is wrong?"

She woke slowly, still looking as though she had not quite come back.

Xiao Huaiyan sat up. He soothed her with a pat, voice gentle. "Did you have a nightmare?"

Jiang Mi looked at him. She pressed her lips together. "Your Majesty — I dreamed the Chǔxiù Palace was on fire. The flames were very large. Would you send someone to check?"

Xiao Huaiyan's hand paused. He looked at her with a complicated expression. Was she worried for him? Was she using a dream as a way to warn him about something from the last life?

He drew her more tightly against him. "Tangtan — it is only a dream. It will not happen." How he wished she could forget everything from the last life, treat it all as a dream and let it go. The Chǔxiù Palace fire — it would not happen in this life. He had cleared out those people before she entered the palace. It would not repeat.

Jiang Mi lowered her eyes. Why was he so certain?

The Chǔxiù Palace had been Consort Jin's quarters. He could not possibly be indifferent to it.

The certainty he spoke with — did he know something?

Xiao Huaiyan soothed her. "Tangtan — go to sleep."

Jiang Mi lay quietly in his arms, but could not sleep.

She was uneasy, listening for the sounds of commotion from the servants, for Li Fu coming to report a fire in the Chǔxiù Palace.

But the night was completely still. Nothing.

By the next morning, when Xiao Huaiyan had gone to court, the Chǔxiù Palace remained entirely quiet.

When she woke, she still could not set her mind at ease, and had someone go and check. They reported back that everything was normal.

Official Sun saw how concerned the Empress appeared to be about the Chǔxiù Palace and said: "Your Highness — the Chǔxiù Palace had a new set of attendants put in before you entered the palace. Nothing will go wrong. Your Highness might like to look over today's birthday gift register instead."

Jiang Mi took the register Official Sun offered, but her mind was more occupied with the matter of the changed attendants. "Why were they changed?"

"This servant does not know either. Not only the Chǔxiù Palace — several halls were assigned new palace maids and eunuchs. Even in the Kūnníng Palace, all the attendants were chosen by the Qiánqīng Palace."

Jiang Mi fell into thought. A certain idea that had been surfacing kept pushing back up.

She collected herself and opened the register in her hand. Her eyes went wide. "Were we not keeping this simple? Why is there to be a night banquet — and foreign envoys coming to offer congratulations?"

chapters.title: After the Wedding, Part Seven
chapters.content:
Jiang Mi's birthday fell on the seventh day of the ninth month — the same month as the Emperor's own birthday celebration.

With no consorts in the inner palace, it was the noble ladies and officials' wives who came to the palace to attend the banquet and offer their gifts.

The attending ladies thought to themselves: every year it was the Emperor's birthday that was celebrated on a grand scale — yet the Empress's birthday celebration appeared to be of an equivalent scale, and the Emperor had even permitted tributary envoys from foreign nations to come and offer gifts. It was grander than last year's imperial birthday.

The Emperor's favour toward this Empress Jiang was plain to see.

Those attending the banquet gathered in the Jiāotài Hall to await the phoenix palanquin.

But the family of the Empress from the Cheng'en Duke's house could go first to the Kūnníng Palace to pay their respects and spend a little time with the Empress privately.

On the way to the Jiāotài Hall, several of the ladies saw Princess An'yang, who had not long been married out of the palace.

The princess had none of the bloom of a new bride. Her face was heavily powdered, and she looked gaunt underneath it, though her expression was forced into a remnant of imperious severity.

Not far from her was the wife of the Zhōngqín Earl's house — her new mother-in-law — staring in her direction with an expression of undisguised anger.

Some of the ladies exchanged looks. They had been at the Dragon Boat Festival banquet. They knew that An'yang had been caught meeting the Earl's fourth son in private, and that the marriage had followed. Though it was also said the matter had some hidden circumstances — that An'yang had not been a willing party — and that since going to the Earl's household she had been making trouble.

One of the ministerial wives said: "Why has Princess An'yang not gone first to the Kūnníng Palace to pay her respects? I noticed the daughters of the Loyal and Brave Marquess's household went over."

As an imperial sister, An'yang should properly have gone to the Kūnníng Palace to greet the Empress and make a show of closeness — yet here she was at this hour already heading to the Jiāotài Hall.

Another lady said quietly: "I heard Princess An'yang and the Empress had some prior friction..."

The sentence was left unfinished, but everyone understood perfectly.

The marriage had been rushed through by the Imperial Household Department to ordinary standards, with no additional gifts from the Emperor, and no apparent concern on his part. An'yang had no imperial brother to protect her, no closeness with the Empress, and her birth-mother the Worthy Dowager Consort was at the travelling palace. Life in the Earl's household must not be going well.

That Worthy Dowager Consort seemed no easy person to deal with either. Once she had taken the measure of the imperial family's attitude toward An'yang, the inner household's way of making someone's life difficult had many methods. An'yang was not especially clever — she had wasted this rare opportunity to repair the relationship. She had only herself to blame.

......

In the Kūnníng Palace, there was warmth and laughter.

Jiang Mi had meant to keep her birthday simple and had left the arrangements to the Imperial Household Department without giving it much further thought.

She had not expected Xiao Huaiyan to do all of this behind her back and hold the Thousand Autumns celebration on such a grand scale.

At first she had been at a loss. She had not prepared anything.

But Official Sun told her there was nothing she needed to prepare — today was her birthday, and she was the one being congratulated and receiving gifts.

Jiang Mi changed into her ceremonial robes under Official Sun's care, had her phoenix crown put on, and stood regal and resplendent.

She looked at herself in the mirror and felt that in the two months or so since entering the palace, she had somehow become a little different.

Before long, the palace attendants led the Jiang family relatives in.

Jiang Mi sat in the seat of honour and was genuinely happy to see family she had not seen in some time.

Everyone bowed together. "We pay our respects to Her Highness the Empress and wish the Empress a thousand years of joy and a birthday celebration that endures through all seasons."

Jiang Mi smiled and told them to rise, and had them seated.

Madam Chen and Su-shi looked at Jiang Mi in her gold and jade magnificence and thought: the palace really does bring out a person. Tangtan's complexion was even more radiant than when she had been at home — a lushness like a peony fully open, that effortless aristocratic elegance and fullness that only the palace could cultivate.

Jiang Wǎn, Jiang Yì, and Jiang Róng each presented hand-made birthday gifts — these were a family's own heartfelt offerings. The formal gifts for the Jiāotài Hall had been prepared separately.

Qín Sīwǎn, prompted by her mother, also offered a double-sided embroidered fan purchased at great expense from a master artisan. She had thought to make an impression — but seeing that the Jiang women had all brought things made with their own hands, her expensive fan was clearly nothing she could have embroidered herself. And did the palace lack valuable things? Everything she saw in the Kūnníng Palace was priceless and exquisite. Even the pearls sewn onto Jiang Mi's embroidered slippers were imperial tribute pearls, to say nothing of the gemstone ring and bracelet on her wrists, or the magnificent phoenix crown. Envy she could not quite suppress showed in her eyes.

Jiang Mi looked at the gifts presented and was pleased with all of them.

She glanced at Jiang Róng and smiled: "A-Róng's embroidered peonies have improved — well done."

Jiang Róng's face lit up with delight. Elder Sister had praised her.

Jiang Yì teased: "The Empress praised A-Róng specially — won't she say anything for me and Sister Wǎn?"

Jiang Mi laughed. "Sister Wǎn's painting needs no words from me. As for yours — are you certain you didn't have Sister Wǎn help with that sachet?"

She was teasing Jiang Yì on purpose.

Jiang Yì immediately set her teacup down and protested. "How could she! Even if I wanted to be lazy about it, Sister Wǎn would never help me — I embroidered that myself for over a month..."

She trailed off, caught Jiang Mi's expression, saw everyone else smiling too, and understood. Her face went red. She shot Jiang Mi a look. "Your Highness is teasing me on purpose. You have been learning bad habits."

In the laughter that followed, Jiang Mi took the embroidered fan and looked at it, then turned to Madam Yú and Qín Sīwǎn as well. "Aunt and Sīwǎn were thoughtful to remember."

Madam Yú stood and said: "We are the ones honoured, as long as the Empress is pleased."

Qín Sīwǎn listened and felt, somehow, that her cousin's tone toward her was somewhat cooler than toward the Jiang family members — not the same warmth at all.

After a while, the time was getting on, and the family took their leave and headed to the Jiāotài Hall.

The moment the Jiang family left, a palace maid came in to announce: "Your Highness — the daughter of the Loyal and Brave Marquess, Gù Xuān, requests an audience."

Jiang Mi said immediately: "Let her in quickly."

She had not seen Gù Xuān since the Dragon Boat Festival banquet and had expected to see her at the birthday celebration — she had not thought A-Xuān would come to the Kūnníng Palace first.

Gù Xuān came in and bowed. "Long life and joy to the Empress, Your Highness."

Jiang Mi went forward and took her hands. "Do not stand on ceremony. I have not had a chance to thank you properly for helping me out at the Dragon Boat banquet."

Gù Xuān brushed it off. "Such a small matter — why should Your Highness think twice about it?"

She looked at the beauty before her with bright eyes.

She thought: the Emperor truly has fortune on his side. And those hands are still as soft as ever.

"Your Highness — I have come to bring your birthday gift, but also to bid you farewell."

Jiang Mi was startled. "A-Xuān — where are you going?"

Gù Xuān felt a warmth at being called that. "Yúnzhōu. This subject has nothing much worth giving — just a few bottles of liquor that are more than usually drinkable. So I have prepared some for Your Highness. But Your Highness must not overindulge."

Strictly speaking, food and drink as gifts were to be avoided — but she had nothing else to give that felt like a genuine gesture. These were bottles she had personally watched over; nothing would be wrong with them.

Jiang Mi cared nothing for what Gù Xuān gave her. She was concerned about her going to Yúnzhōu.

"Why must you leave for Yúnzhōu so urgently? Is there to be fighting?"

Gù Xuān nodded. "Your Highness need not worry. The situation at Yúnzhōu is stable. If there is to be a battle, Great Wei will win. When I have earned my merits and come back, you must help me look among the unmarried young men of the capital for the better-looking ones! I'll ask the Emperor for a match to be arranged."

Jiang Mi felt the helplessness of it, but also nodded. "Very well — I will look out for you in advance."

Gù Xuān knew the Empress was the only one she could rely on. Good old Tangtan. The best.

Jiang Mi watched Gù Xuān's expression of eager anticipation and could not help thinking of the last life — the excitement with which she had spoken of Yúnzhōu when Jiang Mi was still Noble Consort Duān.

She recalled it now: on the boat to the south, when A-Xuān had asked her to drink with her, she had said that she had originally been summoned to the capital to carry out a task inside the palace — and then the task had been called off, and she had come to no longer need to enter as a consort, and had only wanted to go back to Yúnzhōu to earn her merits.

That old question surfaced again. In the last life, Noble Consort Duān had entered the palace — so why had she suddenly not needed to? Had something changed in between? And was that change connected to Xiao Huaiyan?

Gù Xuān saw Jiang Mi had drifted away and waved a hand in front of her. "Your Highness — are you all right?"

Jiang Mi looked up. "A-Xuān — may I ask you something?"

Gù Xuān was surprised. "Your Highness, please speak freely."

"Do you remember mentioning once that you had been going to enter the palace on a task, but suddenly it was no longer needed? Would it be possible to know what that task was? And why it was called off?"

Gù Xuān went still. She had not expected this question. She had almost forgotten it herself.

Could it be that Tangtan minded the fact that she had almost entered the palace as a consort, and was jealous?

But Tangtan's expression did not look like jealousy at all.

Gù Xuān decided not to conceal it. The Emperor had the Empress in his hands now — explaining the circumstances should not cause any trouble.

"Your Highness — do you remember when you were recovering from your injuries at the Fèngchí travelling palace and my brother and I came to escort you back?"

Jiang Mi nodded.

"At that time I had received a secret imperial order in Yúnzhōu calling me to the capital. The order intended to name me as Noble Consort Duān and send me into the palace to purge the remaining spies and hidden operatives left over from the late Emperor's era in the inner palace."

Gù Xuān glanced at Jiang Mi's expression and continued: "Your Highness may not know — when the Emperor first took the throne, he had the three rival princes executed. The late Emperor's Noble Consort and Virtuous Consort and others were also dealt with. The palace attendants were gone over again and again — but the Noble Consort and Virtuous Consort had built deep roots over many years in the inner palace, and it was impossible to guarantee nothing had been missed. The Emperor wanted me to enter the palace and work my way into those networks to sweep out whatever remained in hiding. The Emperor gave me two years at most — and if I completed it, I would have rendered a great service and could return to Yúnzhōu free and easy."

"Only — afterward the Emperor suddenly rescinded the order and sent me south to help suppress the rebels instead."

Gù Xuān saw Jiang Mi's face go somewhat pale and reached out to take her hand. "Your Highness — are you all right?"

Jiang Mi shook her head gently.

She felt certain ideas inside her slowly coming clear.

The fire in the Chǔxiù Palace in the last life — had that been the work of those hidden operatives? At that time Noble Consort Duān had been punished, and the other consorts all feared being implicated. She herself had been avoiding the summons to the bedchamber.

In this life the Chǔxiù Palace had not caught fire and the attendants had been replaced.

She thought of Official Sun's words — several palace halls had had their attendants replaced, and all the servants in the Kūnníng Palace had been chosen from the Qiánqīng Palace.

Xiao Huaiyan would not have changed his decisions for no reason, unless he had known something in advance.

Jiang Mi also recalled: in the last life, the palace maid who had urged her to attend the Emperor had been dealt with not long after Jiang Mi was first summoned to the bedchamber, and Jiang Mi had been more frightened of Xiao Huaiyan because of it.

But since entering the palace this time, she had intentionally looked for that palace maid — and found no trace of her.

Just then a voice sounded: "What are you two doing?"

Jiang Mi looked up. Xiao Huaiyan was walking toward them, his eyes not particularly pleased as they fell on her and Gù Xuān's clasped hands.

chapters.title: After the Wedding, Part Eight
chapters.content:
Jiang Mi had not yet recovered when she suddenly saw him.

Gù Xuān, caught in those sharp knife-edge eyes, quietly released Jiang Mi's hand and bowed properly. "This subject greets the Emperor."

Xiao Huaiyan's tone was level. "The banquet is almost beginning. Why are you still in the Kūnníng Palace?"

Gù Xuān could tell the Emperor was ushering her out — she had merely held Tangtan's hand for a moment and he was already this vigilant. Was it really necessary?

She could only grumble inwardly and follow his lead. "This subject was delayed. I will proceed to the Jiāotài Hall now."

She bowed to Jiang Mi. "Your Highness — this subject takes her leave."

Jiang Mi's mind was in somewhat more disorder now. If she could have, she would actually have preferred A-Xuān to stay — but she had no other reason to keep her, and could only nod.

After Gù Xuān left, Xiao Huaiyan took Jiang Mi's hand and frowned. "Why are your hands so cold?"

Her slender lashes flickered. Her heart was beating very fast.

She looked up and met a pair of deep, still eyes. She said quietly: "I must have been standing in a draft a while. Why has Your Majesty come?"

He had been with ministers in the imperial study — had he not?

Xiao Huaiyan wrapped that faintly cool, soft hand in his, a smile on his face. "Your Thousand Autumns celebration — I came to escort you there together."

Jiang Mi felt the warmth in her hand. She looked quietly at Xiao Huaiyan.

He raised a hand and touched her cheek lightly, curious. "Why are you looking at me like this?"

Jiang Mi saw that his tone was gentle, his eyes smiling, with a trace of enquiry she could not quite read.

She shook her head. "Your Majesty — we should go to the Jiāotài Hall."

Jiang Mi let Xiao Huaiyan take her along onto the imperial palanquin. She tried to look as usual as she could.

Xiao Huaiyan's hand rested idly on her leg, and he felt the tension in her. His fingers tapped lightly twice. "Nervous?"

She could not put into words what she was feeling right now. She lowered her eyes and said yes.

Xiao Huaiyan said lightly: "I noticed you talking quite happily with Gù Xuān — why such constraint when you are with me? Tangtan — what is wrong?"

She had not expected him to be so perceptive — or to ask so directly.

What was wrong? She wanted to ask him the same question. How many things were you hiding from me?

Jiang Mi tightened her hand. She said quietly: "I heard that A-Xuān is leaving for Yúnzhōu and felt a little reluctant to see her go." She swallowed the real question. She changed the subject.

Xiao Huaiyan heard that and thought: in this life and the last, Jiang Mi and Gù Xuān had been close.

He thought of the last life — hearing that Jiang Mi and Gù Xuān had drunk together and stayed overnight in the Yìkūn Palace — and the veins in his hand stood out.

......

The Jiāotài Hall blazed with light and the sound of strings and bamboo flutes.

The hall was filled with noble ladies and official wives, some conversing quietly, some sitting in silence, all waiting for the Empress's phoenix palanquin.

From outside, wave upon wave of eunuchs' calls came through: "The Emperor and Her Highness the Empress have arrived!"

The music stopped. The great hall went still.

More than a few of the ladies were astonished inwardly. The Emperor had actually come together with the Empress? This was unprecedented even in the former dynasties. For the Emperor to simply have gifts sent on his behalf or to drop in briefly during the celebration was already considered high honour. For him to personally accompany her was a show of extraordinary imperial favour.

Everyone composed themselves and rose to welcome the imperial party.

Their eyes moved toward the hall entrance. The Emperor and Empress came in together. The Emperor's bearing was magnificent, his beauty without equal; the Empress wore a sumptuous phoenix robe, dignified and poised, her striking face blazing like a lotus in full bloom.

The two of them looked entirely matched.

Everyone bowed low. "Long life to the Emperor and Empress. A thousand years of joy to Her Highness the Empress."

An'yang, reluctant as she was, had to bow with the other women toward the woman in the seat of honour.

She waited until the word was given to rise.

An'yang looked at Jiang Mi seated at the centre of everything, surrounded by all the court's attention. It came over her in a vague, dreamlike wave: her mother's voice again — however much she resisted it, she could not change the fact that Jiang Mi was now the Empress. She had to be shrewd about her situation if she wanted to survive. But that slap from her mother had not woken her. She had gone to the Earl's household with her hatred and her resentment. In the beginning she could still command a degree of deference by virtue of being a princess — but as time wore on and the palace showed no sign of concern for her, those people began to comply outwardly and resist beneath the surface. She thought of the chaos of that household, the worthless husband she had been given, and felt the misery of it — yet could do nothing. Her brother had given her this marriage as punishment.

Looking at today's joyful birthday celebration, it felt like something from another world. If she had never conspired with Shūróu to harm Jiang Mi — would she have married the man her mother chose for her and lived an entirely different life?

Jiang Mi had barely sat down when Li Fu began reading out the Emperor's birthday gifts — a long list that left even Jiang Mi's ears tired.

Then came the gifts from the noble ladies and official wives.

Everyone seemed to have marshalled their full strength to catch the Empress's eye at this celebration, holding nothing back.

The gifts were dazzling — a coral tree several feet tall, jewels and curios, authenticated masterworks of painting and calligraphy from famous hands, jade Buddhas, ruyi sceptres, a riot of treasures everywhere the eye turned.

Most brilliant of all was the gift from the Emperor: a single pot of peonies fashioned from gold wire filament, with jade-green leaves and pearl-clustered blossoms, each flower made from gemstones of different colours. Counting the blooms, there were exactly seventeen — blazing and dazzling.

After the court ladies presented their gifts, the foreign tributary envoys were next.

Jiang Mi glanced at Xiao Huaiyan. The gifts were already almost outpacing last year's imperial birthday. How had he made it this extravagant?

At last year's imperial birthday there had been talented young women offering performances — nothing like this, all solid and substantial and one gift more precious than the last.

Xiao Huaiyan raised his wine cup and took a sip. Sensing Jiang Mi's gaze: "Is there anything you like?"

She said quietly: "Your Majesty — this is too much."

He smiled. "It is not nearly enough."

He wanted to make up for all the years he had missed, and more. How could it be too much?

"Tangtan — every birthday you have from now on, I will spend with you."

Jiang Mi looked at him for a long, still moment. Her lips moved — she started to say something and swallowed it back.

Just then, the envoys from Gāojùlí were led in by eunuchs. They presented ginseng of a hundred years' age and other valuable medicines.

When the Gāojùlí envoy knelt and bowed, he glanced at the Empress of Great Wei. He thought to himself: no wonder the king had recently tried to send a royal princess over and been refused. This Empress Jiang's beauty — even a royal princess would pale beside her.

Then the envoy from the western Bōsī kingdom came to pay his respects.

Unlike the other nations, the Bōsī delegation this time was led by their Fourth Prince and Seventh Prince.

Jiang Mi was quite taken aback to see a boy of about thirteen leading a child of four or five into the hall — both with high brows and deep-set eyes, and striking blue irises. They bowed. "We greet the honoured Emperor and Empress."

The young man spoke excellent Hàn Chinese, while the small child blinked with long, brush-like lashes and looked up at Jiang Mi.

Jiang Mi found the young Seventh Prince quite adorably young, and could not help smiling.

The young prince presented the Bōsī birthday gifts — rare aromatics, fine furs, precious amber.

Then he said: "Your Highness the Empress, the western lands have one more thing for which we are renowned — if Your Highness would permit our dancers to offer a performance?"

Jiang Mi understood he meant western dancers. She glanced at Xiao Huaiyan.

Xiao Huaiyan looked entirely at ease, as if leaving the decision entirely to her.

Jiang Mi nodded to the young prince. "Granted."

He clapped his hands three times, and a procession of dancers in exotic dress and veils filed in.

Their costumes were sheer, their wrists and ankles ringed with jingling ornamental bands. As the string music began, the dancers moved to the rhythm, their dance wild and passionate, their hands turning out lotus shapes in the air, spinning and leaping with a vigorous, powerful beauty.

Among the ladies at the banquet, reactions varied — some watching with a curious appreciation, some inwardly disdainful and thinking it immoral, and some smugly wondering whether the Empress would regret allowing these western sirens to dance in front of the Emperor — what if he took a fancy to one and brought her into the inner palace?

Jiang Mi had learned the western dance. She had danced it herself. In the last life she had gone to the bedchamber for the first time and danced for Xiao Huaiyan — what she had worn and performed that evening had been far more daring than anything before her now.

She had allowed the western dancers for a reason — it was partly a test of Xiao Huaiyan.

When the dance concluded and the women stepped back, the young prince asked with careful courtesy: "How did the Emperor and Empress find the dance?"

Xiao Huaiyan, who had been silent throughout, said: "I have been fortunate enough to see something more beautiful."

The young prince was at a loss. He had hoped these dancers might be permitted to stay. But the Emperor of Great Wei said he had seen something finer — which meant he was not satisfied with these dancers.

Sitting beside Xiao Huaiyan, Jiang Mi heard those words and felt her heart give a sudden jolt.

She steadied herself. She said warmly to the young prince: "Four Prince has been most considerate. This Palace found it very enjoyable. Let all these dancers be rewarded."

The young prince saw the Empress's gentle smile, and his face went red in an instant. He lowered his gaze quickly. "To bring delight to the Empress is a great honour."

Xiao Huaiyan shifted his position and set down his wine cup. Those dark eyes carried a coolness as they looked at the young prince.

The young prince felt a sudden chill without knowing why. He was about to withdraw with his brother and the dancers when —

The little four-or-five-year-old prince refused to move.

He unclipped the small curved blade worn at his side — set with blue sapphires — and cradled it carefully, holding it out toward Jiang Mi's direction. "For — for the moon."

The Seventh Prince's Hàn Chinese was uncertain, babyish, yet earnest. He blinked his large blue eyes at Jiang Mi, and anyone's heart would have softened.

Jiang Mi watched the exotic little prince holding his blade, wanting to come forward and yet hanging back shyly, whispering again: "Moon — for the moon."

She said gently: "Is this meant as a gift for this Palace?"

The lovely little prince nodded vigorously.

Jiang Mi was about to signal an attendant to go and receive the blade when Xiao Huaiyan spoke. "Wait. That blade — you cannot accept it."

He turned to the young Fourth Prince. "If I recall correctly, your people have a custom — from birth, each person carries a blade of their own, and when they grow up, that blade is given to the beloved of their heart. Is that right?"

The Fourth Prince nodded. "Your Majesty must forgive us — the Seventh Prince is young and does not yet understand. He saw the Empress and thought her pure and beautiful as the moon, and could not help himself."

Xiao Huaiyan's expression carried a trace of lightness as he replied slowly: "She is already someone else's moon. Let your brother wait until he is grown and find a moon of his own."

The words fell.

Jiang Mi went very still.

Among the older noble ladies, faint expressions of astonishment appeared. The younger girls behind them twisted their handkerchiefs, faces pink — envious and admiring at once.

chapters.title: After the Wedding, Part Nine
chapters.content:
After the foreign tribute presentations were concluded, Xiao Huaiyan took Jiang Mi and left the Jiāotài Hall first.

The ladies remaining at the banquet continued their drinking and watched the performers prepared by the Music Bureau. Though the Emperor and Empress had withdrawn, the banquet itself was not yet over.

Jiang Mi was still thinking of the little prince — the way he had looked, almost in tears because his blade had been refused, had been genuinely pitiable.

She said with a soft laugh: "Your Majesty was a little too strict. The Seventh Prince is only four years old — it was very nearly enough to make him cry."

Xiao Huaiyan's gaze settled on her face. "You like children that much?"

Jiang Mi looked up. Seeing his expression was entirely serious, she laughed awkwardly. "This concubine simply thought the little prince was adorable."

Xiao Huaiyan said: "If you like them so much, then we should have a child of our own."

The smile at the corner of Jiang Mi's mouth froze. With his words, a fragment of blurred memory came pushing into her mind.

She had once dreamed of the last life, and had always wanted to know: Xiao Huaiyan, before setting out on campaign, had told her to wait for him to return — and she had not been able to wait. But she had always wanted to know what it was he had been coming back to say.

In that half-waking moment before a dream dissolved, she had thought she heard Xiao Huaiyan's voice.

He had said: wait for me to return, and we shall have a child.

In that instant Jiang Mi had told herself it was a dream, and that the Xiao Huaiyan in the dream was lying to her. She had not dared to believe it. But the Xiao Huaiyan of the last life no longer had the chance to answer her — the one answering her now was the Xiao Huaiyan of this life.

And here he was again, saying the same thing. They should have a child.

Jiang Mi felt her nose sting. Her eyes were bright with unshed tears.

Xiao Huaiyan bent down to kiss away the tear that slipped from the corner of her eye. He took her hand. "Tangtan — come with me."

Jiang Mi followed him, step for step. He led her up to the city wall and they stood on the battlements, looking out over the capital.

She did not know why Xiao Huaiyan had brought her here.

A gentle night wind moved their robes, lifting and settling.

Xiao Huaiyan touched her face. "I have one more gift for you."

There was still more?

"Your Majesty has given this concubine so much already."

"Look first."

He drew a rosewood box from his sleeve. He had her open it herself.

She did as he asked.

What she saw inside was a phoenix-shaped token.

Jiang Mi's pupils contracted slightly. She was not entirely certain, but she thought she knew what she was looking at.

It looked like a military authority token.

Xiao Huaiyan smiled. "You recognised it?"

"This is the Phoenix Tally — it can command the armed guard that Gù Xuān holds. I know that the imperial edict you asked me for, and everything you agreed to in return — all of it came from the unease you carry. This Phoenix Tally is my way of giving you peace of mind."

Jiang Mi bit her lower lip. She looked down at the Phoenix Tally in her hands. Something wet fell onto the smooth surface of the token.

Xiao Huaiyan breathed out slowly. He drew the slender woman before him into his arms. "Tangtan — there is nothing to fear now. You have something solid to hold." If she still had knots inside her, if she still feared what tomorrow might bring — let these things of the world give her enough assurance that she need not worry about the days to come.

Jiang Mi could not help trembling. She breathed in the ambergris scent from him, and something moved unsteadily in her chest. Just then, a sound like muffled thunder broke through the air — a streak of red light shot into the black sky, bursting open like a waterfall.

One by one, more fireworks rose, lighting up the entire capital.

The noble ladies still at the Jiāotài Hall banquet saw the sky blaze red on one side and drifted out of the hall one after another.

Younger women looked up at the blazing colours overhead with excitement. Fireworks were rarely seen.

The great booming sounds, the brilliant riot of flowers above — they sent the people of the capital running out of their houses and into the streets, calling out: "Long live the Empress! Thousand years of joy to Her Highness the Empress."

In the household of Grand Secretary Shen, they were still observing mourning for the late matriarch. The Shen family had not attended the birthday banquet.

A marriage had been found for Shen Yǎowēi in a distant city, but it had been put on hold for now due to the mourning period.

Shen Yǎowēi's spirits had been very poor. No amount of weeping and pleading had changed her father's decision to send her out of the capital. She had been refusing to accept that Xiao Huaiyan had named Jiang Mi as Empress. Since her confinement she had sometimes talked to herself, and her temper had grown sharper.

Now with the old matriarch's death, everyone in the Shen household had their hands full and no time to watch over her.

Shen Yǎowēi's maternal cousin, Hé Xiùxián, had stayed behind to keep her company — and was also hoping to spend a little more time at the Shen household and find opportunities to see Shen Qiānxiū.

When the fireworks went off outside, Shen Yǎowēi had been sitting inside staring blankly. Her eyes moved. She pushed open the door and walked into the courtyard, head tilted back to watch the sky full of fireworks. She asked her maid: "Why are there fireworks? Is it the Emperor's birthday celebration? The Emperor's birthday hasn't come yet."

The maid answered awkwardly: "Miss — this is not the Emperor's birthday. It is the Empress's birthday celebration!"

Shen Yǎowēi's expression snapped. She raised her hand and struck the maid. "What lies are you telling! The Emperor has not named an Empress — there is no birthday celebration!"

The maid did not dare talk back. She covered her face and shrank to one side.

Hé Xiùxián saw what was happening and hurried forward to take Shen Yǎowēi's arm. "Āwēi — calm down." She quietly gestured for someone to come and help.

Shen Yǎowēi looked at those fireworks rising one after another and shook Hé Xiùxián off. "Elder Sister — I need to go out. I need to go and see the Emperor. My sister came to me in a dream. She said the Emperor would take good care of me — she said the seat she never had would be passed to me. The Emperor may have forgotten. Perhaps if he sees me he will remember."

Hé Xiùxián heard her talking nonsense and would not let go. "Āwēi — stop losing yourself in your own fantasies. The way you are is frightening everyone. Āwēi — please come back to yourself."

Shen Yǎowēi could hear nothing of it. She wrenched free with force.

Hé Xiùxián stumbled and fell.

Shen Yǎowēi was nearly at the gate when Shen Qiānxiū arrived with two or three strong servants. He looked at the state his sister was in and felt the weight of failure. "Take the young miss back to her room."

Shen Yǎowēi was grabbed by both arms, and she screamed: "Third Elder Brother — you cannot keep me locked up. You were the useless one. If you had managed to marry that fox-spirit, the Empress's position would have been mine. It was your fault. You couldn't do it, and now you're taking it out on me!"

Treasonous words. The servants hauling her back to her room were so frightened they clapped a hand over her mouth.

Shen Qiānxiū's face was dark. He went to Hé Xiùxián's side and helped her up. "Cousin Hé — are you hurt?"

Hé Xiùxián shook her head. She looked toward the room with worry. "Third Cousin — how did Āwēi come to be like this?"

She was still shaken from what had been said.

Shen Qiānxiū said: "She is ill. Tomorrow I will have another physician called. Cousin Hé — please go and rest."

Hé Xiùxián rarely had Shen Qiānxiū speak to her like this. But something Shen Yǎowēi had said was weighing on her, and she thought of another matter she had been keeping to herself.

"Third Cousin — I have something to tell you." She saw his expression darken and added: "It concerns the Empress."

Shen Qiānxiū brought Hé Xiùxián to the garden pavilion. "You may speak."

Hé Xiùxián weighed it carefully before she spoke. "Third Cousin — do you remember the flower banquet at the Zhèngguó Duke's house last year? The Empress attended, and she fell into the water."

Shen Qiānxiū's eyes sharpened immediately. "Āwēi had something to do with that?"

Hé Xiùxián looked uncomfortable. "Not directly — she wasn't involved herself. It was just that I discovered Āwēi had sent a maid to encourage a manservant to go in and search for the person in the water... at the time I thought it was urgent and that getting the person out was all that mattered... perhaps I was reading too much into it."

Shen Qiānxiū's expression went cold. He sent Hé Xiùxián away and went directly to find Shen Chānghéng.

Shen Chānghéng heard the account and shook his head again and again, his anger and disappointment toward this daughter showing plainly.

"Qiānxiū — what is your thinking?"

"Father — the Shen family cannot weather any more suspicion right now. Āwēi cannot remain in the capital."

Shen Chānghéng's eyes showed exhaustion. "The Emperor is in a moment of great need for talented men. I believe he will call off the mourning leave and summon us back to duty. But the Shen family must be a family of pure loyalty."

Looking at the son before him, Shen Chānghéng felt some consolation.

He looked out at the deep night and said with resolution: "Have people take Āwēi out of the capital tonight. She cannot be permitted to return."

Shen Qiānxiū agreed.

He walked outside. He looked up at the sky.

The fireworks had long since faded.

......

Jiang Mi stood on the city wall and watched the last of the fireworks die away. She lifted her head slowly from Xiao Huaiyan's arms, and her expression was grave and composed.

One thing after another had given her the courage she needed.

She looked at Xiao Huaiyan and asked: "Your Majesty — will you grant me one more wish?"
